articles.title: Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast
articles.summary: Global struggle for control of Bab al-Mandab strait threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war

blocks.text: Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.

Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war.

In a lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.

The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes.

A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo.

blocks.caption: A heavily laden vehicle arrives in Sana’a as people flee frontline fighting.  Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: The most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said.
“Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.”

Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said.

The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularly the fall of the strategic port city of Mocha – widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym​ for chocolate-flavoured coffee.

blocks.caption: Residents fled the strategic port city of Mocha after Houthi strikes which destroyed civilian infrastructure.  Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/Reuters

blocks.text: Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”.
Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck.

Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014.

blocks.caption: Houthi soldiers stand guard next to a makeshift camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs), in Sana’a on Thursday.  Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: By taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-west Houthis hope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. ​

The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through.

​But if ​the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
The fighting in Yemen, as well as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.
The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”.

“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.”

blocks.caption: ‘Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,’ said Joe Lowry of the IOM.   Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: Instability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high.

This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide.

“Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.”
On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock.

“It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.”

articles.title: Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’?
articles.summary:
Many fear chancellor is wrong man for the job at a time when Germany’s defences against far right are crumbling

A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of

blocks.text: A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of Germany’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order.

Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’s win for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment.

With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period.

blocks.caption: AfD co-leaders Alice Weidel (right) and Tino Chrupalla (left) with Saxony-Anhalt lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP

blocks.text: It is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “democracy’s last shot” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany.
The result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected in two more state polls later this month.
“This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all of Germany,” he said on Monday.

Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces. Pivotal elections are due next year in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Poland.

Merz’s many critics say the 70-year-old former BlackRock executive is the wrong man at such a consequential crossroads, calling him a ham-fisted and empathetically challenged leader who is erratic in his messaging.

Only in office 16 months, the chancellor often seemed incapable of one of the basic tasks of leadership: making the case to voters that accepting bitter pills now could lead to a brighter future, said the political scientist Thomas Biebricher of Frankfurt’s Goethe University.

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz: his future as chancellor is uncertain. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The prevailing impression at the moment is that, in terms of communication, he is unable to explain the many reforms – and the sacrifices they entail – to the public, and thereby win their acceptance,” Biebricher said, referring to planned cuts to the statutory pension and healthcare schemes.

The former chancellor Angela Merkel, Merz’s longtime rival within the CDU, has criticised him publicly for his hardline rhetoric on migration and integration but said she took no pleasure in the debacle given the stakes.

“This is a turning point – a real turning point – in the history of the federal republic of Germany,” said Merkel, who left office of her own accord in 2021 after 16 years in power. “As a CDU member it breaks my heart.”

blocks.caption: Merz speaking to Angela Merkel at the CDU federal conference in Stuttgart in February. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: Speaking at a digital affairs conference on Tuesday, she advised Merz to rethink his messaging in a changing political ecosystem in which emotions counted more than facts.

Merkel, 72, noted that the CDU had pointed to data during the Saxony-Anhalt campaign showing that joblessness had fallen and household wealth had risen in the small, relatively poor state. “And then [Siegmund] says: ‘That may be so, but that’s not how it feels.’”

The AfD formed in 2013, during Merkel’s tenure, as a Eurosceptic outfit opposed to bailouts for debt-mired countries. It grew increasingly radical during the 2015-2016 refugee influx, when she left the borders open to more than a million asylum seekers fleeing war and hardship.

Merz took office last year saying he would put the country back on track after the implosion of the previous government under Olaf Scholz. He promised a return to economic growth, a restoration of defence capabilities and urgent repairs to the creaking social welfare system.
His recipe for confronting the far right – one of his key pledges – was competence in governing and solutions for Germans’ most urgent problems.

Merz also promised a rejection of Merkel’s open-border policy in an attempt to rob the AfD of its signature issue. He had infamously accepted support from the far-right party for a tough draft law on migration just before the February 2025 general election, before back-pedalling in the face of protests.

blocks.caption: AfD co-leader Alice Weidel walks past Merz at the Bundestag this week. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: As “irregular” arrivals of migrants have fallen sharply since Merz took office, the AfD has successfully pivoted to a broader range of concerns about deindustrialisation, regional identity, affordability and crime to gain ground far beyond its eastern heartland.

The AfD, widely seen as more radical than comparable European parties, had been relegated to permanent opposition in Germany by the “firewall” strategy of shunning by the mainstream parties. But this policy is now widely seen to have failed, allowing the AfD to snipe from the sidelines about the slow pace of any positive change.
after newsletter promotion
Biebricher said that for all Merz’s weaknesses, replacing him would not be a magic bullet for the mountain of challenges facing German security and prosperity.

blocks.caption: A forensic technician works near a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig airport, where a drone with an explosive device was found last month. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP

blocks.text: As well as the threat from Russia, he cited decrepit infrastructure, the demographic crunch on social welfare benefits, competition from China in once mighty industries such as car manufacturing, and geopolitical upheaval weighing on supply chains and energy imports.
“None of that simply goes away the moment you have someone who communicates better,” Biebricher told public radio.

blocks.caption: Volkswagen employees during a rally against mass job cut plans in Zwickau in July. Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Merz’s centre-right CDU-CSU bloc, divided between conservatives and moderates, is nevertheless known for its internal discipline in times of crisis – if only out of fear of even graver consequences from drastic changes.

The situation is seen as so grim that it has triggered paralysis, with neither the popular North Rhine-Westphalia state premier, Hendrik Wüst, or Bavaria’s ambitious leader, Markus Söder, keen at this stage to snatch the poisoned chalice.
“Merz has now reached a stage where the crisis – which he himself constantly exacerbates – is stabilising him,” said the veteran political journalist Bernd Ulrich of Die Zeit newspaper.
“The CDU and the government (in coalition with the Social Democrats) as a whole are in such a dire state that, as far as anyone can tell, no one wants to take over his post.”
Wüst, 51, leads a coalition with the Greens in Germany’s most populous state and faces a re-election battle next April. If he wins, the calls for Merz to make way for him may grow louder.

Söder, who represents the bloc’s conservative wing, shares Merz’s view that it needs to echo the AfD’s harsh rhetoric on migration in order to win back support – a strategy political scientists have long disparaged as counterproductive.
Yet the dangers of keeping a revolt at bay by betting on a status quo voters so clearly reject are apparent.

Much will depend on how bad the news is from the regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on 20 September. The AfD is polling well in both states, with clear momentum after Saxony-Anhalt, putting pressure on the CDU in particular.

During a fiery clash with the AfD in parliament this week in which he laid out the threat it poses to German democracy, Merz was reflective about how to steer the country – and himself – out of the current straits.
He quoted from a letter he received from the rector of a theological university arguing how many opportunities still lay ahead for Germany and advising him not to give in to despair.
Merz said he intended to take this to heart and stay on as chancellor using a new roadmap: “Admit mistakes, forgive, get back on your feet, shape the future.”

articles.title: Ben Shelton beats fellow American Frances Tiafoe to reach US Open final
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Ben Shelton won the all-American duel with Frances Tiafoe and now he’s the one who can end his country’s long wait for another men’s Grand Slam champion. Shelton pulled…

blocks.text: Ben Shelton, of the United States, reacts after he won his match against Frances Tiafoe, of the United States, during the men’s singles semifinals of the U.S. Open tennis championships Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
NEW YORK — Ben Shelton won the all-American duel with Frances Tiafoe and now he’s the one who can end his country’s long wait for another men’s Grand Slam champion.
Shelton pulled out a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory on Friday and will play No. 1 seed Alexander Zverev on Sunday for the US Open title.
The No. 8-seeded Shelton had plenty of energy left after ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinal match that ended Wednesday at 3:33 a.m., the latest finish ever at the US Open.
Now he needs to stop French Open champion Zverev to give the host nation its first men’s major winner since Andy Roddick at the 2003 US Open.
“I’m going for it here, and I’m going to leave it all on the court,” Shelton said. “I hope you guys come and back me. Let’s do it for the USA.”
Zverev beat Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6) in the first semifinal.
“Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday,” Zverev said.

The Shelton-Tiafoe match drew a star-studded crowd that included stars from sports, including Serena Williams, Jalen Brunson and of course US soccer player Trinity Rodman, Shelton’s girlfriend; and actors Salma Hayek, Ben Stiller and Rami Malek.

Shelton and Tiafoe treated the fans to a good show, after both had to come through match tiebreakers in the previous round. Shelton, a 23-year-old from Georgia who was less than a year old when Roddick won his title, advanced to his first major final.

“This is where we want to be: at the tail end of this tournament,” Shelton said. “This is both of our favorite tournament in the world, our favorite court in the world and to be able to light it up in front of (this crowd) is the best feeling that there is.”
Tiafoe fell to 0-3 in the US Open semifinals, the last two against fellow Americans. Taylor Fritz beat him in 2024 before losing to Jannik Sinner.

After a ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in which a giant American flag was unfurled across the court, it was Tiafoe who played the cleaner tennis in the first set. He committed just three unforced errors to 14 by Shelton, whose double-fault at 4-4 gave Tiafoe the break he needed.
But after falling behind, Shelton started serving bigger, and finished with 20 aces.

Serving with new balls at 3-all in the second set, Shelton started with a 125 mph serve — Tiafoe got his racket up almost in self-defense and ended up getting knocked backward to the court — and followed it with serves clocked at 144, 139 and 140, the last two for aces that gave him the lead for good in the set.

The pivotal moment in the match came in the final game of the third set, when Tiafoe was desperately trying to hold serve. The game lasted 15 minutes and 20 points before Tiafoe put a forehand into the net to end it and move Shelton a set away from the title.

Tiafoe had his own marathon in the quarterfinals, coming from two sets down and then erasing a 3-0 deficit in the fifth set to edge fellow American Alex Michelsen. He seemed to get slightly more cheers early, but the crowd was loud for both players as the match went on.

Zverev, who had long been considered the best men’s player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, where he lost to Sinner, and is 24-2 in Grand Slam matches this season.

“Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I’ve had a lot of struggles at the major level, I was so close so many times, and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court,” Zverev said.

Now he will try to win the title that he still can’t believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the U.S. Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.
Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first No. 1-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

articles.title: Top seed Alexander Zverev holds off Khachanov for US Open final spot
articles.summary: Top seed Alexander Zverev outgunned Karen Khachanov to reach his third straight Grand Slam final on Friday, rolling into the US Open title match with a straight-sets win. Zverev, who followed up his…

blocks.text: Alexander Zverev, of Germany, celebrates winning a match against Karen Khachanov, of Russia, during the men’s singles semifinals of the U.S. Open tennis championships, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)
Top seed Alexander Zverev outgunned Karen Khachanov to reach his third straight Grand Slam final on Friday, rolling into the US Open title match with a straight-sets win.
Zverev, who followed up his maiden major at the French Open with a runner-up finish at Wimbledon, saved two set points in the final tiebreaker to close out the 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) victory.
He’ll face the winner of the all-American semifinal between eighth-seeded Ben Shelton and 11th seed Frances Tiafoe in Sunday’s championship match.

The German predicted an “absolutely epic” contest between the two Americans, after which he’ll be out to thwart the winner’s bid to become the first American man in 23 years to lift a Grand Slam trophy.
“Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday,” said Zverev, who came agonizingly close to the US Open title in 2020 before falling to Dominic Thiem in five sets.
After a somewhat inauspicious start to the tournament, spending nine hours and 26 minutes on court in laborious five-set victories in the first and second rounds, Zverev has steadily upped his game.
He needed two hours and 57 minutes to deny 50th-ranked Khachanov’s bid to become the lowest-ranked Grand Slam finalist since number 54 Marcos Baghdatis at the 2006 Australian Open.
But the Russian, who fell to Zverev in the Olympic gold medal match in Tokyo in 2021, put up a spirited challenge in the second and third sets.
“Straight-set win, but anything but straightforward in a way,” Zverev said. “He played incredibly well, fought incredibly well.”
Unable to make any real headway in the first set, Khachanov fell a quick break down in the second.

The Russian couldn’t resist a grin when he snuck a passing shot by Zverev to open the fourth game, and flung his arm into the air in celebration three points later when a forehand winner gave him his first break chance of the match, which he converted when Zverev double faulted.
From there, they went to the tiebreaker, where Khachanov denied Zverev on two set points with thumping forehand and a brilliant backhand down the line before Zverev closed out the set.

Neither player mustered a break point in a tense third set. But when Khachanov took a 6-4 lead in the tiebreaker he surrendered both set points with forehand errors. Zverev came up with his 15th ace and sealed the win on the next point when Khachanov sent a forehand long.
“Second and third set I think it’s more than obvious that they could have gone both ways,” Zverev said. “I just played a few points better here and there, and I’m happy with the win.”
US Grand Slam drought

A somber note was struck during the national anthem ceremonies of both the day and night sessions on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks that brought down the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York.
Shelton vanquished defending champion and seven-time Grand Slam winner Carlos Alcaraz in an enthralling five-set quarterfinal clash that lasted until 3:34 am — the latest finish in US Open history.
Having notched the biggest win of his career, Shelton is now chasing his first major final.
So is Tiafoe as they duel to have a chance to be the one to end American men’s Grand Slam drought, which stretches back to Andy Roddick’s 2003 US Open victory.
Shelton leads their head-to-head, but they have split two prior US Open meetings, Shelton winning in the 2023 quarter-finals and Tiafoe turning the tables in the third round the following year.

The women’s final is on Saturday, when Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina will try to thwart Aryna Sabalenka’s bid for a third straight title just days after ending the Belarusian’s near two-year reign atop the world rankings by reaching the semifinals.

articles.title: Trapped nine days in a dark tunnel, Nepali man tells his survival story
articles.summary: 'Even if I had to die, I thought, what would be the point of giving up quickly?' says Nepal flood survivor Sanjay Sah, recalling how he recited religious mantras to calm himself

blocks.text: SAH. Sanjay Sah is carried by members of a search and rescue team after being one of two people rescued alive from a tunnel at the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, where two people had been trapped following devastating floods and mudslides that struck the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, Nepal, September 4, 2026.
Nepal Army/Handout via Reuters
'Even if I had to die, I thought, what would be the point of giving up quickly?' says Nepal flood survivor Sanjay Sah, recalling how he recited religious mantras to calm himself

items: Sanjay Sah was trapped in a dark tunnel for nine days after a flood caused by a glacier collapse in Nepal, where he survived by drinking floodwater and reciting the Hindu Maha Mantra for spiritual strength.
During his ordeal, Sah lost track of time and initially believed he had been trapped for only a few days, but was shocked to learn it was actually ten days before his rescue.

Sah expressed deep sorrow for those who he advised to evacuate but were swept away by the flood, highlighting the tragedy of the disaster that resulted in over 1,300 confirmed deaths and thousands missing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

KATHMANDU, Nepal Sept 11 – When Sanjay Sah got trapped in a dark tunnel linked to a hydropower station after a devastating flood tore through the structure in Nepal, he was so scared of injuring his eyes on debris that he kept them closed for days. When a miracle rescue happened nine days later, he could barely open them.

“There was nothing for my eyes to see. Most of the time I kept them closed. I was afraid that if I slipped or hit something by mistake, I could injure my eyes. So I kept them shut for long periods,” he told Reuters in an exclusive interview after being released from hospital on Friday.
“After doing that repeatedly, it became difficult even to open my eyes again.”

Since the collapse of a Himalayan glacier in late August caused devastation in the valleys below, at least 1,300 people have been confirmed dead and more than 5,300 are missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region.

Now recovering at his sister’s place in Kathmandu, the 30-year-old was a mechanical foreman at the run-of-river Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, owned by the state-run Nepal Electricity Authority, for more than three years.
The multi-storied powerhouse he was stuck in for most of those nine days was built deep inside the mountainside.
Sah said he had no food but drank floodwater and seepage water from the mountain rock.

When despair threatened to overwhelm him, Sah said he turned to the Hindu Maha Mantra, a chant central to Krishna devotion: “Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.”

“Even if I had to die, I thought, what would be the point of giving up quickly? So I continued to chant God’s name and recite the Maha Mantra,” Sah recalled. “The Maha Mantra gave me a different kind of feeling, almost a spiritual experience. I wasn’t afraid. Instead, I felt calm and relaxed.”
From the fifth floor of the six-floor powerhouse, there was an opening through which he could look down and shout, trying to find out if anyone else was alive. No one responded.

“At the beginning, I was very confident that a rescue would come. Even as the days passed, that confidence remained. I kept telling myself that I was not alone. I had a family, and they would be suffering greatly outside,” said Sah, father to a 2-year-old girl, whose wife is 26 years old.

“Thinking about them gave me strength and raised my morale. Even if I was destined to die, I thought, what would be the point of giving up quickly in panic? So I kept reciting God’s name and praying.”
He said he had no idea he got rescued only on the 10th day.

“I had completely lost track of time and felt as if I had been living in another world,” he said. “My guess was that only two or three days had passed. I was shocked when I learned it had actually been 10 days.”

He said that in the darkness, he would often bump into things, cut himself on debris or get scraped. Broken tube lights and other objects had fallen around the area, and some of them pierced his feet.
The flood had buried the tunnel under layers of mud and debris, transforming it completely.

“Before the flood I knew every part of it and could have gone deep inside without difficulty. But after the flood, the entire structure had been transformed,” he said. “Equipment had been swept away, boxes were scattered everywhere, walls had collapsed and debris had created mounds and pits. My familiarity with the tunnel was no longer useful.”
He initially tried to move around, but when he realised that he could instead get trapped in an even more difficult place, he stayed put.
“So I turned back and stayed where I believed it was safest,” he said. “That is where they eventually found me. Otherwise, I don’t know what might have happened to me.”
He said he would hear sounds from outside in the final hours before rescue.

“I knew they would come. I knew a rescue operation would be launched,” he said. “I could hear some sounds, like the rumbling of drums. On the day I was rescued, and about 10 to 12 hours before that, once things had quietened down a bit, I started hearing noises from outside.”
He said: “I could hear the excavators working and the clanging of ladders. About 10 to 12 hours before the rescue, I could clearly hear people working. That gave me real hope.”
Kabir Maharjan, 45 years old, was also trapped in the tunnel and hospitalized at the same army facility with more severe injuries. Sah encountered him moments before the flood struck.

“We both had little time left and headed upward instead of going down,” Sah said. “We believed that even if a large flood came, it would not reach that high. We had reached the sixth floor when water began entering from below. First came air pressure, then the water itself. We got separated in the chaos. My mobile phone was swept away. I do not know where Kabir ended up.”
A devotee of Lord Krishna, Sah was rescued on the day when Hindus celebrated the birth of one of their biggest deities.
Sah said he survived but some of the people he had advised to evacuate from the tunnel and who had managed to get outside were swept away by the flood.
“That is the saddest part of all,” Sah said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: National Artist Resil Mojares laid to rest in Cebu on Day of Mourning
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — National Artist for Literature Resil Mojares was laid to rest at the Cebu Memorial Parks and Gardens on Saturday, September 12, as family, friends, relatives, and officials…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — National Artist for Literature Resil Mojares was laid to rest at the Cebu Memorial Parks and Gardens on Saturday, September 12, as family, friends, relatives, and officials gathered to pay their final respects to the prominent Cebuano historian, author, and literary scholar.

The interment was marked by rows of flower wreaths filling the area as mourners gathered for the state funeral of Mojares, whose decades-long work earned him recognition as one of the country’s prominent scholars.
The Armed Forces of the Philippines also attended the funeral and rendered military and state honors during the interment.
Resil Mojares passes on
Mojares died in the early hours of Saturday, September 5, 2026, a day after celebrating his 83rd birthday, according to a statement released by his family.
The family said they had spent his final day honoring and celebrating his life. Mojares, who was also a professor emeritus, was remembered by his family as a pillar of their household.
His wife, Sally, died in 2022. The family found comfort in the thought that the couple had been reunited.
Day of National Mourning
His death was followed by a Day of National Mourning on September 12, the date of his interment, after President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. declared the day through Proclamation No. 1434.

The proclamation, signed on September 10 by Executive Secretary Ralph G. Recto by authority of the President, recognized Mojares’ contributions to Philippine literature, cultural studies, regional history, and the formation of Cebuano and national identity.
It cited his achievements as a teacher, scholar, essayist, fictionist, and historian, as well as his role in promoting regional literature.

As part of the national mourning, the Philippine flag was ordered flown at half-mast from sunrise to sunset on September 12 in all government buildings and installations throughout the Philippines and abroad.

The directive was based on Section 27(k), Chapter 1 of the implementing rules and regulations of Republic Act No. 8491, or the Flag and Heraldic Code of the Philippines, in relation to Proclamation No. 1001, series of 1972, as amended.
In declaring the Day of National Mourning, Malacañang described Mojares’ passing as a great loss to the Filipino people and the country’s cultural and artistic community.
The proclamation also recognized Mojares as a pivotal figure whose work significantly enriched the nation’s understanding and appreciation of its literary and cultural heritage.
Recognitions, contributions

Mojares was a renowned historian, essayist, literary scholar, and educator whose work focused heavily on Cebuano history and culture while also examining broader questions surrounding national history and identity.

Among his major contributions was the establishment of the Cebuano Studies Center of the University of San Carlos, an institution dedicated to the study and documentation of Cebuano history and culture.
The center is now an important research institution that has placed Cebu in the research and documentation map.

Mojares also united and taught scholars and teachers from or based in Cebu in the study of history, literature, culture, and heritage, contributing to scholarship on the region and its place in the broader Philippine story.
As an author, he produced at least six works that received the National Book Award.

His expertise was also recognized through visiting professorships at Kyoto University in Japan, the National University of Singapore, and the University of California at Los Angeles in the United States.
He served on two National Commission for Culture and the Arts national committees — as vice-head of the Committee on Literature and as a member of the Committee on Historical Research.

Beyond his work in Cebuano history and cultural heritage, Mojares was a cultural commentator who used a critical approach in examining Philippine history. His work explored the Filipino way of life and the prominent figures who helped shape the country’s history.
Through his scholarship, Mojares encouraged the formation of Cebuano and national identity and contributed to a deeper understanding of the country’s literary and cultural heritage.

In 2018, the Philippine government conferred on Mojares the Order of National Artist for Literature under Proclamation No. 606, recognizing his achievements as a teacher, scholar, essayist, fictionist, and historian, as well as his contributions to regional literature and history.
On Saturday, Cebu bid farewell to the scholar who spent decades documenting, examining, and championing the history, culture, and identity of the region he called home.///

articles.title: Army sends 342 more troops to secure BARMM polls
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — More boots are heading to the Bangsamoro region as the Army beefs up security ahead of the 2026 Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliamentary Elections.…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — More boots are heading to the Bangsamoro region as the Army beefs up security ahead of the 2026 Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliamentary Elections.

The 10th Infantry Division (10ID) deployed two additional infantry battalions — totaling 342 personnel — to reinforce security operations and augment troops from the 6th and 11th Infantry Divisions in their respective areas of responsibility, Maj. Ruben Gadut, 10IDPAO chief, said in an email to the Inquirer Saturday, Sept. 12.

The deploying contingent from the 27th Infantry Battalion and the 72nd Infantry Battalion moved out alongside 19 military trucks and an ambulance following back-to-back send-off rites led by 10ID commander Maj. Gen. Alvin Luzon.
The 27IB departed on Thursday (Sept. 10) from its headquarters in Paquibato District, Davao City, while the 72IB held its send-off on Friday in Arakan, Cotabato Province.
Luzon told the departing soldiers their mission is to foster a safe, fear-free environment for voters, while sternly ordering them to maintain strict political neutrality and discipline.

“You will be part of a larger effort to ensure that our people can exercise their right to vote in an environment that is peaceful, secure, and free from fear,” Luzon said, reminding troops to uphold human rights.
The deployment brings the 10ID’s total election security commitment in the BARMM to 1,444 personnel, backed by 43 military trucks and eight Wheeled Armored Vehicles (WAVs).
The division said the forces will coordinate closely with partner units and local stakeholders to ensure an orderly, credible electoral exercise. INQ

articles.title: Court case brought by Zionist federation against journalist Mary Kostakidis ended ‘by consent’
articles.summary:
Former SBS newsreader had been accused by Zionist Federation of Australia of breaching Racial Discrimination Act when sharing X posts

Federal court proceedings brought by the Zionist…

blocks.text: Federal court proceedings brought by the Zionist Federation of Australia (ZFA) against journalist Mary Kostakidis have been discontinued “by consent” with “no order as to costs”.

The former SBS newsreader had been accused by the federation of breaching the Racial Discrimination Act (RDA) by sharing two X posts about a speech by the late Hezbollah secretary general Hassan Nasrallah in January 2024.
Last year, Kostakidis had asked the court to strike the proceedings out, arguing the claim failed to identify which race, ethnicity or nationality was offended by her social media posts about Israel.

The chief executive of the ZFA, Alon Cassuto, had alleged the breach came when Kostakidis shared a video of a speech by Nasrallah on X and added: “The Israeli govt getting some of its own medicine. Israel has started something it can’t finish with this genocide.”
A second post sharing the same video was also part of the claim. The complaint was first raised with the Australian Human Rights Commission but escalated to the federal court.
The court said on Friday that the case had been dismissed with the agreement of both parties.

Kostakidis said in a statement she had spent “two years doing nothing but preparing my defence in a case aimed at silencing me” and the discontinuation was a “win for every Australian who values our democratic right to freedom of political expression”.
“I want to thank my fellow Australians who recognised the significance of what we stand to lose, stood with me and stepped up to assist me to launch my defence,” she said.
“The purpose of journalism is to get to the truth – fearlessly – and to hold power to account. This is a win for press freedom, which has prevailed.

“Watching a people livestream their own genocide while the international community responsible for creating this mess offers the victims sympathy and the perpetrators bombs, diplomatic cover and impunity, has been disgusting.”

In a statement published on Friday, Cassuto said his objectives in bringing the proceedings had been “substantially satisfied” after a public apology by Kostakidis in 2025 for the “hurt, distress and pain” felt by Jews and Israelis in Australia who took her posts “as an edorsement”.
after newsletter promotion
“An important reason I brought this matter was to seek recognition of the harm these posts caused ordinary Jewish Australians,” he said.
“Given everything Ms Kostakidis has chosen to publish since her apology, a further apology compelled by a court would ring hollow.

“The issues that motivated me to bring this proceeding are being examined in the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion. The commissioner’s report will be handed down in December following a national examination of how antisemitism became so normalised in Australia.”

Cassuto added: “Ms Kostakidis can make her own accounting of her conduct. The Australian public can make theirs. I do not intend to spend another year taking Ms Kostakidis’ repugnant commentary from the dark corners of the internet and giving it a federal court platform in her pursuit of martyrdom. My job here is done.”

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — On September 5, Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail in connection with the three counts of grave threats filed against her over her alleged assassination threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

Her lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, confirmed that Duterte posted P120,000 bail for each count of grave threat before Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98. Lim said Duterte underwent the booking process inside the court, which includes taking of her fingerprints.
On September 11, the Vice President showed up for her arraignment that the court later deferred following a motion filed by her lawyer.

Meanwhile, Leyte 1st District Representative and former House speaker Martin Romualdez was arrested on September 7, over his P7.44-billion plunder case, but would remain in hospital confinement at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

On September 11, the Sandiganbayan‘s 3rd Division ordered the transfer of Romualdez to the University of the Philippines-Philippine General Hospital for an independent medical examination and then stay at the facility until further orders from the anti-graft court.

articles.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
articles.summary: Access to the burnt-out boat has been slowed by toxic fumes and lingering heat, the country's coast guard says.

blocks.text: The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.
More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.
Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.
The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.
In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.
"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.
"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."
Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.
A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.
The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.
The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.
Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.
"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

articles.title: Cebuano short film ‘Bato’ng Bunga’ mines from memory, digs into exploitation
articles.summary: A grandson turns his lolo's mysterious illness into magical realism in Cebu's lone entry at this year's Sine Kabataan festival

blocks.text: MEMORIES. Bato'ng Bunga official poster by Cebuano artist Edd Dampios
CONTRIBUTED PHOTO
A grandson turns his lolo's mysterious illness into magical realism in Cebu's lone entry at this year's Sine Kabataan festival

items: Bato'ng Bunga is a Cebuano short film directed by Elj Seth Tababa, inspired by his grandfather's life as a miner and the severe skin disease he suffered from due to lack of healthcare.
The film, shot in Tababa's hometown of Pinamungajan, highlights themes of labor rights, healthcare, and the impact of mining on families, despite not depicting mining scenes directly.

Tababa aims to spark discussions about the consequences of negligence towards laborers, using his personal memories to convey the emotional weight of his grandfather's condition and its effects on their family.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
By the premise alone, you’d be fooled into thinking that Cebuano short film Bato’ng Bunga is a fairy tale. After years of labor underground, a miner comes up for air with his skin turned into stone.
But past the magic is a story translated directly from memory, one lived by a real miner whose body paid the price.

It’s the story that Elj Seth Tababa, a third-year Cinema student at the University of San Carlos (USC), brings to the big screen at the 9th Sine Kabataan Short Film Lab and Festival. It’s the sole entry from Central Visayas for this year and marks Tababa’s first time directing at this scale.
“I have director friends who could direct this, but it’s different when I tell this story,” Tababa said. “Because these are my memories.”

blocks.caption: Tababa directs a scene for Bato’ng Bunga. All photos by Stephanie Moran

blocks.text: The memories he speaks about is of living with his grandfather, Geronimo, who spent the sunset years of his life with a severe skin disease caused by his time as a miner.
Tababa could not name the specific condition, as his grandfather’s work provided no healthcare and his family didn’t have the budget to take him to the hospital, even just to diagnose him.
“Hardened na yung skin niya tapos nagpepeel off (His skin hardened and was peeling off),” Tababa said. “Since I was a kid, I always thought para siyang bato (he’s like stone).”
He looked upon his grandfather’s condition with fear. As much as he could, Tababa would avoid his grandfather, fighting with him when they’re together, and likening him to a stony monster.

This image stayed with him even after his grandfather’s death in 2015, resurfacing years later when he finally had the maturity and empathy to write it into a script which turned his lolo‘s scales into actual stones.

blocks.caption: The stone suit ingeniously crafted by the prosthetics team.

blocks.text: The stone suit of lead character Gregor was made out of foam and thrifted clothing. Tababa allowed his prosthetics team to play with the design. His only condition was that it should look like shale, a type of rock he’d often see in Toledo.
Tababa led the production along with Owen Lepiten, who directed Sunog sa Sugbo into three victories, including Best Director, in last year’s Sine Kabataan.
“I asked myself, ‘Why do I have to do this twice in my life?’” Lepiten joked. “It doesn’t get easier.”

They shot the film in Tababa’s hometown of Pinamungajan, a coastal town with mountainous barangays. To make that vision come to life, the crew worked with the local government unit, which was very generous with their resources: assisting them on location, providing tents and chairs, and even granting them a coaster free of charge.
“It’s not every day that a film is being shot in Pinamungajan,” Lepiten said. “They wanted to engage with something like this happening in their own town.”

blocks.caption: The cast and crew of Bato’ng Bunga pose for a picture after a shoot day.

blocks.text: The crew is relatively young, students or recent graduates of USC Cinema, but their lead actors have been in the industry for a while now. Gregor is portrayed by Sol Eugenio, while his wife, Lina, is played by Sharon Ceneta, who hails from Manila. Bato’ng Bunga is her first Bisaya-speaking performance.

Tababa relayed his experience of teaching her the language: “Before the shoot, I had to Google Meet with Ms. Sharon, direct how she should pronounce certain words and develop an accent…I also directed her for emotional tone, so it’s not just words for her; they actually mean something.”

In the film itself, Ceneta gets it right. She hardens the vowel sounds that Tagalog speakers usually soften. It is through her dialogue, and her dialogue alone, that we find out Gregor developed his stony condition from working as a miner.

blocks.caption: Producer Lepiten and actress Ceneta discuss the film in between takes.

blocks.text: Originally, Tababa wanted to center his script on the collapse of a mining pit in Toledo back in 2020, one that killed four people and left six missing during Christmas week. The host barangay had filed complaints about the project to the Mines and Geosciences Bureau Central Visayas a year before the incident, flagging concerns for workers’ and residents’ safety.
But he decided to stick with a story he’d actually lived through, remembering the details: his mother’s caretaking, his grandfather’s illness, the fears he carried as a child.

“Because of the negligence of those on top, yung naapektuhan is mga laborers (the ones affected are the laborers),” Tababa said. “I want to spark discussions about labor rights, proper healthcare, and reparations for affected families.”

There’s no scene of mining anywhere in the short film. It’s set almost entirely in a small house on the mountainside. But you don’t need to see the mine to feel what it’s cost this family. Every sacrifice they make to adjust to their grandfather’s condition stands in for a wound that was never really his to bear alone, and never really healable to begin with.

blocks.caption: A still from the short film Bato’ng Bunga.

blocks.text: An allegory, a metaphor. Call it what you want. But fiction can only go up to a point. Bato’ng Bunga screens more like a preview: nature, after being allowed to be plundered for so long, is due to take back what it’s owed.
Tababa described it succinctly: “Ito yung palaging hinuhukay ng lolo ko (This is what my grandfather was excavating). Now, the mountain is trying to get his body back.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia

image.caption: Zelenskyy's visit to Canada focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year. (Mark Bochsler/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday described the unfolding tension between Canada and the United States as a "strange" sight to behold, drawing a comparison to his own country's fight with neighbouring Russia.
Says Ottawa and Washington need to work out their differences
Zelenskyy calls U.S. threats to annex Canada 'dangerous'
In a wide-ranging interview with CBC News, Zelenskyy described American threats to annex Canada as "dangerous" and said both countries have a duty to resolve their differences.
"Strange," the president told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, speaking to the tension in North America.
"It's very dangerous [when] there are some problems between neighbours and we [Ukraine and Russia] are the example."

Russia and Ukraine are, like Canada and the U.S., neighbours with a lengthy border and history, though their current tensions are vastly different: Moscow's four-and-a-half year invasion of Ukraine is a deadly war, while the issues in Ottawa and Washington are largely economic.
"I think that the United States and Canada, will have to have … very constructive dialogue. They have to have it. It's dangerous. [There's] no choice," he said.
Zelenskyy's remarks come at the end of a visit to Canada, which was focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year.
He spoke about Ukraine's new strategic partnership with Canada, efforts to revive peace talks with Moscow and his view on any potential face-to-face meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelenskyy says war holds no 'win-win' scenario for Russia and Ukraine
100-year partnership with Canada

Canada and Ukraine signed a long-term strategic and political partnership on Thursday that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries. The declaration established a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.
On Friday, Zelenskyy said the length of the deal with Canada, one of Ukraine's most vocal supporters in the war, was chosen as a symbolic gesture.

"It's about roots," he said. "It says that we will be together for a long period of time. Our children and our grandchildren, we will work together. We will share the experience of security [and] a lot of different things."
Why Zelenskyy has no desire to sit down with Vladimir Putin
Zelenskyy's visit to Canada came not only as the relationship between Canada and the U.S. hit another low, but as the Trump administration renews its push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

After U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner discussed potential proposals to end the war during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, Trump said the Russian leader wanted to make a deal.

items: Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it

blocks.text: But on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed doubts the Kremlin is interested in ending the war. He said he believes Russia maintains its goal of occupying Ukraine, but said he would sit face-to-face with Putin if trilateral negotiations came to fruition — though he said he doesn't expect any movement until after Russian parliamentary elections on Sept. 20.

"It's not my wish … Better to sit with my family," he said of a possible meeting with the Russian president. He described Putin as an "enemy," but said sitting down with an enemy "can bring us closer" to peace.

Diplomatic efforts to end the war have been stalled for months, while both countries have escalated attacks on the other. Moscow has continued its bombardment of Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv has intensified its strikes inside Russia in an effort to reduce its economic ability to continue with the war.
"To be honest, there is no win-win in this war. It can't be so because [there's been] so many human losses. It stopped being win-win at the first day of this war between us," Zelenskyy said.
"The most important victory for everybody, it's not for Ukraine and Russia ... For the world, it's peace. To stop this war. And this is a victory for a human lives."
With files from Murray Brewster

blocks.text: EX-HOUSE LEADER. Speaker Martin Romualdez graces the first meeting of the Visayas Caucus of the 20th Congress in the House of Representatives on August 7, 2025.
House of Representatives
The Sandiganbayan Third Division seeks the independent medical examination to determine whether there is a need for Romualdez’s continued hospital confinement

MANILA, Philippines – Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez was transferred to the University of the Philippines-Philippine General Hospital (UP-PGH) on Saturday, September 12, to undergo an independent medical examination amid his request for continued hospital confinement.

On Friday, September 11, the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan’s Third Division ordered the hospital transfer and independent test on Romualdez, who has been arrested over his P7.44-billion plunder case.
In his motion for continued hospital confinement under custody, Romualdez claimed to have various diseases, including hypertension and heart problems.
The former House speaker was arrested in his hospital room at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Monday, September 7.
Following the Friday court order, he left the hospital at past 8 am on Saturday and arrived at UP-PGH at 8:35 am.
Among those who escorted the ambulance carrying Romualdez were personnel from the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology.
The medical test was scheduled at 10 am.
BJMP personnel left the UP-PGH premises past 10 am. BJMP physician Henry Fabro did not give a comment to the media on the state of Romualdez.
Romualdez will stay in UP-PGH until further court orders.

UP-PGH doctors are directed to submit their report and recommendation on the medical examination on Sunday, September 13. They are told to testify on Monday, September 14, as to “whether there is an imperative need” for Romualdez’s continued hospital confinement.
After the resolution on his request for hospital confinement, the former speaker will be detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US rapper Lil Durk found not guilty of murder-for-hire scheme
articles.summary:
Prosecutors accused musician, born Durk Banks, of putting bounty on fellow rapper in retaliation for friend’s killing

Chicago rapper

blocks.text: Chicago rapper Lil Durk has been acquitted of all charges in a murder-for-hire scheme, in which a man was fatally gunned down in 2022.

Prosecutors had accused Lil Durk, born Durk Banks, of putting a bounty on Atlanta rapper Tayquian Bowman’s life in retaliation for the 2020 shooting death of Banks’s friend, fellow Chicago rap star King Von.

The state alleged that associates of Only the Family, Banks’s alleged criminal enterprise and record label, tracked Bowman to a gas station in West Hollywood in 2022, where they opened fire on his car. Bowman’s cousin, Saviay’a Robinson, was fatally shot in the ambush.

Kacey Hester, who said he had been a shooter in the attack, testified, according to Courthouse News, that Banks probed for details on the ambush: “Did somebody get hit? How many times did you shoot? What did you do?”
Banks’s defense attorneys cast doubt over the reliability of Hester’s testimony, saying he was seeking a more lenient sentence.
The rapper’s defense team also sought to portray Kavon Grant, Banks’s former assistant, whose cousin died after an altercation with Bowman’s entourage, as the mastermind of the 2022 shooting.

Prosecutors rebuffed the lawyers’ notion. “No one is saying he was the one on the ground with a gun in his hand in Los Angeles, but you know this story doesn’t happen without him, and it doesn’t make sense without his leadership,” assistant US attorney Ian Yanniello reportedly said.
The Friday federal jury verdict brought an end to a highly publicized case that drew loyal fans and celebrity supporters to the downtown Los Angeles courthouse.
Banks’s legal woes are not over yet. He is due to appear in court for a second trial on a racketeering charge.

“While we are disappointed with the jury’s decision regarding Durk Banks, AKA Lil Durk, we look forward to presenting our evidence at his second trial, scheduled for 5 October, when he will face racketeering murder and firearms charges,” said first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli.

articles.title: Record fairs and borrowed nostalgia
articles.summary: 'We are an obsessive lot, record collectors, touched by a bit of madness and resigned to the reality that our obsession will only be challenged by the onset of arthritic knees and hearing loss'

blocks.text: It was a rainy, habagat-swept afternoon. Dark clouds hovered ominously over the country’s financial district. On the second floor of Makati Square, once a haven for collectors of pirated DVDs, it was all sunshine and good vibes all around. A different set of collectors have taken over. If there was a brewing storm outside, no one seemed to care.

The place hummed with light conversation over music, vinyl, audio gear, and beer. The participants in this quarterly gathering mingled and merged as an obscure Pinoy disco hit from the ’70s blasted from the house speakers.

Twentysomethings, trentahin titos and titas, senior citizens, punks, jazzers, metalheads, city pop connoisseurs, all going through the rituals of record flipping, reading liner notes, checking the vinyl, haggling, putting their purchases in the ubiquitous tote bags. The event was the 50th staging of “Kagatan,” the quarterly record fair that has grown from record swap meet to a cultural touchstone.

To describe “Kagatan” as a celebration of community is to add a beauty filter to what is, at its barest, a gathering of addicts getting their vinyl fix, a dopamine collective shot in 45 and 33 1/3 rpm. Sure, a few kids were there for the scene and the IG content. They are forgiven. You can easily spot the serious diggers, which is to say, almost everyone.

You see them hunched over crates or kneeling to check out the cardboard boxes of used singles on the floor. You can inhale the intensity and vicariously share the joy of finding an excellent Shuggie Otis or Edgar Mortiz album, discovering a rarity for cheap or a grail find, or just a better copy of scratchy placeholder records. No music police here, no uptight self-proclaimed taste arbiter (plenty of those on Facebook), thumbing down on your acquisition. Michael Cretu? Cool find.

We are an obsessive lot, record collectors, touched by a bit of madness and resigned to the reality that our obsession will only be challenged by the onset of arthritic knees and hearing loss. We obsess over artists, producers, engineers, genres, even session musicians and album cover designers. A lot of us are completists, striving to acquire, by all means necessary unless it lands one in jail, a favorite artist’s entire discography, or all the pressings of a favorite album. How many pressings of Steely Dan’s “Aja” can one possibly own? A lot, it turns out.

Record collecting is a personal, irrational human endeavor. That’s an admission against interest or an insanity plea. It lets you inhabit a private space of chosen decades, genres, or artists. It’s also a vow of self-inflicted poverty. And there are collectors who consider it their mission to rescue artists and their works from cultural oblivion, a record collector being a curator of memories and a keeper of pop culture artifacts, both popular and obscure. In the normal world, it’s called hoarding.
Sure, there’s the nostalgia factor. At 64, I have plenty of nostalgia to feed my record obsession.

From the ’70s until the early ’90s, I was a classic rock fascist. Today, my choices are more catholic, inclusive, a bit weird for some. I have developed a love for disco, which I loathed back then, as well as radio-friendly pop, old-school R&B and funk, hard bop, and artists nearly forgotten like Nick Drake and Karen Dalton.

There was no need for record fairs back in the ’60s and ’70s. Vinyl records were available everywhere. Aside from stand-alone record stores you can buy records in department stores and supermarkets. In college, flush with moolah from my allowance as a campus paper editor, I frequented a store in Quiapo selling used rock albums, all imports. For cheap local pressings, the go-to place was the Mareco record label warehouse on the ground floor of a pre-war building in Escolta.

By the ’90s, stocks were drying out at a time when I had disposable income. Vinyl records were becoming collector’s items. The few stores that sold them were Rastro in Greenhills (where I scored a Canadian-pressing of Joni Mitchell’s “Hejira”) and Shop and Lift owned by Ricky Lee.

Ricky Lee’s corner shop was a crash course in the classics. Memorable finds: A UK-pressing of Bruce Springsteen’s “Born to Run” with a misprint of Jon Landau’s name; “His Band and Street Choir” and “St. Dominic’s Preview” from Van Morrison which I have until now. Makati Cinema Square was already the place to go for record collectors, but geographically inconvenient for an often-hungover working stiff from Quezon City.

Other than a few record stores, you can only find vinyl records in garage sales, flea markets, and thrift shops. These were pre-owned, ungraded records you buy blind. You just hope that the previous owner was that rare owner who cared for his or her records and didn’t use them as beer coasters. Those dirt-covered, worn-out records? They may just need thorough cleaning, especially out-of-print classics like “Samba Song” by Bong Peñera.

Thrift shops often sold crates of sealed local pressings for P50 each. Unsealed ones went for P25. When the budget’s tight, I end up looking for small tears in the plastic cover and pull it halfway when the salesperson wasn’t looking. Like I said, by all means necessary and not illegal.

The industry by that time had declared vinyl officially dead as a music format. The entry of Tower Records opened a mouth-watering selection of albums reissued on compact discs. Out went my vinyl records and the turntable (I know, I know) and in came CDs, lots of them. Everyone was raving about the clarity, the extensive catalog, but no one bothered about the barely readable liner notes, the sound compression, the so-called digital distortion, the listening fatigue.

Apostles of digital hailed CDs for the crystal-clear sound reproduction. Vinyl, they said, had surface noise. The British radio DJ John Peel had a perfect retort: “Somebody was trying to tell me CDs are better than vinyl because they don’t have any surface noise. I said, ‘Listen, mate, life has surface noise.’”

I can’t place the exact date, but sometime around 2013 or 2014, something triggered my return to vinyl. Perhaps it was a music player app on the early iPad models that added scratches to the audio. You can even adjust the level of surface noise. It even had this graphic of a needle drop on a record. I started with the few vinyl records I still kept and bought a portable player, much hated by audiophiles, before upgrading to a decent turntable and amp a few months after. There was no turning back.

The local vinyl community did not just survive the official declaration of the format’s demise but had grown. There were more sellers, more physical stores, institutions like Bebop Records, Erick’s Records, NEC, Stereofiles Audio, Backspacer Records, Treskul, Profound Audio and online sellers like Red Records and Frederick Magat. More record fairs like “Kagatan” and local albeit unofficial stagings of Record Store Day. More collectors, new and returning prodigal sons and daughters.

With it came the demand, and over the years, with vinyl emerging as the leading format, came jacked up prices for second-hand vinyl, pricey reissues, and new releases that sound like rubbish. The industry bigwigs and some greedy sellers, having a gold mine handed to them by consumers, are out for a cash grab, choking the very medium that is keeping music and vinyl alive. Sorry for the old man rant.

As a member of the analog generation, I welcome the analog revival among Gen Z. I understand the yearning for the tactile, the touch and feel absent from the sensory experiences of a generation raised on streaming and the dictates of algorithms that rob a person of personal agency. There is genuine satisfaction in seeing younger collectors buying albums from the ’60s, ’70s, and ’80s, a generation with no actual nostalgia for it, just a hunger for the culture and the music.

I had just paid for a copy of Iggy and the Stooges’ “Raw Power” when I felt a presence hovering over my shoulder, not intrusive, more curious. I turned and saw a young lady, tote bag on her shoulder, one hand holding a paper bag, smiling and nodding at my acquisition. I guess that means OK boomer. – Rappler.com

articles.title: NSW police seize 36 illegal ebikes on northern beaches that are now destined for the crusher
articles.summary:
Officers found one 14-year-old’s ebike was capable of hitting 90km/h. Owners have two weeks to appeal the seizure before the bikes will be crushed

  • Get our

blocks.text: Dozens of high-powered and illegal ebikes have been seized by police on Sydney’s northern beaches just weeks after the force was granted new powers to destroy dangerous bikes.
The operation was part of a coordinated push with the New South Wales government to ensure people only ride legal ebikes that have not been modified to reach high speeds.
One of the ebikes seized on Friday belonged to a 14-year-old boy from Warriewood. Police said it was capable of reaching speeds of more than 90km/h.
NSW police said they seized 36 “illegal ebikes”. The operation was launched on the northern beaches “following following recent incidents of illegal, dangerous and reckless e-bike use”.
Assistant commissioner David Driver said police would be launching more operations across the state in coming weeks.
“Most ebike riders do the right thing and comply with the rules; however, police will enforce [the] new legislation if people ride non-compliant vehicles,” Driver said on Saturday.
In late August, NSW police were given new powers to destroy ebikes capable of exceeding the legal speed limit.
Owners of seized ebikes now have 14 days to let police know whether their bike was stolen and being used by someone else on Friday.
After that two-week window, the bikes will be “crushed”, the government says.
The legislation also allowed police to seize ebikes that do not cut power assistance at 25km/h, with non-compliant bikes to be removed from the streets.
The government invested in a number of “dyno units” – portable speed-testing devices – to measure an ebike’s power output.

blocks.caption: A seized ebike is taken away. Photograph: NSW police

blocks.text: The Transport for NSW secretary, Josh Murray, said one of the units was used on the northern beaches on Friday to inspect suspect ebikes.
“We can put an ebike on a machine and test its power and speed very quickly,” Driver said. “When they did that yesterday, the bike showed that just by clicking the throttle it could go over 40km/h.”

Ebikes have been hailed as a climate-friendly solution to city traffic congestion, transport emissions and even youth social media addiction, offering Australians a means to get more exercise and save money.
after newsletter promotion
But they have come with a cost. NSW recorded 226 injuries related to ebikes in 2024. In just the first seven months of 2025, that had already to surged to 233 injuries plus four deaths.
Murray said most people were legally using ebikes but a small group ignoring the rules endangered other road users.

“We are serious about ebike safety and operations like this will continue by NSW police with support from Transport for NSW to ensure all road users are safe and complying with the state’s upgraded laws,” Murray said.
“Ebikes must behave like bicycles, not motorcycles. If your bike can operate like a motorcycle under throttle or go more than 25km/h while being powered, it is not legal to ride in public.
“Before you or your child jumps on an ebike, please make sure it’s road-legal, otherwise you risk losing the bike.”
On Friday, police issued 16 penalty notices and 46 cautions for other road offences, including not wearing a helmet, using a mobile phone or having multiple people on a bike.

The new laws were announced days after about 40 ebikes and e-motorcycles swarmed the Sydney Harbour Bridge. Footage posted online also showed riders – including those on so-called fat bikes – travelling on the Western Distributor, and performing stunts.
That incident led the federal health minister, Mark Butler, to declare ebikes a “total menace”.
“We’ve got to make sure we stop these things coming into the country [and] police are given the powers to crack down, to take them away, to crush them, to destroy them,” Butler said in February.

articles.title: Martin Romualdez transferred to PGH for independent medical check
articles.summary: Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was brought to the Philippine General Hospital on Saturday morning, September 11, for an independent medical assessment that will determine whether he needs to…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 9:49am

An ambulance carrying former House Speaker Martin Romualdez leaves Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Sept. 12, 2026, as he is transferred to the Philippine General Hospital for an independent medical assessment.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was brought to the Philippine General Hospital on Saturday morning, September 11, for an independent medical assessment that will determine whether he needs to remain confined in a hospital or be transferred to a jail facility.
Romualdez arrived at PGH at 8:35 a.m. from Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, where he had been confined since his arrest on September 7.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division ordered the assessment as it considers Romualdez’s request to remain in a medical facility while in the custody of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP).

PGH doctors were tasked to determine whether Romualdez needs continued medical confinement. If they find that he does not require hospitalization, he could be transferred to the New Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory in Payatas.
The BJMP took custody of Romualdez on September 10 after the Sandiganbayan ordered the transfer of his custody from the PNP-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group.
His transfer to the Quezon City jail, however, had not been implemented as the court continued to hear his request to remain at Cardinal Santos.
The prosecution had opposed continued confinement at the private hospital and asked the court to have Romualdez assessed by independent government doctors.
Romualdez’s doctors earlier told the court that he needed to remain in a medical facility, citing fluctuating blood pressure and the risk of stroke.

Cardinal Santos team manager Dr. Rosalio Torres also previously told the court that Romualdez was at high risk of a possible heart attack. He said transferring him could compromise the “golden hour,” or the critical period when medical intervention is needed after symptoms appear.

During an earlier hearing, Cardinal Santos admitting physician Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan said Romualdez’s admission was unusual because he was brought directly to his hospital room instead of the emergency room despite complaining of chest pain.
Sibayan also said he was not allowed to enter Romualdez’s room to examine him, which he described as unusual hospital practice.
Romualdez was also reported to have exhibited signs of depression and anxiety. His doctors have told the court that he has been diagnosed with depressive disorder.
The PGH doctors were ordered to submit their assessment by September 13.
Romualdez faces a P7.44-billion plunder charge in connection with alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects.
State prosecutors accuse him of repeatedly receiving kickbacks and other pecuniary benefits from former lawmaker Zaldy Co on at least 15 occasions between 2022 and 2025.
Romualdez’s arraignment and pretrial are scheduled for September 14. — with a report from The Philippine STAR/Andrew Ronquillo

articles.title: California woman charged with murder after allegedly killing husband with flagpole
articles.summary:
SF Gate reports bond for Vicky Kyung Mi Kim, 65, set at $10m after man found dead at couple’s Palm Desert home

A 65-year-old California woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after…

blocks.text: A 65-year-old California woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after allegedly fatally wounding her husband with a flagpole, according to SF Gate.

On 4 September, Palm Desert sheriff’s deputies responded to an “unknown trouble call” in The Enclave, a luxury condominium community. Upon arrival, officers located an individual with “traumatic injuries” that appeared to be from a physical assault and pronounced them dead.
Vicky Kyung Mi Kim was taken into custody on suspicion of murder. The victim was her spouse, SF Gate reported.
Her bail has been set at $10m, according to court documents.
The events leading up to the deadly incident remain unknown, but court documents show Kim had a history of recent domestic violence.

In January, she pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge of battery of a spouse or cohabitant and a misdemeanor charge of inflicting corporal injury on a spouse related to a separate violation. Kim entered a guilty plea for violating a protective order.
The couple had previous arguments over finances and infidelity allegations, KESQ News Channel 3 reported.

Molly Smith, a spokesperson for the Riverside county district attorney’s office, referenced Kim’s legal troubles to SF Gate: “In January of this year, our office charged Ms Kim with a felony, obtained criminal protective orders, and intended to aggressively prosecute her for her crimes against her husband.”

In a statement, obtained by KESQ, Smith elaborated on Kim’s record. “Despite our office’s clear objections, a judge resolved all of the defendant’s cases as misdemeanors, released her from custody, and terminated all protective orders that prosecutors worked hard to obtain,” Smith said.
The judge could not be immediately identified for comment.
