articles.title: Marcos arrives in India for BRICS Summit
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has arrived in New Delhi, India for the 18th BRICS Summit, according to the Presidential Communications Office on Saturday.

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 8:36am
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has arrived in New Delhi, India for the 18th BRICS Summit, according to the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) on Saturday.
The president departed from Villamor Air Base at around 7:50 p.m. on Friday, Philippine time.
“President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. has arrived in New Delhi, India to take part in the 18th BRICS Summit in his capacity as ASEAN Chair and invited outreach country,” the PCO said in a Facebook post.
The BRICS Summit is an annual meet between heads of state as a means of consultation and cooperation on different global issues.
Marcos vowed to carry the ASEAN’s voice to amplify the regional bloc’s perspectives. He said he would use his time to present the region's priorities to BRICS members.

“We will engage the BRICS community, whose ranks include four of our fellow ASEAN member-states, on advancing our quest for peace, inclusive growth, regional resilience, sustainable development, food and energy security, and a rules-based international order,” Marcos said in his departure speech in Pasay City.

“We will call for fairer global governance, stronger disaster preparedness, the responsible use of new technologies, climate action, and the peaceful settlement of disputes under international law. We will bring lessons from ASEAN’s track record and long-standing commitment to open and inclusive dialogue, while preserving strategic autonomy,” he added.
Marcos had been invited by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and is set to have a bilateral meeting with him. The President said that he will also meet with Indian companies and other key players.
This is Marcos’ second trip to India. In August 2025, he also went to India for a five-day state visit. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Man arrested over death of Mississippi woman found hanging from a tree
articles.summary:
Police have arrested Jacques Ratliff and ruled the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman, as a homocide

Police in Jackson, Mississippi, have arrested a man in the death of Tasia…

blocks.text: Police in Jackson, Mississippi, have arrested a man in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree behind a vacant house last month. The state medical examiner on Thursday ruled Fortune’s death a homicide.

Jackson police chief RaShall Brackney-Wheelock said at a news conference Friday that police had secured search and arrest warrants for Jacques Ratliff and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street.
The state medical examiner’s office determined Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney-Wheelock said, allowing them to execute the warrants they already had on hand.
The killing of the mother of four has attracted national attention, both because of the severity of the crime and Mississippi’s brutal history of racist violence and lynchings.
Brackney acknowledged the media interest, but declined to discuss motive, other than saying the suspect, a 51-year-old Black man, knew Fortune.

“We understand the questions and the desire for answers given Mississippi’s history,” Brackney said. “We understand this case is being viewed through a broader lens, a global lens, and we do not dismiss those concerns. We are taking them seriously.”

“At the same time, we do have a responsibility to make sure that what we say publicly is supported by our evidence and facts,” Brackney added. “We cannot speculate by the nature or the manner in which Ms. Fortune was killed, beyond what has been officially determined by the medical examiner.”
The investigation remains active and more arrests are likely, Brackney said.
Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said Friday after police told her of the arrest that, “I just started crying and told them ‘thank you, thank you, thank you.’”

Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but was asking her daughter’s friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock”.
“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.

Fortune died less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, Mississippi and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg.

articles.title: Ebola outbreak in Congo spreads to a 7th province
articles.summary: KINSHASA, Congo — The Ebola outbreak in Congo, the world’s fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record, has now spread to seven provinces in the African country, local authorities…

blocks.text: KINSHASA, Congo — The Ebola outbreak in Congo, the world’s fastest-growing outbreak of the disease on record, has now spread to seven provinces in the African country, local authorities said. And it’s showing no signs of slowing down.

According to the governor of the northwestern province of Sud-Ubangi, Jean-Rene Galekwa Vundawe, Congo’s national research institute tested a sample and found traces of the Bundibugyo virus, the rare kind of Ebola that caused the current outbreak.

The statement, which was issued on Thursday and reported by local media outlets on Friday, said the sample was from the Bulu health district in Sud-Ubangi. It did not disclose other information about the source of the infection.

Local lawmaker and former health minister Jean-Jacques Mbungani said on X on Thursday a positive case was recorded in Gwaka, a town in Sud-Ubangi province. He said the patient was a 23-year-old man and has died.

Mbungani said in just three weeks the man had departed from South Kivu province — where confirmed Ebola cases have been reported — and then traveled to Rwanda and Uganda. He then traveled to Congo’s Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak.
He then traveled from the northeast of the country to the northwest through the provinces of Tshopo, Mongala and Sud-Ubangi, according to Mbungani.

Doctors and local authorities in Sud-Ubangi were alerted to a patient that had a fever and was vomiting blood, Mbungani told The Associated Press on Friday in a telephone interview, adding that the man had died on Tuesday. Samples were then taken after the patient had died and were sent to the national research institute.
“It worries me. … Our province borders Congo-Brazzaville and the Central African Republic. We fear it may spread regionally,” said Mbungani.

The development makes Sud-Ubangi the seventh province affected by the outbreak — and the first in western Congo — a worrisome spread outward from what was previously concentrated in the country’s east. A case was detected in Kinshasa in May in a person who had traveled from eastern Congo, but the Congolese capital, more than 1,600 kilometers (1,000 miles) away from the epicenter, was not classified as an affected province.
As of Thursday, 7,022 cases and 3,398 deaths have been reported, according to the latest government figures released Friday.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in Ituri province, the outbreak’s epicenter, but risen sharply in neighboring North Kivu and Haut-Uele.

The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions for aid efforts, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The situation is particularly concerning at displacement sites, where residents already live in extremely precarious conditions.

Sud-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic, does not border any of the six provinces in eastern Congo where confirmed Ebola cases had previously been reported. They include Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo and Bas-Uele.
WHO said last month there is a risk the outbreak could spread from Congo to the Central African Republic and South Sudan, which border the affected provinces.
Neighboring Uganda, which had reported 20 cases since May, declared itself free of Ebola in July.

Last month, Congo began vaccinating health and other front-line workers with the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type of the virus called Zaire.
Clinical trials are underway to find a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus.

The vaccination trials started in Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele provinces, Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC’s director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said Thursday. Vaccinations in Ituri are set to start next week, he added.

articles.title: As China rises, Australia is increasingly enmeshed in the US war machine. Is the alliance still worth the risk?
articles.summary:
Australia is being exploited by an ally that could draw it, however unwillingly, into war with China, experts warn

  • Get our

blocks.text: “Physical security matters,” said Kevin Rudd, at his axiomatic best before the National Press Club this week.
“Our first responsibility is to secure our people’s future in this most contested region of the world.”

Prime minister, to foreign minister, to ambassador, Rudd – on his self-declared, self-deprecatory “career trajectory towards infinitesimal demotion” – has an unparalleled perspective on Australia’s place in the world.
In a time of dramatic global upheaval, he argued, the nation’s security alliance with the United States was neither trivial nor sentimental.
“Our alliance with the United States remains a force multiplier for Australia’s defence needs.”

But, Rudd said, it did represent one of the seismic challenges Australia faced: countenancing “the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be in the future”.
Alliance with the US, he said, was necessary but not sufficient for the country’s long-term national security.
“We must also re-embrace national self-reliance to anticipate the full range of future uncertainties.” A Rudd sentence if ever one was said.
And the alliance, like any, carries risk.

Twice in a row, Rudd was asked whether Australia would even have a choice if the US were to become involved in a war with China over Taiwan, which Rudd judged a “one in three” chance in 2028 (the year of Taiwan’s next presidential election).
Or whether, in that scenario, Australian support would be automatically expected.

Both times Rudd declined to answer, even as he was asked directly whether – if US nuclear submarines were steaming from Australian ports, and US bombers taking off from Australian airfields, heading for Chinese sea and airspace – Australia could decline to be part of another American war.
“On Australian responses: I’ll engage in classic duck and weave,” Rudd said.
Growing enmeshment
This week, the Guardian published new data showing the US military and its defence industrial interests control, or have access to, more than 100 military bases across the Australian continent.
The enmeshment of the Australian military within the giant US war machine has hastened over recent years, and is set to grow even further.

US nuclear-capable bombers take off from Australian airfields on missions across the world – potentially carrying nuclear weapons (the US government won’t say, Australia won’t ask). From next year, nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines will port through HMAS Stirling off Perth.

The US remains Australia’s fundamental security ally, but it is also a country currently mired in what many international law experts say is an illegal, unprompted war, and one seen by many in Australia as a superpower in decline and increasingly unreliable.

The federal government maintains the US remains indispensable to Australian security. Marking 75 years of the Anzus Treaty this week, the deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the US “remains our closest ally and principal strategic partner”.
“For more than seven decades, the alliance has underpinned peace, stability and prosperity in our region and continues to contribute to the region’s strategic balance,” he said.

But a growing cohort of military strategists and geostrategic analysts argues Australia’s increasing enmeshment with the US military makes it less safe: that Australia is being exploited by an ally that could draw this country, however unwillingly, into war with China.
‘An automatic target’

David Vine, the author of Base Nation and The United States of War, told the Guardian the expansion of US military presence in Australia was of a scale unprecedented outside the conflicts in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq.

“What’s clear is that the US is preparing for war with China,” he said, “and for Australians, it’s worth thinking about whether they want to go to war with China, especially given Australia’s relative proximity.”

Australia did play – especially through Pine Gap – a significant role in the US global military system, Vine said, but the Australian military’s main role was as “a kind of auxiliary military force for the United States”.
Vine argued the current US-precipitated war in Iran had again demonstrated the “myth of the security umbrella” in hosting US bases.
“Hosting US bases turns a country into an automatic target; it makes host countries immediately complicit in anything and everything the US military might do, including waging war,” he said.
Instead of deterring potential adversaries, Vine said US military presence often escalated the risk of conflict.
“Building up US military power in China’s region and encircling China only encourages the Chinese military to respond in kind, to continue to build up its military power,” he said.

Vine argued that the breadth and scope of US military presence went far beyond any deterrent capability and instead demonstrated that the nation was preparing for a war that “frighteningly, too many people in the US military establishment assume is inevitable”.

“These are the same people who have been supporting a completely failed military strategy globally, who are making the world a far more dangerous place, and making it more likely that the United States and China and their respective allies will go to war.”
‘Every alliance is exploited’

During the presidency of Barack Obama, Dr Van Jackson served as a strategic adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, when Australia took on a new geostrategic significance, part of that administration’s “pivot” to Asia.

“That pivot was about many things in relation to China, but specifically the geographic encirclement of China … in service of war fighting contingencies against China,” Jackson, an associate professor in international relations at the Victoria University of Wellington, told the Guardian.
“At the grand strategy level, it was about ensuring American primacy: global primacy is the principal means and ends of US foreign policy.”
Australia, as an ally, represents to the US an immensely useful piece of geography.

“Australia is this almost-perfect location to be distant enough from the immediate battle space in a Taiwan or an East China Sea scenario, but at the same time, close enough for power projection, for flowing forces, and to function as a kind of rear area base for recovery,” Jackson said.

Jackson noted the US-Australia alliance was often phrased in euphemism, around “mateship”, of shared values and of a commitment to democracy. Australia’s unswerving support for the US was part of that rhetoric too, he said, citing Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of war at the Pentagon, praising Australia for being “with us, even in our less-advisable wars”.
While Jackson believed “that romance” was authentically felt, it was secondary to the US’ interest in using Australia for “very exploitative reasons”.
“Every alliance is exploited … and geography is the purpose Australia serves,” he said.

Given the size of the US military – America’s military budget surpassed that of the next six largest defence budgets on earth combined (including two countries that were actively at war) – the contribution of American allies “in terms of boots on the ground, or the share of aircraft or of frigates, is always a drop in the bucket”, Jackson said.
“When military strategists in the Pentagon think about alliances it’s always about needing access to bases, ports, and airspace,” he said.

“It helps on the margins to have these almost-symbolic military contributions from allies, but it’s not decisive in any way, it doesn’t really ever shift the balance of power, it’s not the difference between victory and defeat: it’s about access.”

articles.title: Palawan ferry fire death toll rises to 35; 53 still missing
articles.summary: The death toll from the ferry fire off Coron, Palawan has risen to 35, with 43 survivors and 53 people still missing, the Philippine Coast Guard said Saturday.

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 7:38am

This handout photo taken on September 11, 2026 and released by the Philippine coast Guard (PCG), shows an aerial shot of the ill-fated M/V June Aster with coast guard boats (L) at the stern off the shores of Coron town, Palawan province.
Philippine Coast Guard handout / AFP

MANILA, Philippines (Updated 8:52 a.m.) — The death toll from the ferry fire off Coron, Palawan has risen to 35, with 43 survivors and 53 people still missing, the Philippine Coast Guard said Saturday.
The latest figures were provided during the PCG's September 12 press briefing, a day after authorities recovered 30 cadavers from the burned vessel.
The PCG earlier said the fire aboard the MV June Aster was declared out at approximately 10:15 a.m. on Friday, September 11.
Authorities then conducted a safety assessment of the vessel, during which burnt remains were observed in the economy accommodation area.
PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the retrieval and transfer of the cadavers began at around 5:16 p.m. on Friday using the BRP Cape Engaño (MRRV-4411).
The recovered remains were scheduled to be transported to the Port of Borac in Coron, Palawan on Saturday morning, with an estimated arrival time of 11 a.m.
Cayabyab earlier said more bodies remained aboard the vessel after the initial 30 cadavers were transferred to the Coast Guard patrol boat.
The fire erupted on Wednesday after survivors reported hearing a loud explosion, followed by smoke and flames.

The fire erupted on Wednesday after survivors reported hearing a loud explosion, followed by smoke and flames. Cayabyab said that the fire spread very quickly, with "everything" happening within seconds.
The PCG earlier said burnt remains were observed in the economy accommodation area during the safety assessment.
The Coast Guard, Philippine National Police-Scene of the Crime Operations and other concerned agencies are conducting the recovery and identification of the remains.
The PCG also deployed oil spill booms as a precautionary measure after an assessment found no signs of oil sheen in the surrounding waters.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry's manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the Coast Guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country's more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.
The M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 sank along nearly the same route where 31 people died in 2023 after a fire broke out aboard the Lady Mary Joy 3 ferry.
Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., the company that owns the vessel, earlier said it was cooperating with the investigation. — with a report from Agence France-Presse

articles.title: 'Canada is everyone, for everyone': Carney meets with Alberta remain campaigners
articles.summary: The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Friday Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a "calm" and "reassuring" presence for Albertans.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, centre left, and Forever Canadian founder Thomas Lukaszuk, centre right, bump fists after posing for a group photo with volunteers following a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Friday Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a "calm" and "reassuring" presence for Albertans.
Prime Minister shook hands with Forever Canadian volunteers on final day of federal cabinet retreat
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 11, 2026 7:20 PM EDT | Last Updated: 23 minutes ago
Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta, said Carney is showing "there is someone at the helm" by standing up for Canadians in trade negotiations with the White House.

Carney shook hands with volunteers from the Forever Canadian campaign on Friday in Banff, Alta. They were invited to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on the final day of the federal cabinet retreat.
The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.
The prime minister wrote "Canada is everyone and for everyone" with a black marker on the campaign's promotional bright pink recreational vehicle, which it's using to travel around the province.
The crowd then broke out in a rendition of O Canada.

items: Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward

blocks.text: Alberta is set to hold a referendum on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a second vote on leaving Canada.
Carney has called for national unity but has not gone out on the campaign trail to loudly make the case for Albertans to stay in Canada.

The prime minister did not take questions from reporters on Friday. On Thursday, Carney said he sees his role primarily as delivering on his economic agenda for Alberta and Canada to further the cause of co-operative federalism.
He also encouraged Albertans to get out to the polls next month.
"Canada is worth fighting for, and fighting for in this regard means showing up on the 19th or mailing in your ballot or participating in early voting," Carney told reporters on Thursday.
Lukaszuk said he expects there will be "a stage in the campaign" when the prime minister will become "much more personally engaged."
Lukaszuk also said he hopes to see the federal Conservatives get more involved in the campaign.

items: Federal Tories launch 'Conservatives for Canada' campaign ahead of Alberta referendum

blocks.text: "The leader of the Official Opposition, Mr. Pierre Poilievre, says that his MPs from Alberta are behind us. You know, I keep looking in the rear-view mirror of this RV. I don't see them," he said.
"But I certainly hope that they get engaged because this is not a partisan issue and this is the time where all hands are on deck."
Federal government acting as a 'strong partner': minister

While the federal cabinet chose to hold their meeting this week in Alberta and to meet with some of the province's mayors, ministers did not spell out any future plans to take part in the remain campaign.
At a closing news conference on Friday, Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, who represents an Edmonton riding, said it's not the job of the federal government to tell Alberta what to do.

"Our role with respect to this referendum certainly is not to tell Albertans how to do anything. It's not to tell Albertans how to vote. It is to make sure that we are a strong partner with Alberta, that we collaborate in terms of projects and other steps that we're taking to build a unified country together," she said.
Conflicting pictures of Alberta separation outlined by reports
Olszewski said the federal government's actions "speak a lot more loudly than if we just stand at a microphone and say some platitudes about Alberta."
But she also said her colleagues are "absolutely" calling for Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

"We are talking to Albertans about the importance of remaining in Canada," she said. "We're showing Albertans that Canada works, that we're doing our best to ensure that our country works for all regions across the country."

items: Calgary will be hit first and hardest by separatist debate, mayor says

blocks.text: On Thursday, Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas credited Carney and his cabinet for putting in "hard work" in his province and for not taking an off-putting approach to the debate over separation.

"If they had just diminished this to transactions, if they had asked Albertans, 'Well, what's it going to take to keep you?' then I think Albertans are smart. We would have been able to see through that," Farkas told reporters.

"They have been present not just in major events like Stampede but also ... visiting rural communities in Alberta. There's many areas of Alberta that haven't seen a member of Parliament from outside of the province — let alone a Liberal member of Parliament — in many, many decades.
"They're showing up to listen, to learn and to be able to support common cause."

articles.title: Military aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outage
articles.summary:
Meltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report says

The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be…

blocks.text: The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours.

According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours.

The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”.

The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday. Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident.

The incident is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical issue led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that outage, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented.

Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”.

Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”.

O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.”

The delays led to some aeroplanes full of passengers were stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany.
Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers impacted were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”.
The Ministry of Defence has said there was no wrongdoing on the part of the military.

A spokesperson from the ministry said: “We do not believe there’s any indication of an error on the part of the military. This is subject to the live Nats investigation, so it’d be inappropriate for us to comment further while that’s ongoing.”

articles.title: North Korea fires projectile toward sea — South Korea
articles.summary: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea fired an unidentified projectile toward the Sea of Japan on Saturday, South Korea’s defense ministry said. The South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it…

blocks.text: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea fired an unidentified projectile toward the Sea of Japan on Saturday, South Korea’s defense ministry said.
The South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launch toward the body of water that Koreans call the East Sea but it gave no details.
The report came a day after South Korea concluded five days of joint maritime drills with the United States and Japan that were focused on North Korea.
Late last month North Korea slammed plans for the so-called Freedom Edge exercises in international waters off South Korea as a “threat” to Pyongyang and other countries of the region.

In its last previous projectile test, the North fired a barrage of missiles into the sea on August 20, despite an overture from US President Donald Trump, who said he planned to meet this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

That launch from the nuclear-armed North came as South Korea and the United States held a shorter edition of their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises, following an order from Trump to scale them back.
Trump’s order alarmed US allies in the region, with the president calling the drills “inappropriate and hostile” towards North korea.
Pyongyang has long condemned US-South Korea joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion, often staging missile launches around the drills.
Trump, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with Kim in his first term, told reporters at the White House on August 19 he plans to meet the North Korean leader this year.
The US president also said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.
It was unusual for a US official to state a specific number on a classified issue. Seoul says the North has around 80-120 nuclear weapons.
Hours after Trump’s remarks, North Korea fired more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area towards the Sea of Japan, South Korea’s military said.
Hours after the launches, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, said Trump’s decision to scale back the drills with South Korea was Seoul’s punishment.

She called it in a statement “an evident disaster brought by the unrealistic and anachronistic security outlook” pursued by Seoul, arguing the South had a “master-and-servant” relationship with the United States.

articles.title: Xi heads to India for BRICS summit overshadowed by war
articles.summary: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in New Delhi on Saturday for a BRICS summit alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in New Delhi on Saturday for a BRICS summit alongside leaders from India, Russia and Iran, as wars, trade and energy test the divided grouping.
The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, along with global trade turbulence and energy security, are expected to dominate the two-day meeting of the 11-nation bloc.
But Xi’s visit will also be closely watched as his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
His arrival comes six years after a deadly 2020 military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said Friday it was “ready to work with India… by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences”.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.
‘Substantial harvest’
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi’s foreign ministry.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
“You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border… but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday — exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 — waving placards against Xi’s visit.
Modi on Friday embraced Russian President Vladimir Putin before talks. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, also in New Delhi on Friday, said that pressure on Iran “has reached a critical and dangerous stage” following the “military aggression by the United States and Israel”.
Modi and Pezeshkian also held talks.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
‘Big constraint’
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi are also to attend.
Brazil is representated by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, with President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva campaigning for a fourth term in October elections.
BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement — the expansion of BRICS — today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.

articles.title: Arrest made over the death of black woman found hanged from tree
articles.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Mississippi in August.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have made their first arrest in the case of a black woman found dead and hanged from a tree, and say they could soon take more people into custody.
Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Jackson in August, but police only announced they were treating her death as a possible homicide earlier this week.
"That arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion," Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said on Friday. "This case remains active."
Fortune's death has worried locals in Jackson, a majority-black city in a state with a history of racial violence and lynching.
During Friday's news conference, Brackney said the medical examiner had confirmed Fortune's cause of death was homicide, adding that a suspected killer would be charged with murder.
Police had arrested one man and "additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence", she said, adding that they had interviewed 15 people in the case.

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, told the BBC that she cried when the police called to update her about the arrest, saying: "I guess I do feel like a little sigh of relief...like a little bit of peace just come over me."
"I just hope that they've got the right person," she added.
The arrest of a suspect followed weeks of what Spivey and residents in Jackson described as relative silence and inaction from local officials.
Combined with the grim nature of Fortune's death and Mississippi's history of racial lynchings, the lack of information about the case had left the community in shock and fear.
Spivey earlier told the BBC she had tried contacting Jackson police several times over the last two weeks, leaving multiple voicemails, and had not heard back.
Brackney addressed the family's frustration on Friday, saying: "We have been in constant contact with the mother and the stepfather, as well as the biological father, throughout this case."

A letter Spivey wrote to officials about the limited communication and speed of the investigation was read during a public city meeting on Tuesday - the same day Jackson police made the announcement about a possible homicide.
"I'm kind of like in awe," Spivey said. "Like, I can't believe it. That was quick."
Fortune's death has been described by a member of the US Congress as part of a pattern of "possible modern-day lynchings".

This week, more than 50 members of Congress sent a letter, external to the FBI and justice department, saying they were "extremely alarmed by reports of black people found hanging from trees in numerous states" and calling for an independent investigation into suspicious deaths of black Americans.
So far this year there have been at least 10 reported hangings of black people in the US, they said, adding that there were more than 70 lynchings documented between 2000 and 2025.

articles.title: Conservative MP holds independent hearings into COVID-19 vaccine injuries
articles.summary: Over four days in Ottawa this week, the independent inquiry held by Conservative MP Dean Allison heard from witnesses who shared their personal stories of vaccine-related injuries.

image.caption: Conservative MP Dean Allison speaks during a press conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Thursday, June 4, 2026, to announce he'd be holding an independent inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Over four days in Ottawa this week, the independent inquiry held by Conservative MP Dean Allison heard from witnesses who shared their personal stories of vaccine-related injuries.
Government did not sanction MP Dean Allison's four-day probe in Ottawa
Over four days in Ottawa this week, Conservative MP Dean Allison held independent hearings into COVID-19 vaccine injuries.

The Allison Inquiry heard from 50 witnesses drawn from more than 1,400 applicants, according to a news release. Most were Canadians who came to Parliament Hill from across the country to share their personal stories of injury.
According to its terms of reference, the inquiry was intended to listen to Canadians and not "make findings of fact or to reach conclusions."
It did not hear from Health Canada and was unsanctioned by the federal government.
Allison, who represents Niagara West in the House of Commons, said the inquiry "was intended to begin a conversation that should've begun years ago."
"No matter what people think about [COVID-19] or the vaccines or public policy, compassion should never be controversial," Allison said on Friday as the inquiry drew to a close.

Over the four days, the inquiry heard from a range of witnesses including Drue Taylor, a 36-year-old massage therapist who called in virtually from Alberta because she said her doctor decided travelling to Ottawa could take too much of a physical toll.

"I actually haven't been able to fly or travel really at all since becoming injured," Taylor told the inquiry. "Any disruption to my very normal could absolutely put me back into a serious flare where I'm bed-bound for weeks to months."
'Really frustrating'

Taylor said she developed postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic nervous system condition that causes symptoms such as rapid heartbeat, dizziness, fatigue and nausea when standing up.

After a year and a half of back-and-forth with the government, Taylor said she received an initial payout of $45,000 from the Vaccine Injury Support Program (VISP) . She called her experience with the program "really frustrating," saying she's been in the program's appeal stage for years.

According to Health Canada, VISP received 3,557 claims and paid out over $21 million to claimants between June 2021 and November 2025. Of the 1,433 claims that were assessed by the Medical Review Board, 252 were approved.
To be eligible for the program, people must have experienced "serious or permanent injury" as a result of receiving a vaccine authorized by Health Canada.

items: Quebec man's COVID vaccine story spurs others to come forward

blocks.text: Following complaints about its administration, the federal government took it over in 2026. The government had previously contracted a third-party administrator, Oxaro, to administer the program, which was later transitioned to the current Vaccine Impact Assistance Program (VIAP).
"They were supposed to replace my income," Taylor said. "The original payout wouldn't have even replaced my income for that year as a professional massage therapist who owned her own business."
While most witnesses were Canadians sharing their personal injury stories, the inquiry also heard from others like U.S. Senator Ron Johnson.

Johnson used much of his time testifying as a witness on Tuesday to attack Dr. Anthony Fauci, who led the U.S. response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Johnson is part of a U.S. Senate committee that voted to hold Fauci in contempt — and to suggest the COVID-19 virus was manmade.

items: We may never know where COVID originated. Here's why

blocks.text: The origins of COVID-19 are a subject of ongoing debate in the scientific community.
Inquiry was 1st of its kind in Canada
Allison said his independent probe sought to fill a void in Canada where, up to this point, no such inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries has been sanctioned by the federal government.

According to the inquiry's website, "more than 30 democratic countries, including many G7 and Commonwealth nations, have launched major COVID-19 inquiries examining lockdowns, mandates, vaccines and government decision-making."
Some medical experts have called on the federal government to launch a full national inquiry into Canada's pandemic response. No such government-led inquiry has happened.
In 2023, some members of the public conducted their own hearings — known as the National Citizens Inquiry into Canada's Response to COVID-19 — which unfolded across multiple provinces.

items: Top medical experts call for national inquiry into Canada's COVID-19 'failures'
Citizen-led inquiry into Canada's pandemic response makes stop in Winnipeg
Feds should devise way to reflect on COVID-19 response, says Canada's chief science adviser

blocks.text: Last month, Canada's chief science advisor, Mona Nemer, said in an interview with CBC's The House that the federal government should come up with a way to reflect on its own response to the pandemic to better prepare for future public health challenges.
"I think we have to respect how people feel, and then we need to meet them and hear them and understand where things stand," Nemer said.
Between December 2020 and December 2023, a total of 105 million COVID-19 vaccine doses were given out across Canada.

Health Canada reported that 58,712 adverse event reports were made in that time — representing 0.056 per cent of all shots — and that 11,702 of those were considered serious, or 0.011 per cent of all vaccines given out.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: A Conservative riding association wants floor-crossers to pay back their campaign costs
articles.summary: A riding association in B.C. is calling on the federal Conservative Party to adopt a policy requiring MPs to agree to repay campaign expenses should they cross the floor or choose to sit as an…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney raises the hand of Michael Ma, a former Conservative member of Parliament who crossed the floor from the Conservatives to the Liberals in late 2025. A riding association in B.C. has drafted a proposed policy that would force floor-crossers to pay back their campaign costs.

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

A riding association in B.C. is calling on the federal Conservative Party to adopt a policy requiring MPs to agree to repay campaign expenses should they cross the floor or choose to sit as an Independent.
The B.C. riding group aims to make its proposal national party policy. But not everyone's convinced it'll work
Crossing the floor to another political party should come at a cost, says the president of a federal Conservative riding association in B.C.

The Similkameen-South Okanagan-West Kootenay electoral district association is calling on the Conservative Party to adopt a policy requiring MPs to agree to repay campaign expenses should they cross the floor or choose to sit as an Independent.

Chris Pequin, the riding association's president, says that when an MP ditches their party mid-term, it's "a slap in the face" to the volunteers who spent thousands of hours and tens of thousands of dollars to get them elected.

"There's a real sense of betrayal," Pequin told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "So we just thought that one of the ways that we could at least protect the members of the party who donated their hard-earned money to campaigns would be to find a way to get that money back."

Four Conservative MPs and one NDP MP have crossed the floor to the ruling Liberals since the April election, helping the party secure a majority in Parliament. B.C.'s provincial Conservative caucus has also seen a recent exodus of lawmakers.
LISTEN | Interview with Conservative riding association president Chris Pequin:
As It Happens6:50This Conservative riding association wants floor-crossers to pay back their campaign costs

Peguin says he accepts that floor-crossing is an established legal tradition within parliamentary democracy, and acknowledges the Conservatives have celebrated the practice when it works to their advantage.

Nevertheless, he says, grassroots party members who donate their time and money deserve to be shielded from the changing whims of candidates who run with the party when it's polling high, only to abandon ship when the tides change.
"I think it'll attract people of maybe stronger character, more integrity, potentially, to the system," he said.
His riding association has written a three-page draft proposal of a contract between candidates and their riding associations called the "Candidate Funding and Party Loyalty Agreement."

It would require floor-crossers to repay riding associations for money spent on their election campaign, minus what Elections Canada reimburses. That money could come directly out of the MP's pocket, he says, or their new party could pay.
"Honestly, I don't think we're as concerned with where that money comes from," he said.

items: The important questions raised by Parliament's game of musical chairs
Poilievre calls foul, but celebrating Liberals don't seem to care how they reach a majority

blocks.text: There are still details to be ironed out, he says, including working with Elections Canada to ensure the repayments can be made in a way that's enforceable and adheres to elections financing regulations.
But overall, he says the proposal was well-received by members of other Conservative EDAs who met to discuss it on Thursday.
"There is a sense of frustration," he said. "As Conservatives, we like to pride ourselves on being grassroots and that our elected members are accountable to the people."
Slim change of passing, says political scientist
But not everyone's convinced the policy stands a chance of passing at a national convention and becoming part of the Conservative Party's constitution.
"Does the national party want the topic of floor crossing in the news?" said Alex Marland, a political science professor at Acadia University in Wolfville, N.S.
"My instinct is they probably don't, because it just creates more conversation about people leaving the Conservatives."
Even if it did pass, he says, there's no guarantee it would work.
"I don't even think that they would ever see any money because they would probably have to go through the courts to get it," he said.
Calls for national legislation
Don Davies, the NDP MP for Vancouver Kingsway, says he understands where the riding association is coming from.
"It's just another approach that speaks to what I think is a fundamental question of accountability and trust that's owed to the voters of this country," he said.

Davies has introduced a bill to Parliament that would require MPs who wish to join another party to first obtain consent from their constituents through a byelection, or sit as an Independent until the next general election.

The last time the NDP introduced a motion like this, the Conservatives and Liberals both voted against it. Given how many MPs the Conservatives have lost this year to Carney, Davies says he hopes they'll have a change of heart this time around.
"I think it all speaks to the same general idea, which is that in a democracy, elected people owe a duty to remain consistent and have integrity with respect to their campaigning," he said.

"And if something material changes, like, for instance, the party that they claim to support or represent, there should be consequences. And I think power must reside always in the voters who send us to represent them."
Interview with Chris Peguin produced by Kevin Robertson
