articles.title: Thai police arrest Buddhist abbot on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m
articles.summary:
Phra Wachirayan Wi arrested alongside woman he was filmed having sex with in latest scandal to hit country’s clergy

Police in Thailand have arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of…

blocks.text: Police in Thailand have arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.

The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in the Buddhist-majority country, after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances.

Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century temple Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, according to the lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan.
A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested.
Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.
Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.
About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.
“But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday.

blocks.caption: Police say authorities seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg of gold bars, jewellery, watches and land title deeds Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/Thai News Pix/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: He said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds.
Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple.
“We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence in Buddhism,” said Nattasak Chaowanasai, the commissioner of Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau.
Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel.
The former abbot, also known as Luang Pho Atichot, was well known for making amulets, with the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, reported to be among those who wore his creations.
The abbot was defrocked shortly after his arrest.
Last year, police arrested a woman accused of blackmailing at least 11 monks she had sex with, extorting nearly $12m of monastery funds from them, in a case that shook Thailand.

articles.title: Dementia patients warned off seeking home care in case Australia’s aged care algorithm cuts funding
articles.summary:
Exclusive: FoI documents show senior health officials were warned of concerns about assessment tool weeks after it launched

  • Get our

blocks.text: People with dementia were warned not to apply for home support because of fears their care would be downgraded by the government’s aged care algorithm.

Documents released to Guardian Australia under freedom of information (FoI) laws reveal the warnings came within weeks of the November rollout of the algorithm, which is used to determine funding packages and priority of need for older Australians requiring home support.
Home support packages are critical to help prevent avoidable hospital admissions, deterioration and early entry into residential care.

Days before the algorithm was rolled out, the government barred aged care assessors from overriding the Integrated Assessment Tool’s (IAT) decisions, even if the level of funding and priority allocated were wrong or inadequate.
Dementia Australia wrote to senior health department staff on 8 December to say that since the addition of the algorithm, “We remain very concerned about the feedback we are receiving”.
The organisation cited the example of a man caring for his wife with dementia who was on a level three home care package, entitling her to around eight hours of support each week.
But her dementia had progressed and she needed to be reassessed so she could access additional care.

The woman’s husband was “advised by his local assessment service not to pursue a reassessment as they have seen a number of people with dementia receiving less or no support following IAT assessment, even if their care needs are increasing”.

The Older Persons Advocacy Network (Opan) sent a paper to department officials in February warning of deaths occurring due to the failing assessment system, and people with “extreme needs” being left without adequate support before their deaths.
“The inability of clinicians to intervene” and “over-reliance on automated decision-making is contributing to preventable deterioration and in some cases, death,” the document said.

In one example given by Opan, the algorithm refused a funding upgrade for a rapidly deteriorating person, forcing them to pay for private care despite the assessor’s view their existing package was grossly inadequate.
A senior health department staff member shared concerns ahead of a meeting between the department and advocacy groups in late December, the FoI documents show.

“Assessment orgs are telling [people] not to get an assessment as there is no guarantee they will get more funding,” the internal email read, adding that assessors were telling advocacy groups they had not been properly trained on the IAT.

Prof Tanya Buchanan, the CEO of Dementia Australia, told Guardian Australia: “We remain concerned about the IAT and the aged care assessment process being able to meet the needs of Australians living with dementia, their families and carers.”
She said she wants the system to include a return of clinical oversight.

A spokesperson from the health department said rather than human override being returned, the government will legislate a new “assessment escalation pathway”, giving assessors the option to raise cases to a system governor – in this case, the secretary of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing.

“It will sit alongside the existing review provision where an older person can request a review by contacting the department,” the spokesperson said. “Assessment organisations themselves will initiate a referral based on the clinical judgement of the assessment delegate.”
Carers and advocates have repeatedly shared concerns that review processes for wrong algorithm decisions are lengthy, and that older people are at risk of deteriorating or dying while they wait.
after newsletter promotion
Opan’s director of policy, Samantha Edmonds, said that without further details of the government’s new escalation pathway “it is difficult to determine the effectiveness of the process”.
“We look forward to clarification and consultation on the proposed changes, and to continuing to engage with government as those details develop,” she said.

“The IAT algorithm has been an ongoing challenge and concern for older people. These assessments have a real impact on an older person’s life, so it is crucial that human oversight remains part of the decision-making and outcomes.”

The FoI documents show that Ageing Australia, the national peak body for aged care, in February sent senior department officials a comprehensive discussion paper outlining issues with assessments including examples of people being under-assessed, especially those with dementia.
“Participants being assessed are being approved for less than or the same level that they are currently receiving,” the paper said.

Among many examples provided were two separate cases of people living with Parkinson’s disease, both with complex care needs, no friend or family supports, and requiring intensive medication, diabetes management and personal care including wound care.
Both were reassessed under the algorithm as requiring no additional support or care despite declining health.

“The assessors advised that the algorithm did not support a higher level and one assessor suggested seeking a new diagnosis … to potentially change the outcome instead of applying for reconsideration,” Ageing Australia wrote.
The organisation included feedback from assessors that the IAT could not understand the nuance of functional changes in people living with dementia.

The warnings from the advocacy groups came alongside concerns and alarm raised by state and territory health department staff including the head of the Western Australian health department, Dr Shirley Bowen. Department staff logged hundreds of cases, provided to their federal counterparts, of the algorithm systemically under-assessing older Australians, while Bowen warned of “catastrophic” outcomes.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman is investigating.
Do you know more? melissa.davey@theguardian.com

articles.title: Iran pursues cautious escalation ahead of US midterms
articles.summary: Tehran appears to be boosting pressure on Washington ahead of the crucial midterm vote, but shows little desire to return to a full-scale war.

image.caption: Brent crude — the global benchmark for prices — jumped to over $100 per barrel this week [FILE: September 5, 2026]Image: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: The war with Iran "is going to end immediately after the [US midterm] election because they can't hold out any longer," US President Donald Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday.

Speaking at the Republican midterm convention, the first such event to be held at a massive arena in Dallas, Texas, Trump described the November 7 vote as "one of the most important elections of your lives," and once again defended the war against Iran.

The US president restated his argument that he had launched the attacks to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would fall as soon as the US had won the war.
But even if Trump's promises are taken at face value, rising gas prices are sure to hurt Republicans' electoral prospects in the midterms.

On Wednesday, Brent crude — the global benchmark for prices — jumped to over $100 (€86) per barrel. The fighting escalated again this week, with the US striking Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for Iran's targeting of a US warship.
Iran's tightrope walk

"Iran still appears to see escalation primarily as a controlled instrument of coercive bargaining, rather than as an end in itself," said Mohammad Ghaedi, a Middle East expert and professor at the Department of Political Science at George Washington University.
"Iran is trying to impose costs on the United States without raising those costs so dramatically that Washington feels compelled to return to full-scale war," he explained.
"That helps explain why the number of missiles fired at US naval vessels has remained relatively limited."

The regime wants to demonstrate that it can threaten US forces and disrupt the maritime traffic in the region, the expert said, "but it also wants to keep the confrontation below a threshold that could trigger a much larger American response."
How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz?
A return to the Islamabad truce?
Tehran's preferred outcome would be a return to the Memorandum of Understanding signed in Islamabad in June, Ghaedi said, referring to a preliminary deal that paused the full-scale conflict.
At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in late August, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated that, if the United States returns to the memorandum, Iran would return as well.
From Tehran, however, this scenario seems increasingly unlikely.
Ghaedi said the first provision of the memorandum presents a major obstacle, as it requires an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon — "something Tehran sees as unlikely before Israel's elections."
Trump reportedly urged to limit US response

Israel is going to the polls to elect a new parliament on October 27, just days before the US is set to hold its midterm vote. In Tehran, many believe that a decisive turning point in the conflict will not come until after these two elections.

On September 2, the Reuters news agency reported that senior advisers to President Trump were urging him to limit any escalation of the conflict, fearing political repercussions for the Republicans at the midterms.
The White House is reportedly considering expanding the military action after the elections.
Is the lull in fighting between Iran and the US over?
Tehran, Ghaedi said, "has little interest in pushing the conflict into a much higher level of escalation."

"If Democrats gain control of Congress and try to constrain Trump's conduct of the war, Iran would be even more cautious about doing anything that could create a rally-around-the-flag effect or push Democrats closer to Trump."
Will Iran bend to economic pressure?
While military developments are hard to predict, the US will likely continue to boost economic pressure on Iran.
But Ahmad Alavi, an Iranian economics professor based in Sweden, warns that economic pressure alone would not result in political concessions.

"If the leadership of the Islamic Republic concludes that the goal of the pressure is not to change its behavior but to weaken or overthrow it, it might view concessions as a greater threat to its survival and resort instead to escalating military actions," he told DW.
Tehran would be more willing to make concessions if there were a genuine prospect of easing pressure and an established channel for negotiations, he added.
Gulf states search for Hormuz solution
Meanwhile, Oman and several other Gulf states are once again seeking a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

The foreign ministers of the Gulf states are planning to meet with their Iranian counterpart in Salalah, Oman, next week, to try to reach a deal that would temporarily ensure the safety of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported.
However, such an agreement would likely require Washington's approval, given the prolonged US naval blockade against Iran.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
Iran keeps up hard line in public
Iran's leaders have continued to signal defiance as the conflict drags on.
"We will continue the war until final victory," Ali Nikzad, deputy speaker of parliament, told reporters on September 9.

Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also demanded on September 8 that the US "completely cease hostilities" and refrain from further threats if it wanted to end the current situation.
At the same time, he threatened a more comprehensive Iranian response should the US attacks continue.

On September 10, the IRGC released a video that, according to Iranian sources, shows the capture of a US Anduril Dive-LD unmanned underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz. The vehicle is said to have been deployed on a covert mine-clearing mission.
This article was originally written in German.
Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?

articles.title: NBI flags foreigners getting PH birth certificates through late registration
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Friday flagged the acquisition of Filipino birth certificates by thousands of foreign nationals through late…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Friday flagged the acquisition of Filipino birth certificates by thousands of foreign nationals through late registration, mostly Chinese, during a Senate hearing.

Matibag raised the issue following recent raids on Chinese-owned steel plants over alleged irregularities, Philippine Sanjia Steel Corporation in Misamis Oriental, linked to Tony Yang—brother of former presidential economic adviser Michael Yang—and the Chinese-owned steel plant in Pampanga that supposedly manufactured substandard steel products.

During the Senate committee on economic affairs hearing, Matibag cited Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) records showing that over 50,000 individuals had obtained birth certificates through late registration.

“Yung PSA po nag-audit sila, noon na-audit nila, there were about like two or seven million who availed of late registration,” Matibag said, noting that the registration mostly took place in two municipalities in Mindanao.
(The PSA conducted an audit; when they audited, there were about two or seven million who availed of late registration.)
“When that audit was done, there were about 5,000 foreign nationals, and the majority of them are Chinese who availed of that registration na naging Pilipino na,” he added.
(When that audit was done, there were about 5,000 foreign nationals, and the majority of them are Chinese who availed of that registration that has become Filipino.)
With this, the NBI Director appealed to the Senate and House of Representatives to look into the Late Registration Law, which he called already “obsolete.”
“Kasi ang nangyayari po rito, nakakalat-kalat siya eh, kahit saan civil registry ka, nagkakapag-rehistro ka. So wala pong enough guards para ma-check po ito,” said Matibag.
(Because what’s happening here is that it’s scattered everywhere, no matter where you go to the civil registry, you’re registering. So there aren’t enough guards to check it.)
Sen. Risa Hontiveros, chair of the economic affairs committee, in response, affirmed that lawmakers would revisit the law, which was passed in 1930. /dp

articles.title: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
articles.summary: New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.

image.caption: Modi will be hosting the leaders of Russia and China for a two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi (file photo)Image: Suo Takekuma/REUTERS

blocks.text: India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
India's difficult BRICS chairship
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains.
New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition
Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.
Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.
"These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW.
However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

blocks.caption: India's geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powersImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.
The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.
Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

"The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha.

"It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations.
BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow
India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.
Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead.
With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

"Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.
"BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added.
Fears of Chinese dominance
The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.
Tracking the tense relationship between India and China

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. At the same time, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.
What is BRICS Pay?
"Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'"
"Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements."
India's 'America Plus' strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.
EU-India trade agreement: consequences for the economy
India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

"India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.
But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.
"A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said.
In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform.

articles.title: Grab, NCMF Region XI partner for easier, more credible halal food discovery
articles.summary: Grab Philippines has partnered with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Region XI, to make halal food discovery easier and more accurate for consumers when ordering food online.…

blocks.text: Grab Philippines has partnered with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Region XI, to make halal food discovery easier and more accurate for consumers when ordering food online.

blocks.caption: Grab Philippines and National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Region XI formally sign a Memorandum of Understanding at Bajada Suites in Davao City, marking a collaboration to improve the discoverability of halal-certified and Muslim-owned restaurants on GrabFood.

blocks.text: Piloted in Davao city, this collaborative initiative equips the Grab app with enhanced search and filtering features, allowing consumers to confidently identify halal-certified and Muslim-owned restaurants that align with their dietary needs.

The partnership was formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signing on September 9 at Bajada Suites in Davao City, bringing together key stakeholders from the Consulate Office of Malaysia, the City Government of Davao, NCMF Region XI, and Grab Philippines.

blocks.caption: The collaborative initiative between Grab and NCMF paves the way for a more inclusive, worry-free ordering experience for Muslim consumers and travelers in Davao City.

blocks.text: “Our vision is to build an inclusive platform that empowers consumers to make food choices with absolute confidence,” said RJ Cabaluna, Grab Philippines Vice President for Cities. “That means going beyond basic food delivery and equipping our app with the right filters and verification systems needed by the Muslim community. We are proud to partner with NCMF Region XI in taking this practical step toward strengthening the local halal food ecosystem and ensuring Grab remains a trusted partner for diverse dietary needs.”

With transparency and credibility as guiding principles, NCMF endorsement is required before Davao City-based halal merchants can be appropriately tagged on GrabFood, ensuring consumers are guided to food choices that align with their needs. This guarantees that when users search for the word “halal,” the results exclusively display merchants that have been vetted by halal certification bodies. The universal “Philippine Halal” logo will also be placed on the merchant’s icon as an additional identifier.
Following NCMF endorsement, Muslim-owned merchants also have the option to display a “Muslim-owned” tag, enhancing their visibility and classification in relevant search results.
Furthermore, Grab is undertaking a clean-up of inaccurate or unsupported uses of the word “halal” in restaurant names, reinforcing the integrity of the platform.
Building an inclusive food ecosystem

While the immediate focus remains on platform enhancements, Grab and NCMF Region XI are exploring future opportunities to strengthen the local halal ecosystem. Potential collaborations under the MOU include halal merchant education, consumer-awareness campaigns, and capacity-building sessions.

“This partnership goes beyond just an app feature—it is about respecting traditions and building a community where Muslim Filipinos and travelers can order food without worry or hesitation,” said Arch. Sherrila Porza-Sawah, Regional Director of NCMF Region XI. “By working directly with a platform like Grab, we are reducing the barriers to discovering certified halal food and ensuring that our Muslim merchants and consumers are supported.”

With NCMF guiding the community’s interests and Grab adapting its technology to meet those needs, both organizations are laying the groundwork for a more inclusive and credible halal ecosystem in Davao City.

articles.title: Pia Cayetano in Singapore: I am not hiding
articles.summary: Sen. Pia Cayetano on Friday said that she is not in hiding, saying that she was merely in Singapore to support the Philippine Padel National Team before the Asian Games.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 9:11pm
Sen. Pia Cayetano on Friday said that she is not in hiding, saying that she was merely in Singapore to support the Philippine Padel National Team before the Asian Games.
The Bureau of Immigration (BI) on Thursday confirmed that Pia Cayetano and her brother Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano have left the country.
They were seen at the airport a few days ago, triggering speculations on why they were leaving the country.
“Itong Singapore, sinadya kong pumunta because this is the tune-up game before the Asian Games,” Pia Cayetano said in a Facebook live.

“Daming nagtatanong kung nasaan daw ako, parang naman nakikipag-taguan ako. Hindi ako nakikipagtaguan, wala akong tinataguan, wala akong reason na magtago, yung gumagawa ng mga kwento, tingin niyo ba na tama yung gagawa ng kwento?” she added.

(A lot of people are asking where I am, as if I am hiding. I am not hiding; I have nothing to hide from. I do not have a reason to hide. To those making up stories, do you think it is right to make up stories?)

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating alleged anomalies in the country's hosting of the Southeast Asian Games in 2019. Alan Cayetano headed the organizing committee of the said games.

The Ombudsman is also conducting a fact-finding investigation into documents and other evidence submitted by Sen. Panfilo Lacson concerning Taguig City’s reclamation project in a portion of Laguna Lake. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
articles.summary: Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling…

image.caption: Uber has become part of daily life for many people across Africa - but financial shrotcomings have forced the ride-hailing app to minimize its footprint on the continentImage: Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: A week ago, Uber unexpectly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending over a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also announced that it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.
With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition."
In the last year, the company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

blocks.caption: Ride-hailing apps have gained in popularity across Africa over the past decade, but not all seem to be profitableImage: Afolabi Sotunde/REUTERS

blocks.text: A difficult market to crack
Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale.
The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.
However, it's not only Uber that is dealing with frustration over the current situation.
Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility in markets like Nigeria.
In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20 — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.
Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers
Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good" while stressing that the high commissions were adding to his existing woes.
He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€ 20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."
"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick another client]," he explained.
"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."
Uber makes UK drivers workers
Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business more.
The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other driver who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.
"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged protests and strikes over soaring operating costs, low fares, and working conditions as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.
Their please and concerns, however, remain unheard as they prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.
Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision, however, it comes amid a backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded purchasing power while pushing millions of people deeper into poverty and the making them less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

blocks.caption: Rising fuel costs due to the war in Iran coupled with Nigeria's abolition of the state fuel subsidy have led petrol prices to skyrocketImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Effiong added that when Uber's cost base is dollar-linked but the drivers' revenue base is the shrinking naira, the maths stop working, forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins — despite the fact that Nigeria's ride hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."
The complex economics of ride-hailing
There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution.
But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit creates a loss of a service many users had considered safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.
Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives.
"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.
Spain restricts ride-hailing services

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber: Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing change to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, at times resorting to violence as part of local taxi wars.
Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?
As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

blocks.caption: In some markets, the competition between ride-hailing apps and traditional taxi services can have brutal consequencesImage: Daniel Irungu/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.

articles.title: Palace on Marcos resignation call: Is VP Sara Duterte in the right state of mind?
articles.summary: Malacañang on Friday questioned whether Vice President Sara Duterte was lucid when she called for President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr."s resignation.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 8:34pm
Malacañang on Friday questioned whether Vice President Sara Duterte was lucid when she called for President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s resignation.

In a "24 Oras" report from Darlene Cay on Friday, Castro is in India for.Marcos’ attendance at the 18th BRICS Summit. There, she responded to Duterte’s tirade against the President when she was in front of the Quezon City Hall of Justice for her arraignment.

“Was she in a lucid interval at the time? Nasa tama ba siyang huwisyo? Nasa tama ba siyang pag-iisip? Baka po ito dala ng sleepless nights and anxiety, kaya hindi na po siya nakakapag-isip nang maayos,” Castro told reporters.
(Was she in a lucid interval at the time? Was she of right judgement? Was she in the right state of mind? Maybe this is brought by sleepless nights and anxiety, so she is not thinking properly.)

“Bakit? Gusto ninyo? Gusto ni Bise Presidente na agad-agad umupo? Kita naman even before ang plano ninyo. So sa ating mga kababayan, alamin ninyo kung sino ang tunay na leader para sa bayan, at sino ang tunay na leader para sa kanyang sarili,” she added.

(Why? Would you want it? Do you want the Vice President to take the seat? Her plans were obvious even from before. For our citizens, you should know who the real leader for the nation is, and which leader is only for themselves.)

Reacting to Duterte’s claim that the arrest of former speaker Martin Romualdez was an act of drama, Castro said that the real drama was outside the Quezon City Hall of Justice. It was clear how Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla handled Romualdez’s situation without delay, the Palace official said.
Castro also thumbed down Duterte’s accusations of drug addiction against Marcos. Her own father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, admitted to using drugs, the press officer shot back.

“Inamin mismo ni dating Pangulong Duterte, pangulo na siya, na siya ay gumagamit ng marijuana. At inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya, dahil masarap daw yung pakiramdam. Cloud nine yung feeling. Noong umamin ba ang kanyang ama sa paggamit ng bawal na gamot, tinawag ba niya ang kanyang ama na adik? Bangag? So kung ano yung ginagawa ng inyong pamilya, huwag niyo ipahid kay Pangulong Marcos Jr.,” Castro said.

(The former president Duterte admitted it himself, when he was president, that he used marijuana, And he admitted to using fentanyl and abusing it because he felt good. The feeling was cloud nine. When her father admitted that, did she call her father an addict? Stupid? Whatever your family did, do not throw it at President Marcos Jr.)
The Palace is not silencing the Vice President, Castro added. She emphasized that Sara Duterte is being asked to speak up and address her case, as well as in the impeachment trial.

“Dito lang kayo lumalabas na matapang magsalita, laban sa Pangulo, pero tungkol sa inyong sariling kaso, o kaya sabihin natin sa Pax Silica, at pati yung pag-iipon ng tubig-ulan, ay wala kayong masabing tama,” Castro said.
(You are only tough now, when you are speaking against the President, but when it comes to your own case, or about Pax Silica, and the collection of rainwater, you cannot say anything right.)
Castro also turned Sara Duterte’s corruption accusation against her, saying that her father has also admitted to stealing from public coffers.
“Umamin siya na siya ay nagnakaw sa kaban ng bayan. Ang sabi niya, naubos na. Kung nagnakaw siya sa kaban ng bayan at inamin niya, kanino kaya napunta? Sino ang nakinabang?”
(He admitted to stealing from national coffers. He said it is gone. If he stole from the country's coffers and admitted it, where did it go? Who benefitted from it?)
Castro told Duterte to focus on working and solving the country's problems. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: How big and small grocery stores are preparing for tariffs to hit shelves
articles.summary: From small, locally-owned stores to national retailers, Canadian grocery aisles will change in the coming weeks as the impacts of tariffs on some American goods take effect.

image.caption: Askews in Salmon Arm, B.C., is a locally owned grocery store with a few locations in the Shuswap region. Some Canadian grocery aisles will change in the coming weeks as the impacts of tariffs on some American goods take effect. (Jacqueline Gelineau / CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
From small, locally-owned stores to national retailers, Canadian grocery aisles will change in the coming weeks as the impacts of tariffs on some American goods take effect.
Grocery aisles will change in the coming weeks as the impacts of tariffs on some American goods take effect
Canadian grocery aisles will change in the coming weeks as the impacts of tariffs on some American goods take effect.
Stores across Canada will manage tariff price increases differently, with factors like supplier contracts, wholesale capacity and consumer preferences impacting what will be stocked.

Some major retailers, like Loblaw, will denote tariffed products with a "T" sign. Others, like the Salmon Arm, B.C.-based Askews, are choosing to offer even more Canadian-made or internationally-imported alternatives to American goods.

items: 'We're stubborn and resilient': Canadian businesses dig in for tariff fight
More tariffs, more sales: How small N.L. businesses are adapting to U.S. tariffs

blocks.text: "We have the flexibility to purchase from whomever we want, basically," said Heather Turner, a store manager at Askews in Salmon Arm. The grocery store is locally owned and operated, with five locations spread across the Shuswap region.
"We're not, limited to dealing with one large wholesaler," she said.
She said customers began asking for Canadian-made alternatives for everything, from shampoo to toilet paper last year, and the store listened.
"If our customers request a product and we have access to that product, we can source it and get it on our shelves," said Turner.

This round of counter-tariffs on American goods was imposed by the Canadian government as part of the ongoing trade war. It will impact items like U.S. dairy, paper products like toilet paper, make-up and hair care products.

items: 'Owners are afraid': New tariffs could cut sales in half for some Canadian businesses

blocks.text: Turner said as a result of customer demands, Askews already stocks Canadian or internationally-made alternatives for nearly every American product that will be impacted by counter-tariffs. She said if there is anything missing, the store will find an alternative as soon as possible.

Turner said in times like these, being independently-owned and able to quickly adjust to customer needs is beneficial. She added the store can work with small suppliers across Canada to bring in products that large corporations can't.

Turner noted that some items, while manufactured in Canada, may contain tariffed products from the USA, and could still see a price increase. Turner said a key product that may increase in price is protein powder, as many Canadian brands source whey from the USA.
In an emailed statement, the Canadian-owned grocery conglomerate Loblaw said the impact of tariffs may not be felt for weeks, as items already purchased and currently on shelves pre-date the tariffs.
"When tariffs drive up our costs, our price will reflect that increase only, " said Youmna Rab, a Loblaw retail communications manager. "Nothing more."

items: Can buying Canadian really make a difference amid the trade war?
How Canadian counter-tariffs could kill some small businesses

blocks.text: She said Loblaw — including its brands such as Shoppers Drug Mart, Superstore, No Frills, Presidents Choice and No Name — will not benefit from tariffs.
Rab said Loblaw is pushing back on suppliers when it believes cost increases aren’t justified, and will do everything it can to keep prices down.
"We are working with our vendor to find alternatives to help keep costs as low as possible," said Rab.
Kara Stokes is the general manager of the Sweláps Market located on Tḱemlúps te Secwépemc land, in the Kamloops, B.C., area. The market is owned and operated by the Tḱemlúps te Secwépemc Nation.
Stokes said, like Askews, Sweláps Market has been able to tailor its inventory over the last year to meet customer preference for Canadian goods. These tariffs are only accelerating that momentum.

items: Retaliatory tariffs could raise costs for Canadian businesses already weathering the trade war

blocks.text: "We have options to look for other local or Canadian suppliers," said Stokes.
She said customers should not expect to see large increases in cost in the store. Where costs may rise when switching vendors to avoid tariffs, she said quality will not waiver.
"Together, we're going to find the best solution."

articles.title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
articles.summary: Rampant Yemeni rebels take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports

blocks.text: Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.

The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.

The Bab al-Mandab links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.

blocks.caption: Fighters loyal to the Houthi authorities march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied ever since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent over 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

blocks.caption: Perim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph. Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./AP

blocks.text: The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, a blockade that is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, leader of the National Resistance forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel prize winner Tawakkol Karman called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Saudi Arabia is now facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

articles.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
articles.summary: The Houthi takeovers of Mokha, Dhubab and Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threaten to push Yemen deeper into the Middle East war. The Iran-backed group has made advances against Yemen's government…

image.caption: Yemen's Houthi rebels are seizing strategic towns near the key waterway Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Will Yemen be pulled into the wider US-Iran war?Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.
The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.

The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.

"This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said.
Houthis 'much stronger'

The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.

The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.

Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented."

blocks.caption: The Houthis targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and said Riyadh retaliated across four provinces in YemenImage: Al Masirah/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's Pakistan's role?

Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said.

The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.
"At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said.
Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost."

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.

Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation."

blocks.caption: Thousands of civilians fled their homes this week, while nearly 200 were killed in the fighting, according to international bodiesImage: AFP

blocks.text: Humanitarian toll rises
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war.

The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.

The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warnedthat around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild."

This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said.

"Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added.
Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia

articles.title: Prosecution team backs ex-SC justices' role in voting threshold debate
articles.summary: House impeachment spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said that the amici curiae have "credibility, expertise, and integrity. So these are perfect experts who have been chosen by the Senate to be…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:49pm
Spokespersons of the House impeachment team welcomed the participation of legal luminaries in the discussion on the conviction voting threshold in the Duterte impeachment trial.

Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban, retired SC Chief Justice Reynato Puno, retired SC Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna, and retired SC Chief Justice Hilario Davide were already named by the Senate impeachment court.

House impeachment spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said in a press conference that the amici curiae have "credibility, expertise, and integrity. So these are perfect experts who have been chosen by the Senate to be part of this process by soliciting their opinions regarding the threshold."

"They have served as former justices of the Supreme Court or chief justices of the Supreme Court. Dalawa po diyan also sat in the Constitutional Convention of 1986 that drafted the 1987 Philippine Constitution," Alonto Adiong added.
Alonto Adiong also said part of the discussion will be "what happened or what transpired during the discussion in the 1986 Constitutional Convention deliberation."
"Baka din po masabi po nila kung ano talaga yung intention, paano nila napag-usapan ito during the deliberation of the framing of the Constitution," he explained.

When asked what the House prosecution panel's stand on the voting threshold is, Alonto Adiong replied, "If you are asking us kung ano yung interpretation natin whether dapat ibaba o dapat remain, yes, there's no official kasi there's no official stand. But ang stand po ng prosecution panel is very clear - we do not engage in vote counting."
House impeachment adviser and spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers believes it is important to consult legal experts on the voting threshold.

"Ako, personally, I subscribe to that kasi mahalaga na magkaroon ng opinion na maaring gawing basehan ng ating impeachment court sa kanilang magiging decision in the future," Barbers said in a press conference.
Barbers said there are differing opinions on what the voting threshold should be and the amici curiae "can give their opinion on the issues."

"Isa diyan sa lumalabas na opinion, it is not fair for a senator-judge to render a decision when he has not seen the evidence, not heard the testimonies of the witnesses, or has not seen the demeanor of the witnesses being presented by both panels," Barbers cited.

"Very important aspect of this trial is when the judges, the senator-judges, will render their decision in this unique situation that we have na kung saan ay marami sa mga senator-judges ay hindi nakapag-participate. Maraming schools of thought na lumalabas," he added.
Whatever the Senate impeachment court decides, Barbers said the issue can still be raised before the Supreme Court.

"The issue can, will just be raised before the Supreme Court if there is already a controversy. I think the objective of this amicus curiae is to get some opinions before the court, as a whole, will decide on whether they will lower down the threshold that would go against the constitutional provision of the concurrence of two-thirds of all members," he explained.

"Ako, personally, ang tingin ko diyan is that though the Senate has the exclusive mandate to try and decide impeachment complaints, when it comes to constitutional provision, it's the Supreme Court that has that mandate to interpret that," Alonto Adiong stated.
The oral arguments on the voting threshold are scheduled for September 23. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte calls Martin Romualdez's arrest 'drama'; Jonvic Remulla says he's stating facts
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday called the arrest of former Speaker Martin Romualdez "drama" days after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that her camp wanted her detained and handcuffed…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:42pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday called the arrest of former Speaker Martin Romualdez "drama" days after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that her camp wanted her detained and handcuffed for dramatic purposes after a Quezon City court ordered her arrest for grave threats.
Asked for comment about Remulla's remarks, Duterte said it was the Interior Secretary who wanted drama.
“Siya yung may gusto ng drama at saka ang totoong drama kung makikita ninyo ay yung pag-aresto kuno kay Martin Romualdez,” Duterte told reporters.
(He is the one who wants drama, and the real drama, if you notice, is the supposed arrest of Martin Romualdez.)
Remulla earlier said that the Duterte camp initially wanted her to be incarcerated after the Philippine National Police (PNP) served a warrant for her arrest over grave threats.
“Ang drama nila, gusto nilang makulong siya. Hindi kami pumayag. We wanted to go according to the rules of law and to the rules of court,” Remulla said.
(They’re making a drama out of it. They wanted her to be jailed, but we did not allow it. We wanted to follow the rules of law and the rules of the court.)
Remulla shrugged off the vice president's remarks and advised that she focus on more pressing matters.
"I think she has bigger things to mind than me. I'm just doing my job stating the facts. She has an impeachment going on," Remulla said.
"Maybe her energies are better focused on real world problems," he said.
Meanwhile, Romualdez's lawyer Ade Fajardo said he "cannot comment at this time" regarding the vice president's remarks about the arrest of his client.

On September 7, police served an arrest warrant to Romualdez over plunder charges in connection with flood control projects while he was confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City. –NB, GMA News

blocks.text: German federal prosecutors on Friday charged seven suspected members of the Islamist militant group Hamas.
The men allegedly plotted to carry out a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets in Germany or Austria.
What are the charges?
The men are accused of helping procure weapons and taking part in preparations for an attack, the Federal Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said on Friday.
Investigators believe the suspects, who were arrested in Germany and abroad over recent months, were already pursuing a concrete attack plan.
The men are accused of helping obtain guns and ammunition for an attack targeting representatives of Israel, Jewish people or people regarded as pro-Israel.
Prosecutors say the plot had become concrete by July 2025 and was intended to take place on the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.
What weapons had allegedly been obtained?

items: one functioning fully automatic rifle

more than 700 rounds of ammunition

articles.title: Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base
articles.summary: The powerful blast registered as the equivalent of a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.

blocks.text: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.
It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge.
The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.
There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.

Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.
Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) showed a fireball lighting up the sky.
"The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC.
"The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."
He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.
Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.

The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives.
"This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram.
"All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."
The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.

The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.
Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.

The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.
Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.
Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.
Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.
Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.
Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.

At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians.
Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed.
Additional reporting by Raffi Berg in London and Samantha Granville and Ghaith Solh in Beirut

articles.title: 9/11 conspiracy theories that continue to circulate
articles.summary: A quarter-century after the September 11, 2001, attacks, they are still the focus of numerous conspiracy theories. Why do people believe them?

image.caption: Almost 3,000 people died in the al-Qaeda terrorist attacks against the US on September 11, 2001Image: akg-images GmbH/epd

blocks.text: The terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, also known as 9/11, were the worst such attacks in history. Twenty-five years on, they have been thoroughly investigated and analyzed — yet many people still believe the conspiracy theories that swirl around the suicide attacks in the United States.

First, a reminder of the event itself. On September 11, 2001, the Islamist terrorist network al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger planes. Two were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York City. A third crashed into the Pentagon, just outside Washington, D.C., the headquarters of the US Department of Defense. The fourth airliner is believed to have been heading for the Capitol in Washington, the seat of the US Congress, but it crashed in rural Pennsylvania after passengers staged an intervention to prevent the hijackers from reaching their target. The suicide attackers killed almost 3,000 people that day, and injured thousands more. Live footage of the attacks was broadcast all around the world.
September 11 was an event that changed the world — not only in terms of terrorism, but also conspiracy theories.

"September 11 was a trigger point that led to so many things: debates in society as a whole that hadn't happened before, security problems no one had had to deal with before," historian Claus Oberhauser explained in an interview with fact checkers from BR-Faktenfuchs.

blocks.caption: One passenger plane was flown into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US Department of DefenseImage: StockTrek Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Daniel Jolley is a professor of social psychology at the University of Nottingham who researches the societal repercussions of conspiracy theories. He told DW that conspiracy theories often spring up around events like this. Even today, many people still wonder how it was possible for the most powerful country in the world to be so utterly blindsided — and some believe conspiracy narratives provide the answer.
20% of Americans believe the government was involved

According to a 2023 YouGov survey, one in five Americans believe the US government was behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It's a claim that has been circulating for decades. Jolley said it shows that many people mistrust institutions and "those in power."

A conspiracy narrative that bolsters this myth is the claim that the twin towers and other World Trade Center buildings were brought down not by two passenger jets — or not by these alone — but with controlled explosions.

Not only does this allegation continue to spread on social media, it is also based on the assertions of a small number of scientists. For example, one of their arguments is that the horizontal clouds of smoke seen when the towers collapsed supposedly indicate controlled explosions in lower floors.

blocks.caption: Both of the World Trade Center towers collapsed about an hour after they were hit by the planesImage: Louis Lanzano/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, there is no evidence whatsoever that explosives or bombs were found at the site. Investigations like the one carried out by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) explain how the two passenger planes crashing into the twin towers caused them to catch fire and collapse. According to the NIST, videos of the attack support the scientific evidence.
Other analyses, like those done by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) or the consultancy firm Weidlinger Associates, reached the same conclusion.
Why do people believe conspiracy theories?
Events like 9/11 can leave certain psychological needs unfulfilled, Jolley explained: "The needs being: to want to feel in control, to want to feel certain, to want to not feel anxious."
Initially, especially with sudden, expected events like this, there are many unanswered questions and gaps in our knowledge. How did the attack happen? Who was behind it?

"These gaps in our knowledge are precisely what encourage conspiracy theories to spring up," said Oberhauser. And then some people start to entertain the possibility that an even bigger conspiracy is behind it all.
Karen Douglas, a professor of social psychology at the University of Kent, confirmed this. "Anyone can fall into conspiracy theories if the circumstances are right," she told DW.

blocks.caption: The south tower was the first to collapse, as New Yorkers watched in horrorImage: Syndi Pilar/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Jolley added that it's not the case that a person wakes up one day and suddenly distrusts the world. "Rather, this may have been a journey based on their life experience; for example, the adversities in their life," he said. The way a person generally deals with crises is also relevant. An anxious person is more likely to succumb to conspiracy theories, he added.

Social networks in particular contribute to the rapid spread of myths. Social media already existed before September 11, 2001, but its big breakthrough came with Facebook in 2004. Apps like Instagram, WhatsApp, Telegram and YouTube are now used by billions of people. They're used to share false information and conspiracy narratives, and the platforms don't always act swiftly to take them down.

"They become part of our everyday content, whether it's on our phones, on TikTok, on other social media platforms, where we can kind of come down that rabbit hole very, very quickly," said Jolley. "Going down a rabbit hole" means taking a very intense interest in a subject, clicking from one link to another, and "falling" ever deeper — like Alice in Wonderland.

blocks.caption: Disproved conspiracy theories continue to circulate about various aspects of the 9/11 attacksImage: akg-images GmbH/epd

blocks.text: Why are conspiracy theories problematic?
There are three main reasons why conspiracy theories are so dangerous.

items: Conspiracy narratives hold out the promise of making people feel less anxious and more secure. But as Jolley explained, the opposite is more likely to be the case. This can result in even greater mistrust of the government, and of other people, resulting in social isolation.

A conspiracy theory mixes reality and misinformation; and, unlike disinformation, it cannot easily be exposed as false as it is not based on clear statements that can be verified or disproved. The very essence of a conspiracy theory is the idea that a group of conspirators are acting in secret and the general public are not supposed to know anything about it.

Conspiracy theories have consequences, and can influence how people act, said Douglas. "Conspiracy theories historically have been linked with prejudice, genocide, risky health behavior, climate denial, and more recently some disturbing behavior related to QAnon and COVID-19 conspiracy theories."

blocks.text: One group has been a particular focus of conspiracy theories around 9/11: Jews. The myth that Jewish people were behind the attacks has been widely shared on social media. This claim can be traced to the antisemitic trope that "the Jews" are a collective supposedly seeking world domination or to control the world. There is no evidence whatsoever to support this conspiracy theory, either.

blocks.caption: Today, a memorial to those who died on 9/11 stands on the site of the former World Trade CenterImage: Piotr Kucza/Fotopyk/newspix/IMAGO

blocks.text: According to Jolley, certain groups — including Jews, Muslims and LGBTQ+ people — are often blamed for crimes they did not commit. Throughout history, Jews in particular have often been the focus of conspiracy myths, and this continues to this day. An example from Germany is that of the right-wing extremist who tried to storm a synagogue, then killed two people at a nearby kebab shop in Halle in 2019. He had been sharing antisemitic conspiracy theories online.
How can societies respond to conspiracy narratives?

In Germany, nongovernmental organizations like the Amadeu Antonio Foundation or the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb) give advice on how to deal with friends or family who believe conspiracy theories. For example: Communicate with each other on equal terms, and conduct research together to find reliable information, and call out antisemitism, racism and other extreme positions, and make it clear that you oppose them. The historian Oberhauser stressed that people need to learn to go back to trusting facts and science.
This article, translated from German, was written as part of a collaboration with the ARD public broadcaster's fact-checking network.
