articles.title: Marcos departs for 2-day BRICS Summit in India
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday left Manila to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:08pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday left Manila to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
In his departure message, Marcos said that his travel to India from September 12 to 13, 2026, was at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The President is set to represent the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) community in the BRICS Summit in the Philippines’ capacity as chair of the regional organization for 2026.

“In this role, I will carry ASEAN's voice to the summit and help amplify our community's perspectives on the issues of our time, guided by the priorities of our chairship, peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment,” Marcos said.

“We will engage the BRICS community, whose ranks include four of our fellow ASEAN member-states, on advancing our quest for peace, inclusive growth, regional resilience, sustainable development, food and energy security, and a rules-based international order,” he added.
During the opening session of the Summit on September 13, Marcos said he will have the opportunity to present the priorities of ASEAN to the BRICS members.

He said he plans to highlight ASEAN’s commitment to deepen its engagement with its partners through established frameworks, and offer views on how partners can and should work to address challenges, especially those that affect developing countries and emerging economies.

“We will call for fairer global governance, stronger disaster preparedness, the responsible use of new technologies, climate action, and the peaceful settlement of disputes under international law. We will bring lessons from ASEAN’s track record and long-standing commitment to open and inclusive dialogue, while preserving strategic autonomy,” the President said.
While in India, Marcos is also set to have a bilateral meeting with Modi.

Marcos said that he and the Indian leader will track progress in the key areas of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and will review the progress in the implementation of the Five-Year Plan of Action for 2025-2029.

“Our discussions will cover defense and maritime cooperation, trade and investment, the proposed Preferential Trade Agreement, health and pharmaceuticals, digital cooperation, tourism, direct air connectivity, and people-to-people ties,” he said.
He also said he would renew the invitation for Modi to visit the Philippines for the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit in November.
Marcos said he will also engage with Indian companies and players.
“We thus embark for India determined to continue the task of translating potential to action,

and action into gains—gains for greater economic security for the Filipino people, for ASEAN and its external partnerships, and for fostering broader practical cooperation among players, even of differing persuasions, to support peace, security, and shared prosperity,” the chief executive said.

“I look forward to another productive visit to India, to engaging leaders, nations, and entities participating in the BRICS Summit, and to opening more doors for the Philippines and for ASEAN,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
articles.summary: The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?

image.caption: This year's BRICS host India has to balance welcoming new members like Iran without appearing to snub the USImage: Qamar Sibtain/IANS

blocks.text: In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.

"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.

"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.
For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.
"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."
Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters
Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.

At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing.
"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.
She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.

blocks.caption: Several heads of state skipped the 2025 gatheringImage: Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.
However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.
"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.

Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".
However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.
"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole.

blocks.caption: The leaders of Russia, China and India will all be present this yearImage: REUTERS/ANI

blocks.text: "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"
Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.

"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."
What is BRICS for anyway?
BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.
The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.

Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.
"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.

blocks.caption: BRICS foreign ministers have already met ahead of the summitImage: ANI

blocks.text: She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.

There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.
What could the BRICS summit achieve?

Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.

While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.
"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."
Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."
He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.
"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

articles.title: Buddhist monk arrested in suspected $3m embezzlement scandal
articles.summary: Thai police also arrested a suspected female accomplice with whom the monk, who had taken a vow of celibacy, was filmed having sex.

blocks.text: Thai police have arrested a Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling 100 million baht ($3m; £2.2m) from his monastery, along with a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.

Phra Wachirayan Wi, a former abbot at the prominent 14th-Century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, allegedly pocketed donations meant for the temple on more than 20 occasions over two years.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions. He was defrocked after his arrest. He has yet to comment publicly.
The latest arrests come just over a year after another sex-and-blackmail case involving senior monks rocked Thailand's monastic community.
The 66-year-old was known for creating a highly-coveted coin amulet. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul reportedly owns some of his creations.
Thailand's Buddhist institution has long been plagued with reports of monks breaking their vow of celibacy, trafficking drugs and committing financial crimes.

In July last year, police opened a hotline for people to report "misbehaving monks" after at least nine monks were found to have had sex with a woman. She then blackmailed them with photos and videos of the acts for nearly $12 million.

Police on Friday said they identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts Phra Wachirayan had issued in the temple's name – one was meant for temple renovations, while the other was payment for amulets and other sacred objects.
"But the money from both streams did not enter the temple's account. Not a single baht," lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan told a news conference, according to reports.

Police found cash and gold bars worth more than 100 million baht while raiding Phra Wachirayan's residence on Thursday, with counting going on until late into the night, Thai news outlet The Nation reported.
While examining CCTV footage in the residence, police found a clip of him having sex with a woman on his dining table.
Authorities identified her as 47-year-old Punyavee Rungrueang, who has been arrested on charges of abetting a state official in illegal activities. She has yet to comment publicly.
Many monks in Thailand receive stipends from the government and are therefore considered state officials.
Police seized 35 gold amulets, along with about 1.5kg of gold bars and jewellery, worth an estimated 6.04 million baht, from Punyavee's home.
Police believe Punyavee helped Phra Wachirayan manage his embezzled proceeds, noting that tens of millions of baht circulated through her bank accounts each year, The Bangkok Post reported.
Investigators say they started looking into the case in mid July, after receiving an anonymous tip alleging Phra Wachirayan of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Two or three other people could be involved in the case, they say.

articles.title: Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
articles.summary: Donald Trump's overtures to North Korea's dictator have gone nowhere, with an emboldened Pyongyang accelerating its nuclear program and solidifying alliances with Russia and China.

image.caption: Kim's dismissive stance toward Trump reflects North Korea's growing confidence that it no longer needs a grand bargain with the US [FILE: June 30, 2019]Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: Last month, US President Donald Trump revived a charm offensive aimed at Pyongyang by drastically scaling back joint US military exercises with South Korea and pouring praise on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The US president said the North Korean dictator "has always treated me with great respect."

North Korea's response to Trump's overtures has been markedly less enthusiastic, ranging from firing a barrage of missiles to publicly denying Trump's claims that Kim has responded "very positively" to a request for talks.
This week, as the US and South Korea, along with Japan, kicked off a five-day military drill, there was no mention of any pullback from Washington, nor any sign of diplomatic progress with Pyongyang.

Instead, Kim on Monday commissioned a naval destroyer, while again emphasizing North Korea must establish a "powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent" and strengthen "maritime defense." Kim also said North Korea would soon unveil a "significant" naval advancement.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
No urgency for deal with US
Unlike the summit diplomacy of Trump's first term, Kim's dismissive stance comes at a time when North Korea has alternatives to a grand bargain with the United States.

"For Kim, the stakes are simply lower than they were in 2019. There is no longer the same sense of urgency in Pyongyang to get back to the negotiating table with Washington," Joon Ha Park, a correspondent at Korea Risk Group in Seoul, told DW.

"North Korea now has a treaty-based alliance with Moscow and is drawing closer to Beijing, while its military capabilities have expanded significantly. That's why a single reduction in ROK-US military exercises is not enough for Pyongyang to be swayed," he added, referring to military ties between South Korea and the US.
Kim rides high
Park agrees that Kim is arguably in his strongest position since taking power in 2011.

Just six years ago, amid crippling sanctions and the coronavirus pandemic, an emotional Kim stood at the lectern marking the 75th anniversary of the Korean Workers' Party and expressed regret for having failed the North Korean people.

Fast forward to today, and North Korea's economy appears to be on a stronger footing. Estimates released last year by South Korea's central bank showed the economy expanded by 3.7% in 2024, its fastest rate of growth in eight years.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North

Kim has brought North Korea closer to Russia and China than the traditionally isolated country has been in decades. This week, both Moscow and Beijing sent messages marking North Korea's 78th founding anniversary and praising the strategic importance of their deepening partnerships with Pyongyang.

Kim's recent spate of good fortune began in 2023 after a summit with Vladimir Putin in Russia's far east. The meeting opened the door for North Korea delivering arms to help Russia fight the Ukraine war, with Moscow sending back aid.
Since then, Pyongyang has heavily ramped up industrial military production, buoyed by fresh financing that skirts international sanctions.
Beijing responds to the Russia-North Korea alliance
China, North Korea's traditional benefactor, quickly took notice of the growing alignment between Moscow and Pyongyang, but initially kept its distance.

"The war in Ukraine has opened up a crucial lifeline for the (North Korean) regime, delivering weapons, ammunitions and soldiers to Russia in return for cash, foodstuff and ostensibly advanced military technology," Alexander Lipke, policy fellow with the Asia Program at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"These warming ties with Russia have also alarmed China, which is also actively attempting to cement its position as Pyongyang's preeminent partner," he added.

By 2025, Russia and North Korea's ever closer ties forced Beijing to pivot and showcase its leading role among the three countries. In September that year, Kim was invited to the "Victory Day" celebrations in Beijing, and for the first time, stood publicly on stage alongside Xi and Putin.

For a regime known for its international isolation, Kim standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of Russia and China was a major milestone. This was again the case when in June 2026, Xi's first foreign trip of the year took him to Pyongyang.
Why North Korea is now Europe's problem
Denuclearization off the table?

Notably, any mention of "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" was omitted from communiques following these high-level meetings, despite the phrase previously being part of boilerplate diplomatic language from Beijing and Moscow.

This diplomatic softening comes as North Korea aggressively takes steps to ramp up its nuclear program. In February 2026, Kim said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "irreversible," while calling for the country's nuclear force to be expanded. Recent analysis of satellite imagery suggests increased activity at known North Korean nuclear sites.

Pyongyang has also insisted on US recognition as a nuclear weapons state as a precondition for any talks with Washington, while emphasizing that any future summits must omit language on "denuclearization."

North Korea is estimated to have nearly 60 nuclear warheads, which is double the 20-30 warheads Pyongyang is thought to have possessed during Trump's last diplomatic episode with Kim in 2018 and 2019.

"North Korea is no longer looking for talks centered on denuclearization or even traditional arms control. It increasingly wants recognition, implicitly or otherwise, as a nuclear weapons state," said Park from the Korea Risk Group.

He added that any Trump summit without denuclearization included as part of the official agenda "could be portrayed by Pyongyang both domestically and internationally as implicit US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status."
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
Sanctions don't matter anymore?

Since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has been subject to a strict sanctions regime, with the UN Security Council having passed nine sanctions resolutions aimed at restricting exports, along with asset freezes.

The last package was passed in 2017. At that point, it was combined with pressure and fiery rhetoric from the first Trump administration, raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula. Kim was under heavy economic pressure and seeking sanctions relief in return for concessions on his nuclear program. But that moment has now long passed.

"North Korea's diplomatic situation has vastly improved, reducing the pressure to come to the table to cut a deal with the US," said Lipke, adding that "independent sanctions enforcement has widely collapsed," with Russia and China no longer actively pursuing their non-proliferation stance of previous decades.
Lipke said North Korea no longer needs a bargain with the US regarding sanctions relief in return for partial denuclearization.

"But the bargain now on the table could potentially be much larger for North Korea, a freeze in nuclear development in exchange for the recognition by the US as a de-facto nuclear state in front of the whole world."

articles.title: Marcos establishes EduPhil program to attract international students
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has issued an executive order establishing the Education Philippines (EduPhil) Program to promote the country as a preferred destination for international…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 6:31pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has issued an executive order establishing the Education Philippines (EduPhil) Program to promote the country as a preferred destination for international students seeking higher education, research, and training.
Under EO No. 124, the EduPhil Program seeks to facilitate the entry, stay, and education of international students in the Philippines through a whole-of-government framework.

It also aims to support and promote Philippine higher education internationally by advancing academic cooperation, research collaboration, innovation partnerships, knowledge exchange, and global engagement.

“The increasing importance of international education as a driver of economic growth, innovation, cultural diplomacy, human capital development, and international cooperation, together with the rapid evolution of digital governance and regional integration, necessitates a modern, coordinated, and digitally enabled whole-of-government framework to streamline the delivery of government services relating to international education and strengthen the competitiveness of the Philippines as a destination for higher education, research, and academic exchange,” the EO read.

The EO also formed the EduPhil Task Force, which shall serve as the principal inter-agency coordinating body for promoting, facilitating, and developing international students' education in the country.
The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) shall serve as the program's lead implementing agency and the task force's secretariat.
The EduPhil Portal shall also be established to facilitate and streamline the delivery of government services relating to the education of international students in the country.
The initial funding requirement for the program implementation will be charged against the current and available appropriations of the CHED and other concerned agencies.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto signed the EO on behalf of the President on September 8, 2026. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Yemen: Houthis tighten control of strategic Red Sea towns
articles.summary: Reports indicate Houthi militants have taken over the port city of Mokha along with Perim Island, which occupies a strategic position on a vital transport waterway in the Red Sea.

image.caption: The port city of Mokha lies near the crucial Bab el-Mandeb strait [FILE: August 10, 2026]Image: Al Joumhouriya TV/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi militia have captured strategic points on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.

In addition to the Iran-backed group's takeover of the port city of Mokha yesterday, Yemeni government sources told several news agencies on Friday that the Houthis have now also captured the island of Perim, also called Mayyun in Arabic.

Reuters reported that Yemeni government forces said they had withdrawn from Perim, and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, located south of Mokha and closer to the narrowest part of the strait.
Mokha is located 80 kilometers up the Red Sea coast from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, while Perim Island is located in the strait itself.
Vital Red Sea transport route vulnerable?
The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted amid the United States' war with Iran, sending global oil prices skyrocketing.

Houthi spokesperson Abdulsalam was cited by the Reuters news agency as saying that freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remain safe and operations are limited to specific targets.
The Houthis have in the past targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, saying it is in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
Meanwhile, Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz.
"The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel was cited by AFP news agency as saying.
Dhubab lies just south of Mokha.

blocks.caption: For a long time, Mokha had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government [FILE: September 2021]Image: Planet Labs Inc./AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting intensifies between Houthis and Yemeni government

Fighting has intensified between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government in recent months after four years of relative calm, with rebels intensifying efforts to solidify their control over the country's coastline.
The capture of Mokha is the Iran-backed militia's biggest territorial gain since a UN-brokered truce signed in 2022.
The Iran-backed Houthis control the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, as well as much of the more populous areas in the country's north and west.
The internationally recognized government has its headquarters in the southern city of Aden and receives considerable support from Saudi Arabia.
Yemen's civil war has killed over 150,000 people and brought others to the brink of famine.

articles.title: Turks in Germany anxious after AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany party's win in Saxony-Anhalt has alarmed people of Turkish origin in eastern states. Will workers and business owners abandon the increasingly AfD-friendly region for the…

image.caption: Ahead of Sunday's election, people of migration background went on a symbolic daylong strike in the eastern state of Saxony-AnhaltImage: Monika Stefanek/DW

blocks.text: The nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's 43.8% share of the vote in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has prompted nationwide alarm. People of Turkish origin are especially worried.

Gökay Sofuoglu, the co-chair of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), told DW that business owners he has spoken with in Saxony-Anhalt have been especially alarmed. "After the AfD's success, some were thinking of shutting up shop and leaving, first Saxony-Anhalt, then Germany," Sofuoglu said.

He said that initial response was emotional. "We've had a chance to speak to some of them again since," Sofuoglu said. "They're going to wait and see: They're waiting for the formation of a government."
'Problem for Germany'

Sofuoglu said people of Turkish descent in Saxony-Anhalt regard the rise of the AfD "as a problem for Germany as a whole." He said the party's election win was a threat to the stability of democracy in Germany.

blocks.caption: Anti-AfD protests were held across Germany after Sunday's electionImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Although the AfD campaigns heavily against migration, Sofuoglu said he believed that the party's true target is Germany's constitution. He said many people of Turkish origin were inclined to see the party's election win as an immediate threat to their communities rather than look at the AfD's wider aims.
"Much as the rise of the AfD affects us, this is a generally anti-democratic development, and we, along with all democratic forces, must act to counter it," he said.

The AfD's victory has also raised concerns about an increase in nationalist violence within Germany. "There's a fear that the coming days could see more attacks like the ones carried out by the National Socialist Underground, and that there will be no clarification of what's behind them," Sofuoglu said, referring a yearslong neo-Nazi terror spree in Germany.
Grasping the root

A feared increase in nationalist violence is only one part of the discussion. "I don't think that just being concerned achieves anything," Alaz Sümer, a lawyer who works with a nongovernmental organization in Berlin, told DW. "You have to think about the causes. I don't think the established parties have sufficiently addressed the problems that allowed the AfD to become so strong."

blocks.caption: According to current polls, 29% of German voters support the AfDImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sümer came to Germany nine years ago to study. He's currently working on a PhD about extreme-right political parties, and advises people from migrant communities on how to get their international qualifications recognized in Germany.
"Saying 'the AfD is bad, the AfD is dangerous' is the easy way," Sümer said. "We already know that."
Win no surprise
Irmak, who asked that her real name not be used, moved to the eastern city of Leipzig to study 12 years ago. She said the AfD's victory was worrying, but not a surprise.

"It was to be predicted that the far right would do well, and would emerge from the election as the strongest party," Irmak said. "But the ground for this result was also prepared by government policies not addressing citizens' needs."

Irmak said the rise of the AfD would not address Germany's structural problems. "Even with a change of government, it won't alter the need for workers and young people," she said, "especially not in a state with an elderly population, like Saxony-Anhalt."
An AfD ban?

Sümer said German authorities would need to be cautious in dealing with the AfD, which he called an extremist party that is now "a reality in Germany." He said banning the AfD, as many have called for, would only make the party stronger.

blocks.caption: Sümer said politicians must try to address the concerns of AfD votersImage: Privat

blocks.text: If the AfD were banned, Sümer said, a new party would be founded, and more extremist members might fall in with less-visible organizations. That would make Germany "even more uninhabitable" for migrants, he said.

Sümer said Germany's other parties should engage with AfD voters to understand their motives. He said the problem of racism in Germany was bigger than just the AfD, and that the issues that migrants face withing the country were not created by to the party.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Saxony-Anhalt had a population of about 2.1 million people in 2025. Approximately 249,000, or just over 10%, had a migration background; 6,120 were people of Turkish origin. There are roughly 3 million people of Turkish origin in Germany.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: China angered by Taiwan VP's visit to EU democracy forum
articles.summary: Beijing has lodged a complaint with Italy and the EU over top Taiwanese officials visiting a democracy conference. The EU is navigating contentious issues with China and high-ranking Taiwanese visits…

image.caption: News of Taiwan Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim's attendence was kept under wraps for security reasonsImage: Chiang Ying-ying/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: China was angered by Italy and the EU on Friday, lodging "solemn ‌representations" with both after news broke that high-ranking Taiwanese officials had traveled to the bloc to attend an annual democracy summit.
Beijing's Foreign Ministry said it firmly opposes official interactions of any form with Taiwan by nations who have ties with China.
Solemn ‌representations is a literal translation of a Chinese term expressing diplomatic discontent.
At issue is a visit by Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, both of whom were welcomed to the Ventotene Conference for Freedom and Democracy in Italy.
China sees democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, which it has vowed to "reunite" with the mainland.
Beijing has previously blasted Hsiao as an "independence diehard" and has criticized her Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) as a separatist outfit.
Taiwan's government has not sought formal independence but Beijing has, nevertheless, threatened to take the island by military force.
How Taiwan is planning to outlast China
EU Parliament VP blasts Beijing 'regime' over interference

European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announced Hsiao and Lin's attendance at the conference early Friday morning, adding that news of the visit had been kept under wraps until they arrived for safety reasons.

The EU's Picierno, who called the visit a "very important message," was defiant on Friday, saying, "No one can decide who is hosted in Ventotene and who is not," and calling out the Chinese "regime" for seeking to interfere.
Though Taiwanese foreign ministers travel abroad, it is rare for an official as high-ranking as the vice president to visit nations with ties to Beijing for fear of fallout for host countries.

Other prominent pro-democracy advocates such as Russian Kremlin critic Yulia Navalnaya, the wife of the late Alexei Navalny, and Belarus opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya are also in attendance.
The conference began on Thursday and is scheduled to wrap up on Saturday.
Taiwan minister to DW: 'You cannot be naive' with China
EU threading needle between support for Taiwan, ties with China
Italy, like most nations, is not among Taiwan's 12 formal diplomatic allies, although the Vatican is.
Still, both Italy and Taiwan have de facto embassies in each other's capitals.
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani will not meet with the visiting Taiwanese officials.
Further details are expected to be made public after the conference concludes.
The EU is walking a fine line between democratic support for Taiwan and relations with China.
Beijing's support for Russia in its ongoing invasion of Ukraine — which also prompted Taiwan to seek closer ties with the EU in 2022 — has been a thorn in the side of EU nations and in Brussels.
Why Taiwan's last 12 allies support it in US-China rivalry

A BBC Eye investigation in 2021 suggested that the syndicate had become one of the most far-reaching and dangerous organised crime groups in the world.
Nigeria is its main recruitment ground and many of its members are university educated and inducted during their schooling.
The group has been on the radar of law enforcement agencies for a number of years.
FBI operations against Black Axe were launched in November 2019 and September 2021, eventually charging more than 35 individuals with multi-million dollar internet fraud.
Since then there have been several other operations across multiple countries targeting Black Axe co-ordinated by the global policing agency Interpol.

Last month, Interpol said during its latest one - which took place between November 2025 and June 2026 - seven sites in South Africa linked to a syndicate involved in romance and investment scams were raided.
It led to the arrests of 39 people, the seizure of money and the blocking of more than 250 bank accounts.

articles.title: Teodoro: Intelligence gathering ongoing amid 'Manchurian candidate' fears
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Friday said authorities continue gathering intelligence amid fears that China might try to influence the 2028 elections and push for the election of…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 5:44pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Friday said authorities continue to gather intelligence information amid fears that China might try to influence the 2028 elections and push for the election of officials who would serve its interests.
In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB, Teodoro was asked whether authorities had received information about candidates being supported by China and who could advance Beijing's interests.

“Well, tuloy-tuloy ang intelligence gathering namin at pakikipag-ugnayan namin sa law enforcement officials. Ngunit kung walang matibay na ebidensya, siyempre, mahirap din na basta na lang pumataw ng bintang,” he told Super Radyo dzBB in an interview.
(Well, our intelligence gathering is ongoing, and we are in contact with law enforcement officials. But it is difficult if there is no solid evidence and we just make accusations.)

The Defense Secretary cited the case of former Bamban, Tarlac mayor Alice Guo, who was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment for qualified human trafficking linked to illegal Philippine Offshore Gaming Operator (POGO) operations.

Teodoro said the public should pay attention to statements made by candidates concerning the West Philippine Sea (WPS) as voters ultimately have the power to prevent foreign-backed personalities from gaining influence.

“’Yan ang pinakamagandang depensa laban sa, diumano, may mga tinatawag na Manchurian candidate sa sine. So, nasa taong-bayan 'yan. Demand yan for national dignity. Demand ’yan para sa pagpatatag ng Pilipinas,” he added.

(That is the best defense against, supposedly, those called Manchurian candidates in the movies. So, that is up to the people. That is a demand for national dignity. That is a demand for the stabilization of the Philippines.)
The term Manchurian candidate refers to a politically influential person who is secretly working for or controlled by an unfriendly power.
GMA News Online is trying to get a comment from the Chinese Embassy and will publish it as soon as it is available.

Teodoro went viral on social media recently after he lashed out at China's massive claims in the South China Sea when he was handed an unsigned note while speaking before a defense and security forum in Seoul, South Korea.
The note said China didn't recognize the arbitral award that nullified its historical claims in the South China Sea.
"Of course. Because you lost,” Teodoro said in a panel discussion at the Seoul Defense Dialog as he responded to the pro-China points raised in the note. It was not clear where it came from.
In a news conference, the Chinese Foreign Ministry, without naming Teodoro address what happened at the forum and said the Filipino "individual" should cut the “provocations and theatrics.”

“I’m not sure what exactly happened at the event, but China’s position has always been clear on the so-called ‘South China Sea arbitration’. The Philippines unilaterally initiated the case, which is a distortion and abuse of the UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea) dispute settlement mechanism. It is the Philippine side that has violated UNCLOS and undermined its integrity and authority,” spokesperson Mao Ning said.

“We urge the certain individual of the Philippine side to cut the provocations and theatrics, and stop undermining China-Philippines relations and stability in the South China Sea,” she added. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: 9/11 families to gather at World Trade Center and Pentagon to remember victims on 25th anniversary – US politics live
articles.summary:
Victims of those killed in September 11 attacks honored at memorials across the US

As clear as that cloudless September…

blocks.text: US marks 25 years since the 9/11 attacks
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
It is the 25th anniversary of 9/11, as Americans come together to remember and commemorate the devastating effects of the attacks, which claimed the lives of 2,977 victims.
Today’s milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names - and volunteer projects in tribute to the day.
“In the course of history, there are a few moments that divide time into, really, what came before” and after, president Donald Trump said at a 9/11 remembrance in Washington this week.
The Republican, who was in New York on 11 September 2001, has often recounted his memories and said he plans to attend the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony later today.

Vice-president JD Vance is expected to attend the observance at the National September 11 Memorial in New York, while other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.

Planned remembrances extend far beyond the attack sites, from beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington to a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium to a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
In other developments elsewhere today:

items: Donald Trump doubled down on his pledge to pay all US adults $5,000 if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in the midterm elections. He’s one of the few people to actually mention the pledge tonight, as many lawmakers and officials – including his vice-president, JD Vance – avoided mentioning the so-called “dividend” altogether. Trump defended his plan: “We can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars.”

In a shorter address to voters than his nearly two-hour speech on Wednesday, Trump again pleaded with voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” in November. In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the audience to commit to voting in the midterm elections at all costs. The president asked Republicans in the arena to repeat: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try. And cheat like hell like they do.” Trump also told those gathered in Dallas that they would “go to hell” if they didn’t vote.

Earlier, JD Vance urged Republicans who may oppose parts of the Trump administration’s agenda not to abandon the party in November’s congressional races. The vice-president pointed to Charlie Kirk – the conservative activist killed a year ago today – to argue that voters shouldn’t “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over “a policy issue here or there”, an apparent nod to dissent over the Iran war that he avoided naming.

Vance’s speech, in many ways, was an audition for a possible 2028 presidential run. He spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, listing the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office.

Meanwhile, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the arena to protest Trump’s policy agenda. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 30m agoUS marks 25 years since the 9/11 attacks

blocks.text: Police officer Casey Kloepfer plans to spend time today at the Brooklyn station house where his father, officer Ronald Kloepfer, reported to work that day before being called to the World Trade Center. He didn’t make it home.
Casey Kloepfer was only four, but he grew up hearing about his father’s affinity for helping people and for a job that enabled him to do so. He became an officer this past June, AP reported
“It’s big footsteps to fill, but it’s definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honor him and be the best police officer I can,” he said by phone this week.
The 29-year-old wears his father’s badge number and even has joined the New York Police Department lacrosse team, which his dad founded.

blocks.caption: David Smith

blocks.text: David Smith

As clear as that cloudless September morning, Jenna Jacobs McPartland remembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.”

A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at its Windows on the World restaurant. “I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.”

Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel, born six days after September 11, 2001. McPartland, then living in Briarcliff Manor, New York, would marry twice more, set up a grief support charity, and become a chef and restaurateur. Each 9/11 anniversary, she has a picnic at the cemetery where a few pieces of bone from her late husband are buried.

Speaking from Fairfield, Connecticut, McPartland says: “Ari was an incredibly joyful person who cherished his life. I made a conscious choice to honour him by living as joyfully as I can. It’s not always easy. I still cry pretty frequently. If there’s a movie with a building getting blown up, or if I’m reading a book and they casually mention ‘post 9-11 this’ or whatever, it catches me off guard. The grief finds a place to live in the heart, and you visit it.”

McPartland and other victims’ families have learned to live with that grief over the past 25 years. But America writ large has struggled to carry the weight of the worst terrorist attack in its history. The world’s most powerful nation responded by inflicting terror of its own, betraying its history as a safe harbour for immigrants, and pitting Americans against one another. The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.

McPartland adds: “It makes me incredibly sad and bordering on angry that the death of my husband has been invoked to cause more violence. It is the othering of people that got him killed in the first place and, when we Americans fail to learn that lesson and choose collectively as a nation to other people, whether it’s immigrants or other nations, that is a deepening of that tragedy that is sickening and unfathomable to me.”

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut will close its doors in Russia on September 13Image: Igor Ivanko/AFP

blocks.text: In recent years, Moscow has declared numerous foreign foundations and organizations "undesirable" and banned them from operating in the country. However, despite the significantly deteriorated relations between Russia and the West as a result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, the Goethe-Institut, which opened in Russia in 1992, had been able to continue operating.
But that's no longer the case. Employees of the Goethe-Institut must stop working on September 13 — and staff members sent from Germany must leave the country by that date.

According to Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, the closure of the Goethe-Institut's three locations in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk comes as a response to the announced closure of the Russian House in Berlin, the minister said. Germany intends to terminate its contract with the cultural and events venue as a punitive measure. The German government holds Russia responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"The announcement by the Russian foreign minister marks the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations," wrote Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut, in a press release. She said it was bad news for people in Russia and that the Goethe-Institut had connected the two countries through culture and language.

blocks.caption: Gesche Joost has been President of the Goethe-Institut since 2024Image: Goethe-Institut / Loredana La Rocca

blocks.text: As early as 2023, the Russian Foreign Ministry had demanded the Goethe-Institut's staff be significantly cut. Cultural exchanges with German artists were limited extent and kept to digital formats. Nevertheless, interest in German-language courses remained high, with around 10,000 students taking part. "Our work in Russia was and remains important," Joost said, referring to learning the German language, the many encounters and mutual understanding between people.
A fresh start after World War II
For the past 75 years, the Goethe-Institut has represented Germany abroad, promoting the German language and sharing German culture with people around the world.

It was founded in 1951, at a time when Germany was seeking to rebuild international trust in the aftermath of World War II and the crimes of the Nazi regime. Originally established as the "Goethe Association for the Further Training of Foreign Teachers of German," the organization initially focused on inviting foreign teachers to Germany for language training.
Its mission soon expanded, however, to promoting the German language abroad.
The first Goethe-Institut opened its doors in Athens in 1952, and just a decade later, the organization had already established 54 branches around the world.

blocks.caption: Language students from Ghana stroll through Murnau with their host family in 1969Image: Goethe-Institut / Michael Friedel

blocks.text: Today, the Goethe-Institut operates a global network of 154 institutions in 100 countries, employing nearly 4,500 people.
Around one million people take an official German exam at a Goethe-Institut or one of its partner organizations each year.

In a speech honoring the institute's 75th anniversary, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier emphasized the significance of promoting German culture abroad, stating, "For countries like ours, which are not great powers, our foreign policy will continue to have to rest on four pillars: yes, military strength, so that we are taken seriously, but also smart diplomacy to devise solutions and forge alliances; wherever possible, an international legal order to provide a framework and direction in addition; and, fourthly, culture and science as soft power, as something we offer to the wider world."

blocks.caption: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier speaking at an event marking the Goethe-Institut's 75th anniversary in June 2026Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: From classical music to jazz

One element that proved crucial to the institute's success from its founding onward is its credibility as an independent association. Although two-thirds of its funding stems from the German Foreign Office, the organization itself determines its programs — and over the decades, these programs have regularly been adapted to be in step with the prevailing political and social climate.

The institute promptly made its ambitions clear to expand its scope beyond mere language instruction by striving to provide a more comprehensive picture of Germany through a range of cultural and informational programs. "And it was also very clear that this was not about exporting so-called German culture to the world," explained Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut since 2024. "On the contrary — the aim was to reflect on how we could have a fresh start and how we want to shape society and the future together."

In its early years, the institute's cultural programs deliberately drew on Germany's rich heritage in the areas of classical music and literature. Figures such as Schiller, Bach and Beethoven had lost none of their international appeal despite the Nazi era.
Then, in the 1960s, German jazz was a hit among the institute's cultural exports — with musician and composer Klaus Doldinger and his band touring the globe.

blocks.caption: Klaus Doldinger (right) also played jazz in Lahore, Pakistan thanks to the Goethe-InstitutImage: Goethe-Institut / Michael Friedel

blocks.text: Over the decades, Nobel Prize-winning authors Günter Grass, Heinrich Böll and Herta Müller also traveled internationally on behalf of the Goethe-Institut.

With the spirit of change ushered in by the generation of 1968, with flower power and student protests, the institute's profile changed once again, and it increasingly incorporated critical viewpoints on social issues into its programs, including efforts to critically examine Germany's Nazi past.
A space for dialogue

In this period, West Germany was redefining itself under Social Democratic Chancellor Willy Brandt. In 1970, sociologist Ralf Dahrendorf, then parliamentary state secretary at the foreign office, announced a new set of guiding principles. Cultural policy was to become the "third pillar of foreign policy."

But Dahrendorf didn't simply wish to give culture a higher profile — he advocated for a new way of thinking. "What we give is worth only as much as our willingness to receive," he said. "Openness toward others is thus a principle of our foreign cultural policy." As a result, the Goethe-Institut moved away from the idea of simply exporting culture and toward dialogue, cooperation and reciprocal learning. That approach continues to guide the organization's work today.

blocks.caption: The late Pope Francis also studied German at a Goethe-Institut: In 1985, he took a course in Boppard, Rhineland-PalatinateImage: Vatican Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: While Germany was divided, East and West also competed to forge political alliances abroad through their foreign cultural policies, especially during the Cold War. In the 1970s, the East German press even spread rumors that Goethe-Instituts were being used to conduct espionage.

After the Iron Curtain fell in 1989, the Goethe-Institut opened numerous new locations in Eastern Europe and the former Eastern Bloc, including in Moscow in 1992. Despite turbulent times, its doors had remained open there until now.

For its part, the Kyiv branch, in Ukraine, has also remained open throughout the war. The institute offers a flexible hybrid scheme for its German courses there: When an air raid alert sounds, in-person classes are moved to a shelter. A range of digital and hybrid options are also available if necessary.
The 'turning point' has already come

"I have the impression that working under crisis conditions has become the norm in many regions," Gesche Joost explained. "Either because democracy is being pushed back, because colleagues are working under censorship or because they are being threatened by armed conflicts." In many Goethe-Instituts, she said, the much-discussed Zeitenwende — or "turning point" — has long been reality.

This term entered public discourse after a famous speech by former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz after the war in Ukraine broke out in 2022 and refers to the dawn of an era marked by geopolitical turmoil in Europe.

"We've recognized that we're important partners for civil society in crisis regions. At the same time, we have to make sure that we act sensitively and diplomatically so that we don't get expelled," added Joost.

In times where freedom of cultural expression, freedom of speech as well as science and education are increasingly coming under pressure, the Goethe-Institut plans to continue providing spaces for dialogue where open debate, critical reflection and cultural exchange remain possible.

Meanwhile, Germany's position on the Middle East conflict is currently making the organization's work more challenging in many countries. Some partners in the Arab world have suspended their cooperation as a result, while Goethe-Institut events have seen boycotts elsewhere.

"Our task then is to explain the German position and the history behind it, but also to show the debates taking place on the issue within Germany," Joost said. "At the same time, we also convey the criticism coming from many countries back to Germany."
The Goethe-Institut's work has also been made more difficult in recent years due to deep cuts in federal funding, forcing it to restructure and even shut down some locations.

At the same time, integrating Germany's growing number of foreign skilled workers presents new challenges; Joost feels her institute plays a crucial role here. "We see that many foreign skilled workers see a future for themselves in Germany. But settling into life in Germany is not always easy," she said. "To support them, we have our welcome coaches who are available to answer questions about living and working in Germany and provide guidance, especially in the early stages. That is an important contribution the Goethe-Institut can make in Germany."
This article was originally published in German on June 22 and updated on September 10, 2026, ahead of the closure of the Goethe-Institut in Russia.

articles.title: Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi
articles.summary: As Brics leaders meet in Delhi, divisions within the bloc make a united response to Washington unlikely.

blocks.text: The US is not a member of Brics, yet President Donald Trump's shadow will loom large over the group's summit in Delhi this weekend.

Leaders from 11 Brics nations - including host India, China, Russia, Brazil, South Africa, the UAE and Iran, with Saudi Arabia attending as an invited member - will hold talks on a wide range of issues. But few will be as consequential as the impact of President Trump's policies.

The war in Iran and the ever-present threat of White House tariffs, directed at both US adversaries and allies, have destabilised global energy markets and has often left the global economy guessing the future.

It is against this backdrop that Brics leaders are meeting. Yet the group is unlikely to produce a consensus statement that openly calls out the US or lays out a coordinated strategy to counter President Trump's policies and geopolitics.
That is partly because Brics itself is deeply divided over how far it should go in challenging Washington.

"India cannot afford to have a joint statement that rails against Washington," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. He expects any criticism of US policies to be "vague and indirect", reflecting the sharply divergent interests within the expanded group.
While Russia and Iran may push for the group to take a clearer stand against President Trump, the geopolitical realities within Brics are likely to make that difficult.

India, which is reportedly in the final stages of a trade deal with the US, will not want a statement that could upset the White House. China, too, may be wary of being seen as using Brics to target Washington.

Then there is the UAE, which has come under Iranian attack during Tehran's retaliation against US and Israeli strikes. The Gulf state, which hosts US military bases, is unlikely to support a statement that helps Tehran's cause.
Kugelman says Brics has become more significant through its expansion, but that has also made consensus harder.
"You've added a number of members that don't get along," he said, describing the challenge for India as bringing together countries with "a wide array of views and positions on the global order".
Trump has also been quite vocal against Brics, particularly its efforts to reduce global trade's dependence on the US dollar, commonly known as de-dollarisation.
He has often warned the group against trying to come up with an alternative currency or take measures to weaken the dollar's dominance in global trade.
In one such threat, Trump said in November 2024 that Brics countries would face "100% tariffs" if they backed another currency to replace the "mighty US dollar".
Under these circumstances, what can the group realistically deliver?

Brics' geopolitical and economic heft has grown substantially over the past decade. While it will be reluctant to take an openly anti-US or anti-Western position, the group will be looking to build on its existing achievements and demonstrate that it can emerge as an alternative blocs like the G20 and G7.
Brics now accounts for 49% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of international trade, according to BBC Monitoring's analysis.
Its most tangible achievement remains the New Development Bank - which has approved billions of dollars in infrastructure and development projects - many of them in countries of the global south.
The group has also created a $100bn contingency reserve arrangement to help members facing financial crises, although it has yet to be tested.
The leaders are also likely to explore ways to make cross-border payments in local currencies easier. That will be of particular interest to Moscow and Tehran, both of which face severe US sanctions.

Brics is also expected to continue positioning itself as a voice for the developing nations, collectively pushing for reforms to institutions such as the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which many developing nations feel do not accurately reflect the new global order.
For India, in particular, the summit offers an opportunity to strengthen its claim to leadership of the global south.

Many of Delhi's own foreign policy priorities, including multilateralism, a more multipolar world, greater representation for developing countries and freer global trade, align closely with Brics' wider agenda.
But India will also have to find ways to work around China's considerable influence within Brics and its stronger presence across much of the developing world.

The Modi government has placed a strong emphasis on becoming a "leader or a voice of the Global South", Kugelman says. But India's efforts have had "limited success" in making deeper inroads in Africa and Latin America, where China has been more successful.

With most Brics members coming from developing economies, Kugelman says the expanded grouping gives India an opportunity to deepen ties with countries such as Ethiopia, Brazil and Indonesia and build a stronger profile across Africa and Latin America.

For Delhi, the test will be whether it can secure a consensus statement - often seen as a measure of a host nation's diplomatic success. That will be difficult given sharp differences over the Iran war, relations with the US and the future of global trade.

The scale of the challenge was evident in May, when Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement after their summit because of differences over the Iran war, leaving host India to issue a chair's summary instead.
India will take confidence from its experience as G20 host in 2023, when it managed to secure a joint declaration despite deep divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine.

But Delhi will also want substantive announcements and to highlight what Brics has already achieved. On this, members are likely to agree: none will want the grouping dismissed as merely a "talk shop".

Leaders are expected to explore ways to strengthen financial cooperation and may make substantive announcements. They are also likely to address major geopolitical developments, with any language on the US is expected to be carefully crafted to avoid confrontation.
Washington, for its part, will be watching closely.

The summit will also provide the setting for several important bilateral meetings. Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday will be keenly watched. The two countries have been slowly rebuilding ties, although progress has been more cautious than either side might have hoped.
Modi is also due to meet President Vladimir Putin, with the war in Ukraine likely to feature prominently in their discussions.

Modi made a highly public appeal for peace when he met Putin last month on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek. While some interpreted his remarks as a rebuke to Moscow, Russia did not see them that way and publicly welcomed Modi's efforts.
Beyond geopolitics, India's growing trade deficit with both Russia and China is also likely to feature in the bilateral discussions.
But in the end, the group's focus will be on concluding a successful summit as it would add further weight to Brics' influence.
And for host India, it would also be a diplomatic and geopolitical achievement at a time when Delhi is seeking to reassert its international influence.
Kugelman says the stakes are particularly high for India at this summit.
Delhi, he argues, has been somewhat overshadowed by Pakistan's recent diplomatic role in the Middle East, including its involvement in mediation efforts around the Iran war.
"This is an important opportunity for India to reassert its global significance and its global leadership," he says. "That is one reason why the stakes are high."
The summit, he adds, is in some ways "more important for India as host than it is for the Brics grouping as a whole".

blocks.text: Live

Polling suggests the far-right AfD is carrying its momentum into another upcoming state election. Meanwhile, former Chancellor Angela Merkel has urged people not to take democracy for granted. DW has more.

blocks.caption: The AfD is leading opinion polls just over a week ahead of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state electionImage: Frank Hormann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is three points ahead in a new poll for the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
The poll comes after the AfD thrashed the center-right CDU in Saxony-Anhalt's state election
Former Chancellor Angela Merkel has warned that truth and lies are increasingly being blurred, including by people in power
Merkel acknowledged that some decisions during her time as chancellor helped fuel support for the AfD

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, September 11, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
September 11, 2026
Merkel: 'There is no free lunch' for democracy

blocks.caption: Merkel has rarely made public appearances since leaving office in 2021Image: Jens Krick/Flashpic/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has urged people to actively defend democracy and freedom, warning that democratic principles cannot be taken for granted.
"There's no free lunch — nothing comes for free," Merkel told around 1,200 people at a reading from her memoir "Freedom" in Peenemünde on the Baltic Sea island of Usedom.
"You are getting a small assignment too," the former leader of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) told the audience.
Merkel read from a passage in her book in which she argues that truth and lies are increasingly being deliberately blurred, including by people in positions of power in democratic countries.
"Freedom needs democratic conditions. Without democracy, there is no freedom," Merkel said.
She urged people to defend democratic institutions against those who threaten them.
"If we want to live in freedom, we have to defend our democracy against those who threaten it," Merkel said.
She added that this could succeed "if we work together, if we get involved together, each of us individually and all of us for one another."

Merkel acknowledged that some of the decisions made during her time in office had contributed to support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), including her response to the 2015 refugee crisis and her policies during the eurozone debt crisis.

articles.title: Hong Kong Tiananmen activists jailed for up to 7 years
articles.summary: Three pro-democracy activists who organized annual commemorations of China's deadly 1989 Tiananmen crackdown were charged under Hong Kong's Beijing-backed national security law.

image.caption: Vigils commemorating Tiananmen massacre are essentially outlawed under Hong Kong's security laws [FILE JUNE 2021]Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Hong Kong court on Friday sentenced three pro-democracy activists who organized annual vigils marking China's deadly 1989 Tiananmen crackdown to between five and seven years in prison under the city's national security law.
The sentences handed down were:

items: Lee Cheuk-yan, 69 — seven years
Chow Hang-tung, 41 — seven years and three months.
Albert Ho, 74, — five years and two months, after pleading guilty

blocks.text: The three were convicted in August of "incitement to subversion" over their activities with the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, which received a fine of HK$1.5 million ($191,304, €164,768). The alliance had organized annual Tiananmen vigils in Victoria Park.
Defendants deny charges
Judges cited the group's call to "end one-party dictatorship," saying it challenged the legitimacy of Communist Party rule in the Chinese special administrative region.

blocks.caption: Lee Cheuk-yan, Chow Hang-tung and Albert Ho were charged under Hong Kong's controversial national security lawImage: Peter Parks/Anthony Wallace/AFP

blocks.text: Lee and Chow denied the subversion charges under Hong Kong's controversial national security law. The defendants also insisted the alliance had not asked people to do anything illegal.

The court rejected arguments that the defendants believed they were acting within the law given Hong ​Kong's freedoms of speech, which have been severely curtailed since Beijing imposed the law in 2020 following a crackdown mass pro-democracy protests the previous year.
The vigils, once a major annual event in Hong Kong, have been effectively banned under the law.
Chow, a barrister who represented herself, raised both arms and waved at supporters as she was escorted out.
Her mother, Medina Chow, addressed her supporters saying, "For today's verdict, you do not need to be overly saddened. Do not lose heart. And above all, do not ​feel guilty."

blocks.caption: Chow told a hearing last month that she had 'nothing to repent for' [FILE: June 5, 2021]Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the international reaction?
The convictions have drawn criticism from foreign governments and rights groups.

"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks.
Germany and France last month had condemned the verdict against Chow saying that "peaceful advocacy for human rights does not constitute a crime."
Chow was the recipient of Franco-German Human Rights Award in 2023.
Among those arrested under the security law are pro-democracy former media tycoon Jimmy Lai and former student leader Joshua Wong.
Hong Kong activist pleads guilty to foreign collusion
