articles.title: Magyar vs. Moscow: Hungary toughens stance toward Russia
articles.summary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar has abruptly ended the era of his predecessor's warm relations with Russia: Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats. The Kremlin is considering halting gas supplies in…

image.caption: The close and friendly ties between Hungary and Russia ended when Peter Magyar became prime minister earlier this yearImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: While Viktor Orban was in power, no other EU member state was as pro-Russia as Hungary. Indeed, the prime minister's apparent eagerness to be of service to the Russian president earned him the nickname "Putin's pinscher" or "Kremlin agent."
For years, Hungary was seen as a security risk both in the EU and NATO. Russian spies were able to operate in the country largely unhindered for a long time.
In February, it came to light that Peter Szijjarto, Orban's foreign minister from 2014 to 2026, had passed on confidential information from EU meetings to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
All this came to an end in May, when the government headed by Peter Magyar took office.
An unambiguous signal to Russia
In a clear departure from the government line under Orban, Hungary's new prime minister has already heavily criticized Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine several times.
The government also recently declared Russia a threat to Hungary's national security.

This week, it took its biggest step yet against the Kremlin, expelling 10 Russian diplomats for engaging in activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," as announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban (no relation to the former prime minister).

blocks.caption: Foreign Minister Orban announced this week that Hungary was expelling 10 Russian embassy staff for activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention"Image: Daniel Vogl/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Although Orban did not provide any more details, the phrase is generally understood to mean that the diplomats in question were spies.

Orban said the decision "protects Hungary's security and sovereignty." She added: "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules."
Restoring old alliances

The minister's brief announcement immediately generated a huge number of headlines and comments — hardly surprising given that this was not only evidence of a 180-degree turn on the government's policy toward Russia but also one of the toughest diplomatic sanctions targeting Moscow since the collapse of communism in 1989/1990.

Speaking to Hungarian news website Index, secret service expert Peter Tarjani said this was "not a diplomatic conflict, but a serious secret service matter" and that with this decision, Hungary was simultaneously returning "to the mainstream of its allies' security policy."

Political scientist and leading Hungarian Russia expert Andras Racz told the Hungarian national news agency MTI that Hungary was the only EU and NATO member not to have made such an expulsion in recent years.
Racz said such a step "should really have been taken four and ahalf years ago." He added: "Hungary is now settling its old debt with its allies."
Reliance on Russian gas?
Under Viktor Orban, Hungary was the only EU country never to unreservedly condemn Russia's all-out war against Ukraine.
Indeed, during the final two years of his rule, Orban even blamed Ukraine and the West for Russia's aggression.

blocks.caption: The Russian Embassy in BudapestImage: Aled Betts/cc-by/Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text: But long before that — even after he came to power back in 2010 — Viktor Orban took a markedly pro-Russian line, which he justified, among other things, with the claim that Hungary was more dependent on Russian energy supplies than almost any other country in the region.

His government's repeated assertion that Russian gas was cheaper has long been disproved. What's more, the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant with Russian support will cost Hungary dearly for decades to come.
In the light of all this, Orban's close ties to Russia remain a mystery.
Absurd situations

For Hungary, this closeness to Russia often led to absurd situations in which the country's national security was put at risk. At the same time, Orban repeatedly told his critics that it was they who were a threat to Hungary's sovereignty.
For example, Russian secret service agents for years took part in military-style training exercises in the far-right scene right up until 2016.

Starting in 2012, Russian secret service operatives for years stole huge amounts of data from the Hungarian Foreign Ministry and other Hungarian authorities without the government ever publicly condemning it.

In 2019, Russia got permission to move the headquarters of the International Investment Bank (IIB) to Budapest. The IIB was known as the "spy bank" because its leadership was made up of individuals linked to or associated with Russia's FSB intelligence service. It was only after the US imposed sanctions on the bank in 2023 that it left Hungary again.

Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has warned multiple times in recent years that Hungary had become a "logistical center and deployment zone for Russian secret services," thereby putting the whole region at risk.
Rejection of Orban's pro-Russian course
Orban's strictly pro-Russian course was laterally rejected by many Hungarians.

blocks.caption: Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban (left, pictured here with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2025) maintained close ties with Russia while he was in powerImage: Alexander Nemenov/Pool/AFP

blocks.text: The decidedly pro-European and pro-Western orientation of Peter Magyar and his Tisza party had a considerable role to play in their election victory earlier this year. The EU flag was often seen and spontaneous cries of "Russians, go home" often heard at election rallies last spring.

Unlike Viktor Orban, Magyar and leading politicians in his Tisza party are convinced that Hungary's place is exclusively in Europe and that the country should only maintain pragmatic, low-level relations with Russia.
Nevertheless, many observers and experts are surprised at how radically the Magyar government has turned away from Russia.

Andras Telkes, the former deputy head of Hungary's foreign intelligence service (IH), wrote in the newspaper Nepszava that the expulsion of diplomats shows that the presence of Russian secret services in Hungary obviously runs "very deep" and that the country has a serious problem.
Telkes says that the expulsion of 10 diplomats will help rebuild trust in Hungary in the eyes of the secret services of its NATO allies.
At the same time, he emphasizes the scale of the move: "Expelling two or three people would have been a sign. Expelling 10 people already means war."
Telkes went on to say that the move creates a serious security problem for Hungary.
Will Moscow turn off the taps?

The spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry condemned the expulsion of Russian diplomats in unusually strong terms: She spoke of a "Russophobe lobby in Budapest" and announced a "hard and painful" response.
Russian lawmaker Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma's Defense Committee, said that halting gas supplies to Hungary would have to be considered.

Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban knows more about such Russian threats than anyone else in the new Hungarian government: She wrote her doctoral thesis in 2007 on Russia's energy policy in Central Europe. A year later, she published a book entitled "Power, Energy, and the New Russian Imperialism."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
articles.summary: The revelations in Anthropic's threat intelligence report come after a former top researcher at the company warned of the risks of AI to humanity.

blocks.text: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.

The findings, made in the firm's recent threat intelligence report, is the latest in a growing series of warnings from AI researchers and industry insiders about the technology's potential risks to humanity.
The warnings have prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.
President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".
The company published its latest threat intelligence report, external on Thursday. Other AI firms publish similar reports.

This includes Google, which wrote on Tuesday, external a person had attempted to use its AI tool Gemini to obtain a "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".
Anthropic's AI model Claude was also used by actors linked to a Russia-based cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to Anthropic's report.
The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.
Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities.
The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology.
"Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.

None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.

As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.
The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".
Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said.
"The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.
Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times, external it was "an incredibly nuanced situation".
"You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" he said.

The report also noted six cases where Claude was used "to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them".
The report indicated that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers have increasingly used its technology to assist their operations.
Hacking group ShinyHunters, as well as China-based labs, were among those named in the report.

The report also said that a hacking group whose work is consistent with the Russia-based Midnight Blizzard allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote code until it evaded detection.
The California-based company said it had incorporated its findings into its processes "to better prevent, detect, and disrupt these activities in the future".
Anthropic said it had shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate.

The report - the company's first this year - comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
In an article published on 6 September, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for the industry to implement "voluntary slowdowns" until safeguards are set.

"I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Pachocki said, adding that OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, will continue its work on building safeguards, though broader interventions are required.

The warning prompted an open letter to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI and a call for governments to collaborate about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.
In the US, Democratic lawmaker Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to ban AI superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development.
"When scientists tell you there is a chance, a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he said on Thursday on BBC's Newsnight.
With additional reporting from Osmond Chia.

articles.title: Jean Chrétien says ‘we bow to no one’ in stirring 9/11 speech in Gander, N.L.

image.caption: Former Prime Minister Jean Chrétien received multiple standing ovations during his speech in Gander. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien drew thunderous applause on Friday during a fiery and patriotic speech in Gander, N.L, where many had gathered at a sports arena to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks
'Never mistake our kindness for softness,' former PM says
'Never mistake our generosity for weakness,' Chrétien says at 9/11 memorial

Former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien drew thunderous applause on Friday during a fiery and patriotic speech in Gander, N.L., where many had gathered at a sports arena to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and the legendary humanitarian response as thousands of stranded air travellers had their flights diverted to more than a dozen Canadian airports.

Chrétien was the final speaker during a lengthy and nationally televised event. He began his speech by describing Sept. 11, 2001 "like a nightmare … one that can never be erased." And then recounted how Canadians stepped up, fought side-by-side with U.S. troops in Afghanistan — which drew loud applause.
But then, Chrétien's became the first person to speak on a subject no one else who stepped to the microphone would: the fractured political relationship between Canada and the United States.
"We bow to no one," Chrétien said to an audience that included Pete Hoesktra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada.
"And the more we are insulted or threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united."

items: We can make a difference in a 'sometimes broken world,' says Gander mayor at 9/11 ceremony
One woman survived 9/11. Another helped out in Gander. Now they’re as close as sisters

blocks.text: It was a powerful moment in an two-hour event filled with stories of remembrance, honour and sacrifice.
Trade war ongoing

U.S. President Donald Trump initiated a trade war with Canada, and has hurled insults at Prime Minister Mark Carney. Trump has also threatened Canada’s sovereignty by expressing his desire to make Canada’s the 51st U.S. state.
Hoesktra has amplified the rhetoric through his own public comments and by sharing Trump’s social media posts.

Hoesktra avoided the issue of trade and tariffs during his visit to Gander, and praised the longstanding partnership between the two countries. He offered thanks for the kindness and compassion shown to thousands of stranded American travellers in the wake of the terrorist attacks.

"This is to say one more time, thank you," he said, when asked about his visit to the central Newfoundland town. "We’ll get back to the economic issues from, at least our standpoint, when we get past 9/11."
Chrétien, 92, described the U.S. as a "neighbour and our closest friend," and said a massive rally in Ottawa in the days after the 9/11 attacks was "one of the most emotional moments of my life."

Chrétien’s government initiated the process in 2001 to invoke the so-called Article 5, which stipulates that an attack on one member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is an attack on all members.
Chrétien also ordered Canadian troops into battle in Afghanistan, fighting alongside U.S. allies, and 158 of those soldiers were killed, including 13 from Newfoundland and Labrador.
"Our friends were hurt, and we were hurting with them," Chrétien said. "I was proud of how we stepped up."
He described the response to 9/11 as "the Canadian way."
But 25 years later, the world has changed, and Canada’s relationship with its powerful southern neighbour has also grown more distant.
So Chrétien concluded his speech — which received no less than three standing ovations — with a strong message "to our American friends."
He said Canada is an open, generous country, and the response to 9/11 in communities such as Gander is an example of this. But he said Canada’s generosity should not be mistaken for weakness.
"Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never mistake our kindness for softness. We know who we are and we are proud of it," he said.
Chrétien said building a country like Canada, welcoming people from around the globe, and caring for the weakest, "is a sign of strength."
Chrétien said his "honest" message was "from one friend to another," and he called on the U.S. to "respect the friendship" and "be a good neighbour."
He concluded with the following words in French: "Long live the United States and long live Canada."

articles.title: Inside the New York lab using genetic genealogy to identify 9/11 victims’ remains
articles.summary: Forty per cent of the 2,753 people who died at Ground Zero on 9/11 have not had their remains identified, including approximately 10 of the 24 Canadian victims. Last month, the lab announced it made…

image.caption: Monica Iken-Murphy had only been married to her husband Michael Iken for 11 months when he died in the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center. (Submitted by Monica Iken-Murphy)

blocks.text: This lab is still trying to identify 9/11 victims. Not everyone wants to know
Inside a lab in Manhattan, forensic scientists in white lab coats are still diligently working to keep a promise made 25 years ago.

They're extracting DNA from thousands of pieces of human remains recovered following the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, trying to match them to samples from toothbrushes, razors and other sources provided by family members of victims.
What has changed is the science they're using to draw out the DNA from the remains, and the evolving forensic investigative techniques that didn't exist in 2001.

"When … after years of pushing that science, you're finally able to figure out who it is and return that loved one to their family … that's powerful," said Mark Desire, assistant director of forensic biology at the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.
Forty per cent of the 2,753 people who died at Ground Zero have not had their remains identified, including approximately 10 of the 24 Canadian victims.
Last month, the lab announced it made its first identification of previously unknown remains using a breakthrough technique.
The woman's family chose to keep her name private. It's the first identification the lab has made in a year.
The technique combines DNA testing with genetic genealogy — which uses family tree research conducted by members of the New York City Police Department.
"I think it is sort of a new frontier," said Dr. Jason Graham, New York's Chief Medical Examiner.
"We had really found a breakthrough innovation that's going to open the door, I hope and I believe, likely to many other identifications."

items: Sharing story of 9/11 'only way I can survive,' says first responder visiting Gander
How Gander, N.L., took care of ‘the plane people’ on 9/11

blocks.text: For Monica Iken-Murphy, whose husband Michael Iken died in the collapse of the south tower where he worked as a bond trader, this development brings renewed hope.
"I didn't get a ring, I didn't get an ID. People got cards. They found papers with their names on it," she said. But for her, "it's like he went to work and that's it. Nothing."
Challenges of excavating, preserving remains

Desire was a rookie scientist in the New York crime lab back on Sept. 11, 2001, and was sent to the scene to preserve evidence soon after the second tower was hit. He had never worked on a mass fatality before.
"One of the … first victims I saw die that day landed right in front of us."
Soon after Desire and his colleague arrived, he heard a sound he described as a "crack," and he realized they were far too close to the south tower as it began to collapse.

items: Trump's 9/11 statements come under scrutiny again
Amid trade tensions, Americans visiting Gander for 9/11 distance themselves from their president

blocks.text: He sprinted toward a nearby building to take cover and barely made it in time. Debris fell on him just as he was escaping into the building through a broken window.
"It just fell across my legs, shattered my foot — the most violent moment of my life."
He survived, and made it his mission to keep the promise made by then-chief medical examiner Dr. Charles Hirsch to preserve and identify the remains of all the victims.
The World Trade Center was reduced to a 21-metre hill of debris that for visual reference, if spread out, could cover approximately eight city blocks.
Plans were made to excavate debris from the site and move it for sifting and sorting at a landfill site on Staten Island in hopes of preserving whatever remains they could.

"Everything that destroys DNA was present at Ground Zero: the fire, the water to put out the fire, the jet fuel, the diesel fuel, the chemicals in the building, the chemicals on the ground, sunlight, mold, bacteria," said Desire.

items: 'We'll never be able to finish this project': the difficulty of IDing 9/11 victims
Reporting on 9/11: The day the world changed

blocks.text: Excavation work officially ended in 2002, but scientists continued to search for DNA in the remains they had.
Four years later, more debris was found on the roof of a nearby Deutsche Bank building, where more than 700 bone fragments were recovered.
That led to reopening searches in the area that lasted until 2014, leading to approximately 2,000 additional bone fragments being recovered.
At first, the remains were preserved by freezing them.
Later, as best practices for handling remains for forensic purposes changed, they began drying the bone fragments out to preserve them longer.
Nearly 22,000 pieces of human remains have been recovered since 2001.
The science behind identifying remains
During the early years, victims were identified using fingerprints, dental records and what was then considered cutting-edge DNA technology.
Since then, science has advanced such that more DNA can be extracted from bone fragments. But it still hasn't advanced far enough.
Bone, Desire says, is the toughest material to get DNA from.
"Blood and hair and skin cells — easy. Bone … you have to pulverize it."
He says thousands of samples that still need to be identified haven't even had DNA extracted because they're so badly burned.
Inside the lab working to identify 9/11 victims

One of the challenges scientists face is whether to keep testing a sample. Each time remains are tested, some of the material is consumed and can't be re-tested. Doing too many tests on one sample risks losing it altogether before a match can be made.
"It's very stressful, because we have remains today that we've tried 10, 15 times over the years," said Desire.
That's why this new technique brings so much hope.
The process involves sending DNA from unidentified remains to an outside lab that can generate a whole genomic sequence.

Then, similar to genealogical methods that have been used to generate new leads in cold cases, New York police conduct family tree searches. If a prospective match is found, it would come back to the medical examiner's office to confirm a relation through DNA testing.

items: Genetic genealogy is cracking cases once thought unsolvable. Not all police forces can afford to use it
5 Canadian cold cases solved with help of genetic genealogy

blocks.text: Desire noted that there were 47 sets of remains for which they have full DNA profiles that don't match any of the 17,000 reference samples provided by family members.
So the individuals may have relatives that never contacted the lab or provided samples.
"Using genealogy to help identify them, that was an excellent next step."
The chief medical examiner's office is renewing its call to families to provide samples — in hopes it can help make more matches.
Families face tough decisions
Despite the lab's ongoing work, many families of victims whose remains have never been found don't want to know if a match is made.
"That can be very traumatic," said Jennifer Odein, the World Trade Center anthropologist at the New York City Medical Examiner's Office.
She is the direct line between families and the lab, and says some families are contacted multiple times because their loved one has been matched multiple times to their remains.
"And if they've already had phone calls in the past they might have said, 'OK, we've had enough, we've had our ceremony … we're OK with not getting the notification.'

items: U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to visit Newfoundland for 25th anniversary of 9/11
Canada-U.S. ties 'so much stronger' than trade war divisions, Manitoba premier says ahead of 9/11 anniversary

blocks.text: Long ago, Abigail Carter, a Canadian expat whose husband Arron Dack died while attending a trade show at Windows on the World in the north tower, decided she didn't need to know if his remains were ever found.
"I know he was there," said Carter. "He called me and that was good enough for me."
She has found her own way to honour him.
Canadian recalls losing her husband on 9/11

At their daughter's wedding this past summer in France, where Carter now owns a chateau, they placed a framed photo of Dack on a chair, and later added a martini — shaken, not stirred, just as he liked it — to make sure his presence was felt.
"He was very funny and very charismatic. He had different personas a little bit. He had a very, very silly, silly side," she said.

Iken-Murphy understands that complexity of grief. She hopes that one day, her husband Michael's remains will be matched to samples provided to the lab, but says she wouldn't want to keep them herself.
"I want to remember Michael as a whole human. With his beautiful face and his blue eyes and his smile."
Instead, she says they'll stay at the repository in the 9/11 Memorial and Museum at Ground Zero where all the unidentified remains are stored by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

articles.title: Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
articles.summary: CBC News readers, viewers and listeners have been sending in questions about the trade war, often asking how Canada can turn up the heat on the U.S.

image.caption: Boats sit idle in Lake Ontario close to the Welland Canal on Oct. 26, 2023. (Tara Walton/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
CBC News readers, viewers and listeners have been sending in questions about the trade war, often asking how Canada can turn up the heat on the U.S.
CBC News answers your questions about export taxes, sales bans and toilet paper
Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That

Reading through the emails that readers send to CBC News, one gets the impression they don't want just "elbows up" in the Canada-U.S. trade war, but also sticks, knees, skates and whatever else might be lying around.
One of the most common questions is some variation of, "Why isn't Canada doing X?" — where X is a tactic or tariff the reader supposes will hit the U.S. where it hurts.
Here's a look at some of those suggestions and what key players or observers have had to say about them.
Why doesn't Canada put export duties on energy as the cost is borne by Americans not Canadians?

Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, told CBC News late last month that export taxes are an option. Former prime minister Jean Chrétien said this week that an export tax on oil, gas, electricity and potash might be needed.
In 2025, Canadian commodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81 per cent of imported electricity, 99 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.

However, Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa, warned that the long-term effects of such a move could be severe for Canada, both through lost revenue and damage to the relationship with its biggest customer. The U.S. could respond much as Canada has to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs: by trying to diversify away from a partner it can no longer count on and finding new suppliers.

items: Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs

blocks.text: University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe and Christopher Ragan, founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy, made the same point separately: targeting U.S. energy could play into the hands of the U.S. administration and unite Americans against Canada.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said in July he doesn't "see the value" in using energy exports as a bargaining chip. Carney said being a reliable supplier is important.
"Canadians are reliable. Canadians can be trusted," he said.
Why not ban sales of certain goods in Canada?
This has mostly already happened at a provincial level with alcohol, in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan this week added a retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol.
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has shown no interest in that sort of approach, stressing that Canada's response will be proportionate, strategic and targeted.

items: Poilievre tells U.S. TV Canadians are 'wounded' and 'confused' to be in America's crosshairs
Trade war, Alberta referendum loom large as Carney charts cabinet's year forward

blocks.text: The U.S. may, of course, reply in kind to any ban, as it has with alcohol: Most imports of Canadian-made alcohol will be banned from the United States on Sept. 29.

Tombe, discussing tariffs, told CBC News late last month that Canada has to be careful when selecting products to target because they need to be items Canadians can replace relatively easily but Americans cannot.

If tariffs are applied to harder-to-replace items — "a particular type of circuit board, say, or piece of machinery," that merely complicates life and increases costs for the Canadian importer, Tombe said.
Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war?
Can Canada stop U.S. ships using the Welland Canal?

The Welland Canal is on the western half of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which connects the St. Lawrence River to the Great Lakes. The canal links Lake Ontario to Lake Erie using eight locks, all in Ontario, that can be filled with water or drained to move vessels between different water levels.
But the seaway is overseen by both the U.S. and Canada.
The Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation administers the seaway on the American side as a federal agency within the U.S. Department of Transportation.
In Canada, the federal government owns the Canadian portion of the seaway, but it is managed by the non-profit St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation.
The U.S. also controls several important locks, including ones in New York state between Lake Ontario and Montreal and others in Michigan that connect Lake Superior and Lake Huron.

John Boscariol, a Toronto-based co-head of international trade and investment law at the Canadian law firm McCarthy Tétrault, told CHCH News in Hamilton that closing the canal would be "shooting ourselves in the foot" and would hurt Canadian businesses just as much as U.S. businesses.

Trump critic Jennifer Hillman, formerly general counsel at the Office of the United States Trade Representative under then-president Bill Clinton, told CBC News Network it would "absolutely be a total violation of international law, and I think not really a good idea because you're blocking both sides' goods.
"I would hope that's not a road anybody would go down."
What questions do you have about the latest tariffs? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC's Peter Zimonjic, Darren Major and Evan Dyer and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Dutch tour bus overturns in Switzerland, several people dead, police say
articles.summary: GENEVA — A Dutch tour bus overturned in eastern Switzerland in a serious accident that left several people dead and others injured, police said. The bus overturned Thursday afternoon between the…

blocks.text: GENEVA — A Dutch tour bus overturned in eastern Switzerland in a serious accident that left several people dead and others injured, police said.

The bus overturned Thursday afternoon between the villages of Susch and Zernez in the Alpine canton of Graubuenden, and rescue teams were responding to the scene, authorities said. The police did not specify the number of dead and injured.
According to Swiss media, 48 people were on the bus. A spokeswoman for ANVR, a Dutch travel industry association, told the Blick newspaper that the passengers were Dutch.
A police spokesman said the coach collided with the crash barrier and then overturned. No other vehicles were believed to be involved.

Oad, a travel agency behind the trip, said in a statement in Dutch that it was “deeply shocked and devastated by the tragic bus accident” and its thoughts were with those involved and their loved ones.

The Dutch Foreign Ministry said it was too early to know the number of victims. Swiss President Guy Parmelin, writing on X, vowed that Swiss authorities would ensure a “comprehensive and thorough investigation” of the case.
Several ambulances and five helicopters were deployed to the location, according to Swiss media./dp

articles.title: ‘Magnitude slowly hit’: 9/11 remembered 25 years on
articles.summary: CANBERRA, Australia – A political reporter has recounted being in Washington with an ex-prime minister a quarter of a century ago when terrorist attacks on the US changed the world. What should have…

blocks.text: CANBERRA, Australia – A political reporter has recounted being in Washington with an ex-prime minister a quarter of a century ago when terrorist attacks on the US changed the world.
What should have been a routine international trip with the prime minister quickly devolved into chaos and the start of a new era of global paranoia.

James Grubel was AAP’s chief political reporter covering then-prime minister John Howard’s first meeting with then-US president George W Bush in Washington DC for the 50th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty.
Day one of the visit had gone smoothly.
Day two was to start with a press conference before the prime minister was to deliver a speech later in the day.
News of two planes striking the World Trade Centre in New York had reached the press pack in Washington moments before Mr Howard spoke to the media.
“It had become a little bit more obvious that this was a serious event,” Grubel told AAP.
“The prime minister gave his condolences. And still, at that stage, we were thinking the day was going to go ahead as as normal.”
But as the curtains were opened in the Willard Hotel at the close of the press conference, smoke was billowing from across the Potomac River.
A third plane had struck the Pentagon just 5km away.
The gathered journalists were forced to evacuate, walking one mile down the road to the Australian embassy as thousands of people scrambled to get out of the city.
“The whole of Washington was in gridlock,” Grubel said.
“There were armed police and soldiers on the corners … I think every building in Washington and everybody was evacuating.
“It was a totally different city to the one that we’d been wandering around in for the past couple days.”
The mood in the Australian embassy was sombre according to Mr Grubel as journalists continued writing for the media back home.

“The magnitude of this awful event slowly, slowly hit, and you had to occasionally stop yourself and just focus on what you were doing and try and put it out of your mind so you could write about it clearly.
“Otherwise, you’d kind of get a bit caught up in it.It was very unclear whether there were going to also be attacks on on London, on Paris and Sydney, on Canberra.”
Ten Australians were among the almost 3000 people who died when al-Qaeda militants hijacked four planes on September 11, 2001.
The hijackers flew two planes into the twin towers at the World Trade Centre in New York and one into the Pentagon just outside of Washington.
The fourth plane crashed into a field in rural Pennsylvania.
John Howard decided to invoke the ANZUS treaty three days later on the advice of his foreign minister. If the United States was under attack, Australia had an obligation to send troops.
It’s a poignant end to an event which Mr Grubel says has rippled out to the present day.
“Now with AUKUS, we’re still going through these issues and these debates about our national security,” he said.
The shift in political rhetoric to security and defence bolstered support for the Liberal government heading into the 2001 federal election which it ultimately won.
A quarter of a century on, Mr Howard said the lesson to be learnt was in being vigilant to the world around us.
“We must be alive to the threats that face us but not live in constant fear,” Mr Howard said in a statement.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who was a Labor backbencher at the time of the attack, said it remained a harrowing anniversary a quarter of a century on.
“Alongside the many Americans who lost their lives, were people from nations across the world, 10 Australians among them,” Mr Albanese told the parliament on Thursday.
“America was shaken to its core, but it did not yield. It did not break.”/dp

articles.title: Princess Diana's 'revenge dress' goes up for auction
articles.summary: Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to $300,000 (£220,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December.

blocks.text: A dress worn by Princess Diana to a party in London hours after a documentary was televised in which the then-Prince Charles admitted to committing adultery during their marriage is going up for auction.
Her dramatic arrival at the Serpentine Gallery in 1994 in a custom-made black silk evening dress by designer Christina Stambolian became an iconic pop-culture moment.
The media dubbed her outfit the "revenge dress".
Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to $300,000 (£220,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December.
A press release from Sotheby's said it is the first time the dress has been offered at auction since 1997, when the late princess sold 79 of her dresses to raise money for charities.
Morgane Halimi, Sotheby's Global Head of Handbags and Fashion, said in a statement that Princess Diana "understood instinctively" that fashion can be a language in its own right.
"On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life," Halimi said.
"She walked into a moment in which so much of her story was being told for her and, through what she chose to wear, reclaimed the narrative for herself."

articles.title: Philippine rescuers board ferry 40 hours after blaze began
articles.summary: Thick, toxic fumes and extreme temperatures pose a challenge to rescuers who have boarded the ship.

blocks.text: They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said.
"The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the ship [as] there is still a visible, thick smoke," the coastguard's spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab told the BBC earlier.
"No matter how we try to push through, high temperatures and toxic smoke remain a severe risk to our personnel," she told local media earlier.
Smoke resulting from incomplete burning contains dense, lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide.

Earlier, authorities reported that 86 were still unaccounted for, but as of Friday morning, the figure stood at 84 – two passengers whose names were on the ship's manifest did not go onboard, authorities say.

Rescuers have widened their search area, Cayabyab says, adding that the coastguard has deployed one of its largest ships and done radio broadcasts to vessels in the area. The search teams are also accompanied by divers and nurses.
A local diver in Coron told the BBC on Friday that he and his team were on standby to help out and awaiting instructions from the coast guard.
The coast guard also conducted an aerial survey of waters near the disaster site.
The plan is to resume firefighting efforts, first from the cargo hold of the ferry, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, Cayabyab said.
Earlier, the coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that was where the fire started. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.
A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat had described the frantic cries on board the passenger-cargo vessel when the fire erupted on Wednesday evening.
Roland Lerma recalled falling while scrambling to get off the burning boat.
"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," the 30-year-old told the BBC.

He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea. Lerma said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.
"It was cold [in the sea] If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," he said.
The ferry, which set off from Manila, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, in the province of Palawan, when it caught fire.
The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.
Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.
"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

articles.title: Spies, strategies and missed opportunities: How the lessons of 9/11 are still being learnt
articles.summary: Twenty-five years on, the attacks have come to define a generation of foreign, security and intelligence policy, the BBC's security correspondent writes.

blocks.text: ByFrank Gardner
Security correspondent

The first duty of a government, countless leaders over the decades have said, is to safeguard its population. On 11 September 2001 the US manifestly failed to do that. The intelligence was there, yet tragically, nobody joined up the dots in time.
9/11, as the attacks on the US became known, came to define – along with the response – a generation of foreign, security and intelligence policy for the first two decades of this century.

On 11 September 2001, as al-Qaeda's suicide pilots flew those hijacked planes into the World Trade Center, I was just finishing a deployment in our Middle East bureau. As a Palestinian taxi driver drove me through the pine-clad hills west of Jerusalem to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport he suddenly turned up the car's radio. "Something big has happened in America," he said. He wasn't exaggerating. 2,977 victims died that day.

The attacks did not come out of nowhere. The CIA had been aware of the al-Qaeda network and its exiled Saudi leader, Osama Bin Laden, for years prior to 2001. It even had a taskforce dedicated to hunting him down.
Nine days after the 11 September attacks, then US President George W Bush declared the "War on Terror".

In the ensuing 25 years there have been numerous intelligence successes as well as failures on both sides of the Atlantic. The successes include plots that have been foiled, suspects who have been arrested, brought to trial, convicted and jailed.
But what of the bigger picture? How has intelligence-gathering, counter-terrorism and strategic planning changed in the 25 years since the worst terrorist attack in US history?

blocks.caption: Image caption, George W Bush was in a school in Florida when the attacks happened

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
George W Bush was in a school in Florida when the attacks happened
A colossal intelligence failure

No one can question that 9/11 was a colossal intelligence failure, or to be more specific, a failure of imagination in the US intelligence community. At the time both the CIA and the FBI were in possession of information which, if shared properly, could have prevented what happened.

The 9/11 Commission Report that followed blamed "failures of imagination, policy, capabilities and management" on the US government. The CIA and FBI, the report concluded, failed to properly assess intelligence and share information with each other and take sufficient steps to disrupt the plot.

This most basic of lessons has since been largely – although not completely – learnt, and sharing between Western intelligence agencies is infinitely better than it was in 2001. The old rivalries between say, MI5 and Police Counter Terrorism have dissolved, first with regional 'fusion centres' dotted around the UK and now, most recently, with the establishment of the high-security Counter Terrorism Operations Centre in London. Here MI5 intelligence officers might find themselves sitting literally right next to police officers whose job it is to take the executive action to stop a terrorist plot. Equally, they might find themselves sitting next to a US federal agent from the FBI or a language specialist seconded from GCHQ.

Since 9/11, there has also been a root-and-branch reorganisation of US intelligence with the establishment of a National Counter Terrorism Center just outside Washington DC and a Director of National Intelligence to ensure that information is shared where it needs to be between the 18 separate US intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and its UK counterpart, the Secret Intelligence Service (better known as MI6) is perhaps the closest one in the world. This is supplemented by the Five Eyes alliance that pools intelligence between the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Yet disastrous failures of intelligence, assessment and strategic planning have still occurred since the planes hit the Twin Towers. In the run-up to the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, MI6 unwisely allowed its intelligence to be politicised, leading to the organisation suffering its worst reputational setback since the days of betrayal by the double agent Kim Philby and other Soviet moles in the 1950s and 60s.

blocks.caption: Image caption, MI6 was roiled by an intelligence scandal

blocks.text: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
MI6 was roiled by an intelligence scandal

Against a backdrop of overwhelming political pressure from Washington to produce evidence that Iraq, under its President Saddam Hussein, still possessed 'Weapons of Mass Destruction' (WMDs), MI6 supplied Prime Minister Tony Blair's government with what turned out to be flawed intelligence. Iraq did indeed have WMDs in the past, but it was all destroyed after the 1991 Gulf War.

Following the Iraq invasion of 2003, MI6 then underwent a complete revamp of how it assesses the raw intelligence, known as CX, that comes in from agents in the field. Today there is a clear separation between the agent runners - whose job it is to gather that intelligence from sources in places like Iran, North Korea or from inside proscribed terrorist groups such as al-Qaeda - and the reports team, whose job is to check and challenge that intelligence, often sending it back to demand more substantiation.

"The [2003] Iraq war was based on deeply flawed intelligence," says General Sir Richard Shirreff who served in Iraq as a divisional commander. "Have we learnt from it? No, I think we're bad at learning… It was so obvious as a Commander that we were heading for strategic failure".

After the Iraq invasion an inquiry followed once again, culminating in the Butler Review. This concluded that the UK's intelligence on Iraq's alleged WMD programme "was seriously flawed and heavily reliant on unverified sources".

The Security Service, MI5, has also had its own failures, amid numerous undoubted successes, in foiling terrorist plots. "After 9/11," says Lord Jonathan Evans, who ran MI5 from 2007-2013, "the assessment was that by far the most pressing security threat to the UK was the terrorist threat from al-Qaeda and associated individuals and groups".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tony Blair joined George W Bush in the 'war on terror'

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Tony Blair joined George W Bush in the 'war on terror'

But with a database back then of more than 20,000 "Subjects of Interest" and a high number of investigations running concurrently, MI5 faced – and still does – a daily challenge of which leads to prioritise. It has not always got it right.

In 2005 it failed to prevent the 7/7 London suicide bombings that killed 52 people. The Security Service was aware of Mohammed Sidique Khan, the man who turned out to be the ringleader, but it was unaware of what he was about to carry out. The Manchester Arena bombing of 2017 was another more recent lapse.

Today the threat from terrorism has not gone away but, says Lord Evans, "the picture has changed. Non-state terrorism remains a serious concern but state threats… have become increasingly serious and are at least as severe a national security concern as non-state terrorism. These threats come, in different forms, from Russia, Iran, their proxies and from China."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The war with Iran has been seen as a strategic miscalculation

blocks.text: The war with Iran has been seen as a strategic miscalculation

It could also be argued that US President Donald Trump's decision to join Israel in attacking Iran this year was a failure of intelligence imagination. All America's allies in the Gulf knew there was a serious risk Iran would retaliate by closing off the Strait of Hormuz. The warnings were all there and yet Trump appeared to lack a counter-strategy when Iran did exactly what it had threatened to do, causing huge disruption in global energy markets.
Moral calculations

In the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 attacks there was a widespread fear that a second wave was coming. In fact al-Qaeda itself promised "a swarm of planes" that was going to attack more buildings. In the rush to pre-empt such an attack numerous human rights abuses were committed by the US and its allies. Suspects were swept up in Afghanistan or Pakistan, often on the flimsiest of tip-offs. Hundreds were flown, bound, blindfolded and wrapped in nappies, halfway across the world to a makeshift cage prison on the US naval base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where they were incarcerated without trial.
Human rights groups denounced this as a stain on the moral conscience of America.

Scandals over the abuse of prisoners in US custody in Iraq and Afghanistan have duly come to light and some of the individuals involved held to account, but critics say more senior figures escaped consequences. Nevertheless, the US still practices detention without trial at Guantanamo Bay, and when it deported more than 200 men from the US to El Salvador's controversial Terrorism Confinement Centre in 2025.

The immediate period after 9/11 had its stains on human rights for Britain too. In 2004, MI6 was complicit in the abduction and rendition of a Libyan Islamist, Abdelhakim Belhaj, and his wife from Thailand to Libya. There he spent years in prison and was tortured by Colonel Muammar Gaddafi's regime. The case eventually came to light and it resulted in a fulsome public apology delivered to Parliament by the Attorney General in 2018. Today, in-house lawyers are said to be the fastest growing department within the agencies.
Russia and China rising

"We spent the first 20 years of this century focussing almost entirely on counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency," said Sir Alex Younger, who was Chief of the Secret Intelligence Service from 2014-2020. The late MI6 Chief was speaking to me at a literary festival shortly after leaving the top job, adding: "We missed the rise of China as a military power and as a strategic challenge".
Similarly, General Shirreff wrote the political thriller "War With Russia" in 2016, in which he foresaw Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In the aftermath of 9/11 and the ensuing "War on Terror" - while Western nations were busy fighting the Taliban, ISIS or trying to sort out the messy occupation of Iraq - Russia and China embarked on colossal rearmament programmes with innovations in hypersonic missiles, for example, that have seriously eroded the military advantage once enjoyed by Nato.

"The West's mistake was not simply that it was distracted by counter-terrorism after 9/11," concurs Sam Olsen, Chief Analyst at the security intelligence firm Sibylline. "It also misunderstood the nature of China's rise, assuming that economic integration would lead to political convergence."

China, just like Iran, Russia and North Korea, is considered a "hard target" for intelligence gathering. Back in 2001, biometric data was still in its relative infancy but the subsequent use of facial, iris and gait recognition have all contributed to the considerable modern-day challenge of getting agents and agent runners across borders undetected.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China and Russia have ascended in the last two decades

blocks.text: Image source, Host Photo Agency via Getty Images
China and Russia have ascended in the last two decades
So how well – or not – does Western intelligence understand China?

Along with Russia, China today is a top intelligence target for MI6. "Western intelligence understands a great deal about China," says Sam Olsen of Sibylline. "The bigger danger is that it sees the individual pieces without always understanding what they add up to. Chinese power is no longer just about ships, missiles and troops. It increasingly lies in semiconductors, critical minerals, batteries, ports, telecommunications and industrial capacity... So the problem is often less a failure of intelligence collection than a failure of strategic interpretation".

Twenty-five years ago, on the day of the 9/11 attacks, US intelligence agents did have pieces of the jigsaw – an analogy that spies love to refer to – but collectively, they failed to fit it all together and see clearly what was coming down the tracks. It is no good having great intelligence gathering if you can't apply it for strategic gain.
A world beyond recognition

Clearly, the world of intelligence and counter-terrorism has changed almost beyond recognition in the quarter century since that cloudless blue September morning in New York. With the advent of AI and quantum computing it is only going to go on changing, and in some areas, at exponential speed.

However, in a world full of conflicting narratives and interests, Western nations do not have a monopoly when it comes to failures of intelligence, oversights or strategic miscalculations. Other noteworthy instances include Russia's disastrous full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and what some have described as Israel's "own 9/11" – the Hamas-led raid from Gaza on 7 October 2023.

Ultimately, it is in the big, strategic, national decisions that questions are still being asked. Was it right for Britain to join President Bush's invasion of Iraq? Was it right to join the US-led Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan and then abandon the country to the Taliban in a dash for the exit two decades later? These, and many other questions, continue to reverberate.

articles.title: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
articles.summary: Hong Kong used to be one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could gather to mark the 1989 crackdown.

blocks.text: Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years.
Two of the defendants - Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41 - were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law.
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January.

For years, Hong Kong was one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen Square crackdown - a topic that is highly sensitive and heavily censored in mainland China.

These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.
Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear.
Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction.
On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison.
As the court session started, Chow and Lee stood up and smiled at the public gallery, which was full of people. Ho wore a serious expression.
After their sentences were handed down, Lee appeared to pray as he was led out of the dock, while Chow blew a kiss to those seated in the public gallery.
According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power".
Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.
A key part of the trial concerned the group's slogan of "ending one-party dictatorship", which the court said had incited people to undermine the Chinese Communist Party.
Lee's wife, Elizabeth Tang, told Reuters that it was a "sad day" for her.
"I cannot imagine that he has to spend another three years in jail, it is really unacceptable," she said, adding that Lee intended to appeal his sentence.
Chow's mother Medina told a crowd outside the court not to be "overly saddened" about the verdict. "Do not lose heart. And above all, do not feel guilty," she said, Reuters reported.
Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy".
The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies.
Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.
Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.

The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout.
On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance.

"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks.
"The harsh sentences against peaceful Tiananmen vigil organisers expose the cruelty and insecurity of a government afraid of memory and the people," Human Rights Watch said in a statement.

articles.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
articles.summary: The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fears about the reliability of the US, but equally important is the need to keep gold closer to home in the…

image.caption: In an age of geopolitical unrest, more and more countries want to have easy access to their gold reservesImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where about half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security.
To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the United States as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane.

The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move about 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis.
The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness."

France also removed its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that it was not politically motivated.

blocks.caption: The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of EnglandImage: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS

blocks.text: Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves, respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns about the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy toward the European Union, including threats to annex part of Greenland.
The gold rush

Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, told DW the outright seizure of assets is an "extremely remote risk" for European central banks. However, he said, there are growing concerns about ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty.
"The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he said.

In general, said Krishnan Gopaul, of the World Gold Council, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs.

A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-tonne average over the preceding decade.

Because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign-debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset, Gopaul said.
"As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he said.

The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the United States and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis.

Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location.
"Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximize resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," Tillett said.

Gopaul said reserve management had become "incredibly important" and that, while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure that the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub that moves fast.
He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the United Kingdom is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market."

"The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he said. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold."
The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion).
The US question

While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making.
Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries.
That decision seems to be driven by concern about US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors.
Tillett said gold remained sensitive to decisions by the US Federal Reserve and general concern about US financial markets meant that gold holders are looking to move their assets.

As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric about Greenland and continued veiled threats toward the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around.

blocks.caption: US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leadersImage: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Yet the United States, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan, in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved about 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the United States.
Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves."

articles.title: JRT Foundation launches Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub for Bulacan Students
articles.summary: JRT Foundation, the charitable arm of Coolaire Consolidated Inc. (Coolaire), launched the Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub and donated 20 complete sets of desktop computers to Heritage Homes Integrated…

blocks.text: JRT Foundation, the charitable arm of Coolaire Consolidated Inc. (Coolaire), launched the Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub and donated 20 complete sets of desktop computers to Heritage Homes Integrated School in Marilao, Bulacan, on August 14, 2026.

Both the technology hub and the foundation, named after former Coolaire president Jerry R. Tugade, are committed to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 4: Quality Education, by advocating for digital literacy and expanding access to technology in Philippine education.

“In the Philippines today, 78% of public schools do not have functional computers, 48% of Filipinos do not have internet access, and only 18% of Filipino children above 10 have used a computer,” said Joel Ryan E. Tugade, Vice Chairman of the JRT Foundation and the President of Coolaire. “It’s important the private sector partner with the government to help with the educational system.”

The initiative also advances other sustainable goals, namely: SDG 10 Reduced Inequalities and SDG 17 Partnerships for the Goals, since the event is supported by the Departments of Education (DepEd) and Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Region III.
Bringing digital access to HHIS

Heritage Homes Integrated School (HHIS), with more than 1,100 students, is the only public high school in Marilao without a computer laboratory. Therefore, DepEd Region III volunteered them as the technology hub’s first beneficiary.

“I learned na gumagraduate ng senior high school (SHS) ang mga students na walang experience sa computer kasi wala silang equipment. Thirty percent of these learners, di na magkokolehiyo. Kaya tuparin natin ang promise ng K-12 na dapat job-ready sila pag-graduate,” explained Dr. Charies N. Dela Peña, Regional Education Program Specialist and Head of Regional Delivery Unit of DepEd Region III.

Before the donation, students relied largely on laptops donated by DepEd years ago. Of the 45 laptops previously provided, only 20 remained functional, according to HHIS school principal Dr. Nica Mae Magisa. With scarce equipment, several students resorted to using their mobile phones for schoolwork instead.
For Grade 12 student Mark Hero Domingo, the new computers will be especially useful.

“Makakatulong po sa amin sa practical research, lalo na sa paghahanap ng RRL. Noon, cellphone lang gamit namin, pero mahirap pa rin kasi mag-edit. Kaya malaki po talagang tulong ang donation,” Domingo said.
The facility will also support teacher development, allowing teachers to improve their digital skills.
“May mga teachers pa rin na hirap sa ating technology. Gagamitin ito ng mga guro natin para i-train ang kanilang digital literacy skills. Kaya walang maiiwan, lahat ay aangat,” Dr. Magisa shared.
Beyond digital literacy

The Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub is just one of JRT Foundation’s many robust projects for education. Among them are the TIKYO Scholarship Program, which has seen a 200% increase in its scholars all over the country, receiving a total of Php1.5M+ in investments for their education.

Beyond financial assistance, the foundation has also launched its Caring Initiative Series with workshops on mental health, spiritual values formation, and drug abuse prevention and awareness for its youth beneficiaries.

The foundation has likewise collaborated with organizations such as the University of the Philippines Engineering Research and Development Foundation, Inc. (UP ERDFI) to support emerging mechanical engineering scholars, hoping to contribute to the development of professionals in the field.

The variety of these projects reflects the JRT Foundation’s overall advocacy for education: that the effective development of young students must not only include financial assistance but also focus on their holistic development across multiple aspects.

“This partnership with DepEd provides us with an opportunity to make a more impactful and meaningful influence in the lives of students and teachers in advancing their skills. It is our hope that we join hands in building a future where no one is left behind,” emphasized Joel Ryan.
ADVT.
This article is brought to you by JRT Foundation.

articles.summary: Zeshan Hamdani, who lost his older brother in the North Tower, is speaking out after push back against New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani attending the 25-year memorial.

blocks.text: This year’s 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks has become embroiled in divisive politics. There are controversial calls for the city’s first Muslim Mayor to sit out the commemorative event, including from Rudy Giuliani who was New York’s mayor on the morning of 9/11.
