articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Here are INQToday’s top stories this afternoon: Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has been ordered to appear before the Sandiganbayan on September 10 as the anti-graft…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Here are INQToday’s top stories this afternoon:Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has been ordered to appear before the Sandiganbayan on September 10 as the anti-graft court hears his plea to remain hospitalized while facing a non-bailable plunder case.
Meanwhile, Vice President Sara Duterte has appointed lawyer Paolo Panelo as her assistant spokesperson, adding a new voice to her communications team amid her ongoing legal and impeachment battles.
And 14 Filipino seafarers who survived an attack on a Saudi Arabia-flagged oil tanker near the Strait of Hormuz are now back in the Philippines. /dp

articles.title: P1.79-M shabu confiscated from high-value suspects in Taguig, Valenzuela
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Police on Wednesday confiscated suspected shabu or methamphetamine hydrochloride with a combined value of P1.79 million, and arrested five suspects during separate…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Police on Wednesday confiscated suspected shabu or methamphetamine hydrochloride with a combined value of P1.79 million, and arrested five suspects during separate buy-bust operations in Taguig and Valenzuela cities.
The confiscated substances had a combined weight of 263.6 grams, the National Capital Region Police Office said.
According to law enforcement, the arrest happened after an undercover police officer purchased alleged shabu from a 37-year-old newly identified high-value suspect.
Police also arrested his other accomplices, including two newly identified high-value individuals aged 35 and 20, and a 28-year-old high-value individual.
Seized during the operation were six heated-sealed plastic sachets of suspected shabu, a mobile phone, and other personal items.

The authorities also confiscated a Glock 14 Gen 5 pistol with one magazine and seven rounds of live ammunition from the 37-year-old suspect, facing another charge aside from drug trafficking for violating the Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act.
The four suspects arrested in Taguig were taken into police custody and are expected to face charges for violations of the Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002.
The seized drugs and other evidence will be subjected to forensic examination.
Anotherbuy-bust operation in Barangay Punturin, Valenzuela City, at 4:49 a.m. resulted in the arrest of a 45-year-old high-value individual and the confiscation of P432,480 worth of alleged shabu.
Authorities recovered two plastic sachets allegedly containing 63.6 grams of suspected shabu.
Under police custody, the suspect faces charges of violating Sections 5 and 11 of Republic Act No. 9165 and will be referred to the City Prosecutor’s Office for inquest proceedings.

NCR Officer-in-ChargePolice Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano said that the back-to-back operations show the NCRPO’s efforts to disrupt illegal drug activities and prevent firearms from being used in further criminal acts.

“We will continue to focus our operations on high‑value individuals and areas being used for illegal drug activities. The recovery of a firearm in one of these operations further underscores the need for sustained, intelligence‑driven police actions to prevent more serious crimes and protect our communities,” Abrahano said in a statement. Martina Nieyandra Calica. Inquirer.net trainee /mr

articles.title: Mimaropa cops plant over 31,000 trees under environmental project
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police planted 31,592 trees across the Mimaropa region since launching an environmental initiative in July, the regional police office said in a statement on…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police planted 31,592 trees across the Mimaropa region since launching an environmental initiative in July, the regional police office said in a statement on Wednesday.

The latest tree-planting activity was held on Sept. 8 in Barangay Sta. Isabel, Pinamalayan town in Oriental Mindoro, where nearly 300 participants planted more than 100 narra seedlings and over 100 fruit-bearing trees.

Oriental Mindoro Police Provincial Office (ORMIN PPO) led the activity, bringing together police personnel, firefighters, local government representatives, civic organizations, and other community partners.

Brig. Gen. Christopher Dela Cruz, MIMAROPA police director, joined the activity and said environmental protection forms part of the police’s broader responsibility to help build safe and resilient communities.
“Hindi lamang tayo nagtipon para magtanim ng puno. Nandito tayo upang magtanim ng pag-asa, malasakit, at pananagutan para sa kinabukasan,” Dela Cruz said.
(We did not just gather to plant trees. We are here to plant hope, compassion, and accountability for the future.)

The police regreening initiative, called Project T.R.E.E. (Take Responsibility for the Enhancement of the Environment), was launched on July 6 as part of Dela Cruz’s F.I.G.H.T. C.R.I.M.E.S. framework./coa

articles.title: Intent to nab dela Rosa not waning amid ‘negotiations’ – PNP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors”…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors” for his surrender.
“It will take as long as it will take,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co said in a press briefing in Camp Crame on Wednesday.
“Our efforts did not wane, will not wane, and we will not deviate from serving the warrant of arrest,” he insisted.
Dela Rosa was ordered arrested by the International Criminal Court in a warrant issued last November.
The warrant was only publicized in May and it was in connection with his alleged involvement in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war against illegal drugs.
On Tuesday, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that the government was in negotiations with dela Rosa’s “protectors,” whom he only identified as “powerful people.”
The senator’s legal counsel, Israelito Torreon, however, denied any personal knowledge of the supposed negotiations nor the protectors.
For its part, Co said the PNP’s search for dela Rosa are continuous, but the spokesperson refused to provide further details, citing operational matters.
He further noted that 91 of the 117 firearms registered to dela Rosa are still unaccounted for.
“Our FEO is continuously coordinating with the family for the surrender of the guns. Legal police action will be initiated,” Co explained.
The PNP FEO revoked dela Rosa’s firearms license and gun registrations in June as part of the bid to capture him.
Dela Rosa was last seen leaving the Senate premises and was supposedly dropped off in Makati City in the early hours of May 14, after a shooting in the chamber.
Remulla previously said dela Rosa’s last known location was in Mindanao. /apl

articles.title: Zamboanga City marks ‘Day of Remembrance’ for bloody 2013 siege
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands of residents.
Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso issued Executive Order KHYM 183- 2026 on Tuesday, declaring Wednesday a “Day of Remembrance” to honor the lives lost and the sacrifices made during the 2013 Zamboanga Siege.
The order recognizes the heroism of the security forces who defended the city and remembers the civilians caught in the crossfire during the three-week conflict 13 years ago.
Olaso highlighted the selflessness of the military, police, and emergency personnel who stood on the frontlines to safeguard the city’s democratic ideals and way of life.
Pursuant to Sangguniang Panlungsod Resolution No. 1019, dated Sept. 2, 2014, the declaration formalizes Sept. 9 as an annual day of commemoration.

The mayor urged local businesses—including major department stores, restaurants, public conveyances, entertainment centers, and resorts—to observe the occasion by offering customers a 20% discount every September 9, with special emphasis on active security personnel, as a gesture of solidarity and appreciation.
The September 2013 siege remains one of the darkest chapters in the city’s history.

Sparked by an influx of Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) fighters identified with the Nur Misuari faction, the three-week standoff directly affected six barangays and displaced 22,196 families—or 122,226 individuals.

The urban armed conflict claimed the lives of 25 military and police personnel, alongside 13 civilians, while 266 others were wounded. Rebel casualties were reported at 153 killed in action, with 278 individuals arrested.
The physical and economic destruction was massive.

At least 9,722 homes were burned or destroyed, causing an estimated P200.83 million in damages, while the closure of the city’s airport and seaport paralyzed trade links across Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, and the broader Zamboanga Peninsula, resulting in an estimated P331 million in daily economic losses.

Despite the lingering scars, local officials emphasized the resilience of the city’s constituents. Rebuilding and recovery efforts have relied heavily on support from the national government, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and international partners.

In his declaration, Olaso offered eternal prayers and condolences to the families of the victims, reassuring residents that the memory and heroism of those who served—including prosecutors from the Department of Justice who pursued legal accountability—will remain permanently etched in the hearts of every Zamboangueño./ca

articles.title: 68 Itogon families evacuate amid prolonged rains in Benguet
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the enhanced southwest monsoon raised safety concerns in several communities.

As of Monday, a total of 227 families, or 874 individuals, have been affected by the continued rains across Itogon’s nine barangays, according to the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office (MSWDO). It said 81 houses were also reported damaged.

The evacuations were carried out as residents in high-risk areas responded to government advisories to seek safer locations amid weeks of rainfall brought by weather disturbances Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Obet, and Pilandok, as well as the monsoon.

Barangay Ampucao recorded the highest number of affected families at 65 (256 individuals, followed by Loacan with 47 families (211 people). Gumatdang reported 46 affected families, while Poblacion had 44 families (134 individuals).

The MSWDO distributed 238 family food packs and hygiene kits to affected residents. The provincial government also provided 200 five-kilogram rice packs, while the Office of Civil Defense in the Cordillera provided nonfood items and fuel assistance for emergency response operations.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development also extended cash assistance to affected families in Gumatdang, Virac, Tuding, and Tolibeng in Loacan. The Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office provided additional nonfood items to families in Tolibeng.

Mayor Bernard Waclin, together with the MSWDO and disaster risk reduction councils, led the assessment and relief efforts. The municipal government said no casualties had been reported in Itogon amid the prolonged rains and successive weather disturbances. Maureen Matayew / Contributor/coa

articles.title: ‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodies
articles.summary:
Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada

The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico…

blocks.text: The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.

Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.
Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.
“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”
“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.
Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.
Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.
“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”
Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.
A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.
The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.
“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.
The trial is expected to run until the end of September.
Rhoad’s widow, Natalie, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.

articles.title: ‘No executive suite for Romualdez if transferred to PNP hospital’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH) in Camp Crame.
“May room nang naka-ready sa kanya,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co explained in a press briefing in Camp Crame.
(There is a room waiting for him already.)
“Wala ditong executive suite. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms,” he stressed.
(There is no executive suite here. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms.)
Romualdez was arrested on plunder charges on Monday night while confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for various purported ailments.

On Tuesday, however, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the PNP will ask the Sandiganbayan to transfer Romualdez to the PNPGH to show that the former speaker is not receiving special treatment.
“Our doctors have been coordinating with the doctors of Cardinal Santos for practicing rights so we can assess him independently,” Co said.
“And then, they will confer for us to be able to assess if the former Speaker will be physically fit to face the Sandiganbayan,” he added.
Romualdez has since requested the Sandiganbayan to allow his continued hospital confinement.
But earlier on Wednesday, the Office of the Ombudsman opposed the motion while asking that another team of government doctors assess whether he needed to be confined.
“We welcome them to erase any doubts or suspicions of special treatment,” Co said.
“The more, the merrier. We very much welcome additional doctors to assess the situation or the health status of our former speaker,” he added.
Romualdez is charged in connection with over P7 billion in alleged kickbacks in various government projects from 2022 to 2025. /gsg

articles.title: Iloilo City mayor secures power pledges to strengthen local grid
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build grid redundancy for the fast-growing city.

In a statement released on Wednesday from South Korea, where she is currently on official travel, Treñas said the city government is proactively pursuing long-term solutions to safeguard local power stability despite regional supply challenges.
“We know how frustrating these continuing interruptions and rotational brownouts are for our people,” Treñas noted.

She added: “Even while the manual load shedding implemented by the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) is not directly within the control of the city government, we will not just wait around.”
To address Panay Island’s vulnerability as it sits at the tail end of the national power grid, the mayor outlined three major power generation projects to strengthen the island’s electricity supply.

The mayor said Panay Energy Development Corporation (PEDC) has committed to expanding its generation capacity, with the additional power targeted to become fully operational by 2028. Meanwhile, cleaner energy provider PH Natural Gas is preparing to establish operations in Iloilo City, which is expected to help diversify the local energy mix.

In nearby Guimaras, MORE Power is also set to operate a 40-megawatt (MW) floating power barge by the first quarter of 2027. The facility is expected to provide immediate backup power and help improve the reliability of electricity supply in Panay.
Treñas noted that building redundancy—having multiple, independent sources of electricity—is essential to sustaining Iloilo’s rapid economic expansion and insulating it from wider grid failures.

“These are the investments we must continuously pursue because we cannot depend on just one source of power,” Treñas stressed. “Especially here in Panay, being at the tail end of the grid, having more generation, more sources, and more redundancy is vital.”

To ensure these projects proceed without unnecessary delays, the mayor called on the national government and regulatory bodies to fast-track the required permits and approval processes so construction can begin immediately.

She reaffirmed that the city administration will continue engaging with power utilities, private investors, and regional stakeholders to build a more resilient energy infrastructure for Iloilo City./coa

articles.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
articles.summary:
Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems

Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in…

blocks.text: Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.
Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.
Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.
Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”
The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.
While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.
“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.
The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

articles.title: DTI-Bukidnon cracks down on social media promos, flags 5 firms
articles.summary: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Five business establishments in the cities of Valencia and Malaybalay have been slapped with show-cause orders by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Bukidnon…

blocks.text: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Five business establishments in the cities of Valencia and Malaybalay have been slapped with show-cause orders by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Bukidnon provincial office for allegedly running unauthorized sales promotions on social media.

The DTI-Bukidnon, through its Consumer Protection Division (CPD), intensified its monitoring after noticing a spike in online promotional offers, including contests and discounts advertised digitally.
Junar Merla, DTI-Bukidnon CPD chief, said that digital campaigns must not bypass regulatory frameworks.

Operating a sales promotion without a valid DTI permit violates Article 116 of Republic Act No. 7394. Violators face potential administrative fines ranging from P500 to P300,000 under Article 164, alongside penalties upon conviction under Article 123(b).

While the show cause orders demand formal explanations from the establishments to ensure due process, DTI-Bukidnon emphasized that the enforcement actions aim to uphold fair marketplace transparency and protect consumers from unlawful practices.
It did not name the five business establishments ordered to explain.
The provincial office plans to sustain its monitoring efforts across online and physical platforms./coa

articles.title: Yellow rainfall warning up in Metro Manila, 5 areas in Luzon
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The state weather bureau placed Metro Manila and five other areas in Luzon under a yellow rainfall warning on Wednesday due to the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The state weather bureau placed Metro Manila and five other areas in Luzon under a yellow rainfall warning on Wednesday due to the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat.

In its Heavy Rainfall Warning No. 18 issued at 11 a.m., the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the following areas were under the yellow warning level:

items: Metro Manila: Caloocan, Malabon, Navotas, Valenzuela, Quezon City, Makati, Mandaluyong, San Juan, Pasay, Marikina, and Manila
Bataan
Rizal: Rodriguez and San Mateo
Zambales: Olongapo, Subic, Castillejos, San Marcelino, San Narciso, San Antonio, Iba, Botolan, Cabangan, Palauig, San Felipe, Masinloc, and Candelaria
Bulacan: Meycauayan and Obando
Pampanga: Floridablanca and Lubao

blocks.text: Areas under yellow warning tend to experience rainfall between 7.5 mm and 15 mm within one hour and can continue in the next two hours.
The yellow warning level likewise indicates a need for the public to “be alert,” with flooding in flood-prone areas identified as its associated hazard, Pagasa said.
Several local government units have already suspended in-person afternoon classes this Wednesday due to the forecast rains.
Meanwhile, according to Pagasa, light to moderate rains with occasional heavy rains were expected within the next three hours over Laguna, portions of Rizal, Bulacan, Tarlac, Batangas, and Quezon.
The same rainfall conditions were affecting portions of Nueva Ecija, Zambales, Pampanga, Cavite and Metro Manila, which may persist within three hours and could affect nearby areas.
Pagasa will release its next rainfall warning at 2 p.m. /jpv

articles.title: Northern Mindanao cops seize P19-M contraband, net 126 drug pushers
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — The Police Regional Office-10 (PRO-10) seized around P19 million from alleged illegal activities and netted 126 suspected drug pushers in a span of about two weeks. Brig. Gen.…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — The Police Regional Office-10 (PRO-10) seized around P19 million from alleged illegal activities and netted 126 suspected drug pushers in a span of about two weeks.

Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr, newly installed PRO-10 director, shared the achievement as he marked 12 days in office during his first press briefing on Tuesday at Camp 1Lt. Vicente Alagar in Barangay Lapasan here.
He sent a message to criminals that “they will not find any breathing room” in the region.
“Our provincial and city directors are very good. These first days have set the direction for my leadership of PRO-10,” Babagay told reporters in mixed Filipino and English.

He noted that consistent with the priority agenda of PNP Chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. and the directives of Interior and Local Government Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla Jr., PRO-10 will remain focused, visible, intelligence-driven, responsive, and accountable.
“We will prioritize sustaining efforts to make Northern Mindanao peaceful,” Babagay said.

Under the Enhanced Managing Police Operations framework, PRO-10’s anti-narcotics campaign chalked the biggest haul, confiscating 1,141 grams of suspected shabu valued at an estimated P7.7 million and arresting 126 drug suspects across 104 operations.
Babagay said P6.7 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes and P4.4 million worth of equipment and minerals from alleged illegal mining activities were seized in just about two weeks.

The region-wide campaign also curbed loose weapons and underground betting. Under Oplan Kontra Boga, police carried out 73 operations, arresting eight individuals and seizing 71 firearms. In contrast, 10 anti-illegal gambling operations resulted in 18 arrests and the recovery of P5,911 in proceeds and gambling paraphernalia.

Manhunt operations accounted for 107 wanted individuals, including 32 classified as most wanted persons. On the counterinsurgency front, Babagay reported that five communist personalities surrendered, turning over three firearms to authorities.

Babagay also highlighted urban order under the “Safer Cities Initiative,” which logged 10,030 ordinance violators, with 4,853 individuals fined and 4,897 issued warnings. He said that PRO-10 will maintain maximum visibility patrols, checkpoints, Oplan Bakal, Oplan Sita, Oplan Bandillo, and other area-specific policing interventions.
According to him, only one of the 10 most wanted persons in the region has not been arrested./coa

articles.title: Ombudsman opposes Romualdez’s bid for continued hospital arrest
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday said it will oppose the motion of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez for extended hospital confinement after his arrest, adding that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday said it will oppose the motion of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez for extended hospital confinement after his arrest, adding that it will request a team of government doctors to assess whether his declared illnesses could be managed outside the hospital.

This was the response of Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano after Romualdez on Monday filed a Manifestation of Hospital Confinement and Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement for continuous lawful custody at the hospital “for so long as inpatient confinement remains medically necessary, certified by his attending physical, until he is medically cleared for transfer.”

“The prosecutors will strongly oppose the motion. In fact, the prosecutors will ask that not just one doctor but a team of government doctors assess whether or not the illnesses declared need confinement or can be managed outside of the hospital,” Clavano said in a statement.

Clavano also said that if Romualdez’s illnesses could be managed outside the hospital, the prosecutors would move for his transfer to a regular detention facility, including the other co-accused in the charges.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former lawmaker Zaldy Co, and two others last Monday for plunder over allegations that they received more than P7 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.
Romualdez was arrested in the hospital and he is currently confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said that according to the former House Speaker’s doctors, he suffered from a cardiovascular event, and was having an anxiety attack and unstable blood pressure. /jpv

articles.title: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?
articles.summary: (Part 1: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means) (Last of two parts) MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has struck down the government’s specific system for electronically…

blocks.text: (Part 1: SC voids vessel tracking rule: What the decision means)
(Last of two parts)

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has struck down the government’s specific system for electronically monitoring commercial fishing vessels, but it did not erase the Fisheries Code’s broader requirement for vessel monitoring.
That distinction now sits at the center of a debate over what happens next.
For commercial fishing operators, the ruling removes a regulation the Supreme Court found overly intrusive and unsupported by sufficient legal and scientific basis.

For the government, fisherfolk groups and fisheries advocates, however, the decision raises a different question: How can authorities enforce fishing restrictions and protect municipal waters if they cannot continuously see where commercial vessels are operating?

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: Graphics by Ed Lustan/Inquirer.net

The Fisheries Code continues to prohibit commercial fishing in municipal waters except in cases allowed by law. It also gives municipal and city governments jurisdiction over municipal waters and responsibility for their management, conservation, development and protection.
So the ruling does not give commercial fishing vessels a new license to enter or fish in municipal waters.
What it changes is the specific monitoring mechanism the government had put in place through FAO No. 266.
Here’s what that means.
Does the ruling mean commercial vessels can now fish in municipal waters?
No. The Supreme Court struck down FAO No. 266, the regulation implementing the VMM and ERS requirements. It did not repeal the Fisheries Code.
The amended Fisheries Code continues to prohibit commercial fishing vessels, except in specified cases, from fishing in municipal waters. Section 86 states:
“Except in cases specified under this Code, it shall also be unlawful for any commercial fishing vessel to fish in municipal waters.”

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: The law also provides:
“Preference shall be given to resource users in the local communities adjacent or nearest to the municipal waters.”

Municipal and city governments have jurisdiction over municipal waters and are responsible for their management, conservation, development and protection. They are also tasked with enforcing fishery laws, rules and regulations and valid local ordinances.

So the ruling does not create a new right for commercial vessels to enter or fish in municipal waters. What it removes is the specific FAO No. 266 mechanism requiring Philippine-flagged commercial vessels to be monitored and electronically report information under that regulation.
Why are small-scale fishers worried?
The law continues to prohibit unauthorized commercial fishing in municipal waters.
But enforcement depends on the government having ways to determine where vessels are operating and what they are doing.
Oceana argues that real-time VMM gives enforcement agencies information they would not obtain from conventional manual reporting.

In a statement, Oceana said VMM provides enforcement agencies with timely vessel-location data that can help them monitor compliance with fishing restrictions, unlike manual reporting, which it said is more vulnerable to manipulation.

“Without VMM, it will be harder for agencies to detect if commercial fishing vessels intrude into restricted areas like MPAs, municipal waters, and closed fishing areas because manual reporting can easily be manipulated,” Oceana Vice President Von Hernandez said.
The group has also argued that VMM should be paired with proper safeguards for access to and use of the information.
Oceana said it has consistently called on BFAR to share real-time vessel data with enforcement agencies capable of protecting municipal waters from illegal commercial encroachment.
That concern was echoed by small-scale fisher Pablo Rosales, who is also a petitioner in the case.
In a statement issued through Oceana, Rosales challenged the argument that commercial fishing operations are entitled to trade-secret protection.
“What gave them the right to declare as trade secret their fishing operation and when our waters and the resources extracted from these are public good and thus be managed by the state?”
Rosales added that a commercial fishing license comes with responsibilities, including transparency in reporting required data.
Is VMM really different from manual reporting?

The Supreme Court focused on the evidence presented to it about the effectiveness of VMS compared with existing reporting mechanisms. It found that the government failed to establish that VMS was more effective, or even as effective, as manual reporting for detecting certain violations.

Oceana, however, disputes that characterization. In its briefer responding to the ruling, the organization said VMM is not the same as manual reporting because electronic data can arrive in real time, are much harder to fake and can provide vessel tracks, while manual reports do not provide the same continuous picture of vessel movements.

“Without VMM, it becomes much harder for enforcement agencies to detect if vessels enter restricted areas like the marine protected areas (MPAs), municipal waters (the zone that the law sets aside for small fishers), or fish during closed fishing seasons,” the group explained.

“Manual reports do not provide vessel tracks and only indicate general fishing grounds rather than exact locations. By the time a manual report is submitted, any illegal operation may long be over,” it added.

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: Oceana’s position is supported by assistant professor Joshua Regalado of the University of the Philippines Visayas’ Institute of Fisheries Policy and Development Studies.

“A fully functioning vessel monitoring system is a key part of effective fisheries management. It allows authorities and managers to know where fishing activities are taking place, conduct enforcement efforts more efficiently, and assess the compliance to fisheries laws and regulations,” Regalado said.

This distinction matters because the Supreme Court was evaluating whether the government had established the effectiveness and necessity of the particular system required by FAO No. 266, while Oceana is arguing from the perspective of how real-time monitoring can function as a fisheries management and enforcement tool.
What does the Fisheries Code say about monitoring?
The wording of the Fisheries Code is broader than FAO No. 266.
Section 14 says the monitoring, control and surveillance system must cover “all Philippine flagged fishing vessels regardless of fishing area and final destination of catch.”
Section 119 likewise refers expressly to municipal, commercial and distant-water fishing vessels:

“No municipal, commercial or distant water fishing vessel shall engage in fishing activity without complying with the vessel monitoring measures promulgated by the Department in coordination with the LGUs.”

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: That language was also discussed in the Supreme Court decision.

Some justices viewed the statutory provisions as indicating that the law contemplated a monitoring framework covering different types of fishing vessels, while others emphasized the legal distinction between municipal and commercial fishing and the separate roles of LGUs and BFAR.
The disagreement illustrates why the ruling does not simply reduce to “the Supreme Court banned vessel monitoring.”
The Fisheries Code still contains a vessel-monitoring mandate. The constitutional problem identified by the majority was with the way FAO No. 266 implemented that mandate.
Could the ruling affect seafood exports?
Oceana has also raised concerns beyond domestic fisheries enforcement.

The organization said VMM and electronic reporting are part of the traceability systems used to demonstrate that seafood is legally caught and properly documented. It pointed to the Philippines’ previous experience with the European Union’s fisheries “yellow card,” which was lifted in 2015 after the country strengthened its monitoring and traceability systems, including through measures under Republic Act No. 10654.

“With this gap created by the Supreme Court decision, our fisheries are subject to stricter scrutiny, higher costs for exporters, slower catch certification, and at worst, a possible red card that would shut Philippine seafood out of the EU entirely,” Oceana said.

“On average, a yellow card cuts a country’s EU fishery exports by about 23%, and a red card by around 83%. The Philippines exports over $225 million worth of fishery shipments to the EU annually,” it added, citing a 2024 study published in Marine Policy.

Oceana also pointed to the Philippines’ obligations under international fisheries agreements and regional fisheries management organizations, including the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission and the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas.
The extent to which the Supreme Court ruling will affect those commitments, however, remains a matter for the government and relevant international bodies.
What about the Philippines’ fisheries crisis?
The case comes amid a reported long-running decline in the country’s fisheries.

Based on the latest fisheries assessment by Oceana, capture fisheries production in the country fell from 2.6 million metric tons in 2010 to 1.9 million metric tons in 2023. It also said 147 of 166 assessed fish stocks, or nearly 88%, were overfished across the country’s 12 Fisheries Management Areas.

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: The decline has also been felt by municipal fishers. Their output fell to 802,770 metric tons in 2024, down 8.8% from the previous year and the lowest level recorded since 2002, according to data cited in an earlier report.

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: The group said this is the broader problem that FAO No. 266 was intended to address: illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, overfishing and weak enforcement of fisheries rules.

“IUUF is the harm that VMM is built to catch, and it is not a distant threat. It is already in the waters. Boat-detection technology has tracked commercial vessels intruding into MPAs and municipal waters year after year,” it said.

“VMM is a more efficient, transparent, honest, and time-sensitive reportage of that intrusion. Take it away and the intrusion is almost impossible to catch, and the small fishers with the least protection are the first to feel the impact of that loss,” it added.
Does the Fisheries Code still require vessel monitoring?

Yes. The Fisheries Code still requires the government to establish a monitoring, control and surveillance system and expressly says fishing vessels must comply with VMM promulgated by the DA in coordination with LGUs.
The Supreme Court did not declare those statutory provisions unconstitutional.
It struck down FAO No. 266, the specific regulation issued to implement them, because the majority found constitutional and procedural deficiencies in the regulation.

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: This is also why the court ordered the DA and BFAR to take “immediate steps to rectify deficiencies in Fisheries Administrative Order No. 266.”
The decision therefore leaves room for the government to pursue vessel monitoring through a framework that addresses the defects identified by the court.
What happens next?
The Supreme Court’s ruling is not necessarily the last word on the vessel monitoring system.

The DA, through BFAR, is seeking reconsideration of the decision. The government argues that commercial fishing is a privilege subject to regulation and that VMS remains an important enforcement tool against illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said the government was confident the court would reconsider the ruling and allow the use of VMS, which relies on electronic data rather than manual reports.

“BFAR respects the Decision of the Supreme Court and we are filing a Motion for Reconsideration (MR),” the bureau said, adding that any future monitoring framework would be aligned with constitutional safeguards.
For its part, Oceana has backed BFAR’s appeal, warning that removing FAO No. 266 would leave the problem it was intended to address unresolved.
“With the FAO 266 removed, the systemic problem it meant to solve remains,” Hernandez said.

“How can the enforcement agencies protect what they cannot see? We support the move of the BFAR to defend vessel monitoring now because it is our most effective tool to enforce the law, protect our marine resources and ensure that our children inherit a living and abundant ocean,” he added.

Oceana also reiterated its call for VMM data to be shared in real time with enforcement agencies tasked with protecting municipal waters, particularly against possible commercial encroachment. It argued that without VMM, authorities would have a harder time detecting vessels entering restricted areas because they would have to rely on manual reports.

Municipal fisherfolk have also asked the court to reconsider the ruling. Rosales and Ronaldo Reyes argued that removing effective vessel monitoring could affect the rights of small-scale fishers whose access to municipal waters is protected under the Constitution and the Fisheries Code.

“When commercial fishing vessels possess substantially greater capital, vessel capacity, fishing gear, mobility and technological capability, the absence of effective monitoring does not produce a neutral regulatory environment. It may reproduce an existing asymmetry. For Rosales and Reyes, it would mean empty nets,” they stated in a 29-page motion for reconsideration filed Aug. 14.

Rosales and Reyes said in their motion that the high court “focuse[d] exclusively on the asserted privacy interests of Royal Fishing et al. without considering the corresponding constitutional rights of municipal fisherfolk whose legally protected access to municipal waters depends upon the effective enforcement of the Fisheries Code.”

blocks.caption: After FAO 266, who will watch Philippine waters?

blocks.text: Fisherfolk, fisheries experts and local government representatives join a press forum on Aug. 11 to discuss the Supreme Court ruling declaring Fisheries Administrative Order No. 266 unconstitutional and its implications for municipal fisheries and coastal communities.
The international fisheries transparency community has also thrown its support behind the appeals.

The Coalition for Fisheries Transparency (CFT) said the absence of a clear legal framework requiring vessel monitoring could weaken the Philippines’ ability to enforce fisheries laws, meet regional commitments and satisfy documentation requirements in major seafood markets.

“Without a clear legal framework requiring vessel monitoring, the country’s ability to combat illegal fishing, meet regional fisheries commitments, and provide the assurances increasingly demanded by seafood markets is weakened,” CFT Director Ryan Orgera said.

The coalition also warned that the European Union requires VMS data for flag-state verification under its rules on illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and may request raw VMS records for seafood shipments entering the European market.

“Continuous, open, and transparent vessel tracking is an essential foundation for sustainable ocean governance—it provides all stakeholders with the objective data needed to protect a country’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ), supporting compliance, and safeguarding marine resources,” Global Fishing Watch similarly said.

Meanwhile, the DA has continued investing in vessel-monitoring infrastructure. On July 27, the department and BFAR turned over new VMS workstations at the National Maritime Center as part of efforts to strengthen digital monitoring of fishing vessels.

The department said the system can provide authorities with real-time information on the location, speed and direction of registered fishing vessels and help detect IUU fishing and enforce closed fishing seasons.
The new equipment, however, does not by itself restore FAO No. 266. The legal question remains before the Supreme Court.

For now, the central question is no longer whether the Philippines can monitor its fishing vessels. The Fisheries Code says it can and must. The question is how the government can do so in a way that protects fisheries, gives enforcement agencies the information they need and, at the same time, satisfies the constitutional limits laid down by the Supreme Court.

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. is Vice President Sara Duterte’s new spokesperson, according to the Office of the Vice President (OVP). “We are pleased to announce the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. is Vice President Sara Duterte’s new spokesperson, according to the Office of the Vice President (OVP).
“We are pleased to announce the appointment of Atty. Paolo Panelo as the spokesperson for Vice President Sara Duterte,” the OVP said in a statement on Wednesday.

“In this capacity, Atty. Paolo will serve as the official point of communication, representing the views and positions of the vice president and engaging with the media and public on relevant matters,” it added
Panelo was also Duterte’s legal counsel in connection with the multiple perjury complaints she recently filed against Ramil Madriaga.
His appointment comes as Duterte faces continued scrutiny over matters involving her grave threats case and the ongoing impeachment trial against her.
The new spokesperson is the son of lawyer Salvador Panelo, the former chief legal counsel and presidential spokesperson of Duterte’s father, former President Rodrigo Duterte. /gsg

articles.title: Teenager rescues juvenile PH eagle in Sarangani
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY – A juvenile Philippine serpent eagle (Spilornis holospilus) was rescued by a teenager after the large raptor landed at the terrace of their home in Barangay Sapu Padidu, Malapatan,…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY – A juvenile Philippine serpent eagle (Spilornis holospilus) was rescued by a teenager after the large raptor landed at the terrace of their home in Barangay Sapu Padidu, Malapatan, Sarangani province on Monday, Sept. 7.
The bird was reportedly attacked by crows before finding its way to the house of the Mejares family.
Joy Ologuin, Sarangani Provincial Environment and Natural Resources Office (PENRO) head, said the distressed raptor landed on the terrace and was found by Xian Mykee Laure Mejares.
The young resident, aware that the bird is endangered, immediately secured the bird and sought assistance from authorities.
He posted on social media his image while holding the beleaguered raptor, calling on authorities to come and rescue the eagle.
Personnel from Municipal Environment and Natural Resources Office (MENRO)-Malapatan immediately responded and rescued the eagle, which measured 53.34 centimeters from snout to vent.
The raptor was released to the wild on Tuesday after it was assessed to be in good physical condition.

Maria Elvira Lumayag, Department of Environment and Natural Resources-12 (DENR-12) OIC regional executive director, commended Mejares and his family for their responsible action, as well as MENRO-Malapatan for its prompt coordination.
“Their response highlights the important role of communities in protecting the country’s wildlife,” she said. /jpv

articles.title: PNP hospital ready if Sandiganbayan OKs order to transfer Romualdez
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez assured that the hospital inside Camp Crame is prepared if the Sandiganbayan approved a proposal to transfer…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez assured that the hospital inside Camp Crame is prepared if the Sandiganbayan approved a proposal to transfer former House Speaker Martin Romualdez there.
“The PNP will await Sandiganbayan’s action on the proposed transfer… and maintain the required security and custodial arrangements,” Nartatez said in a statement on Wednesday.
“Our facilities and personnel are ready to provide medical care while ensuring proper custody under the law,” he maintained.
Romualdez was arrested for plunder at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Monday night, following an order by the Sandiganbayan Third Division.
The former Speaker’s camp has since asked the court to keep him in hospital confinement for various ailments. The Third Division set a hearing for the motion on Thursday.
Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Tuesday said their agency would request the Sandiganbayan to transfer Romualdez to the PNP General Hospital.
“The PNP assures the public that there will be no special treatment regardless of an individual’s position or status,” Nartatez said.
“Our duty is to uphold the rule of law and strictly observe the legal processes,” he added.
Romualdez’ warrant was returned to the court on Tuesday, alongside a certificate of detention, a medical certificate, a spot report, a booking form and his mugshots, the PNP chief noted.
The former Speaker is accused of involvement in over P7 billion worth of alleged kickbacks in various government projects from 2022 to 2025.
He has since denied wrongdoing and pledged to face the allegations against him according to the law. /jpv
